title: Jules Verne’s Paris in the Twentieth Century — Blue Continuum
content:
EARTH · REMEMBERING THE FUTURE
Jules Verne’s
Paris in the Twentieth Century
Jules Verne’s lost novel got the machines of 1960 right. He never imagined that Paris would keep its poets
BY
John Steele
PUBLISHED
October 28, 2026
READ
10 minutes
LISTEN
AUDIO VERSION
TRANSLATE
Paris at sunset. Adobe Stock.
In 1863, Jules Verne did something he would almost never do again. He looked not toward an undiscovered island, the bottom of the sea, the interior of the Earth or the far side of the Moon, but directly into the future. He imagined Paris almost a century ahead, in the year 1960, and asked what sort of civilization the nineteenth century might become if its faith in science, machinery, commerce and efficiency were allowed to run to its logical conclusion. The result was Paris in the Twentieth Century, a book so unlike the Verne we came to know that his publisher, Pierre-Jules Hetzel, refused to publish it. Hetzel thought the prophecy implausible and the tone too bleak. Verne put the manuscript away. It remained unpublished for 131 years, until it was recovered from a family safe and finally appeared in France in 1994.
We commonly describe Verne as a great predictor of the future, but most of his famous novels are not actually set in the future. Captain Nemo's Nautilus, the projectile to the Moon and Phileas Fogg's race around the world are inventions placed within Verne's own century. He enlarged the technological possibilities of the present rather than transporting his reader into a future society. After Hetzel rejected Paris in the Twentieth Century, Verne largely avoided the full-length futuristic novel, although he later wrote a few shorter speculative pieces. That makes Paris in the Twentieth Century his one sustained attempt to imagine a whole civilization produced by machines.
The future Verne imagined is a technological triumph. Paris in 1960 has become a vast, smoothly functioning organism. Elevated railways, driven by compressed air rather than steam, circle the city on four concentric rings. Gas cabs roll silently over asphalt, each costing less per day than "one eighth the price of a horse." At a single moment, the hundred thousand streetlamps of Paris come on. Calculating machines do the work of clerks, stock quotations flash between the exchanges of Paris, London, New York and Calcutta, and what Verne calls "photographic telegraphy" transmits facsimiles of documents, so that contracts "could now be signed at a distance of five thousand leagues." The city has spilled past its old walls into what had once been its suburbs. And its inhabitants scarcely notice any of it.
Some of this now looks prophetic, but Verne's method was closer to extrapolation. He looked at technologies already struggling into existence and asked what would happen if they succeeded. The engine in his gas cabs is Étienne Lenoir's, which Verne himself notes was invented in 1859. His photographic telegraph is Giovanni Caselli's, and he names him. Telegraph networks were already shrinking Europe, and elevators and mechanical calculators already existed. Verne's imaginative leap was to see that, joined together, these things would alter the rhythm of urban life. He says as much in the novel, chiding one of his orators for "forgetting that the wonders of his century were already germinating in the projects of its predecessor."
The real Paris followed him quickly. The first line of the Paris Métro opened in July 1900, only thirty-seven years after Verne wrote the novel, and by the eve of the Second World War the network had spread across much of the capital. Unlike Verne's imagined system, much of it ran underground rather than above the boulevards, and it was powered electrically rather than by compressed air. But the essential insight was right. The twentieth-century city would depend upon rapid mass transit, moving enormous numbers of people through a network that would become almost as fundamental to Paris as its streets. Today several Métro lines run with no driver at all, which is further than even Verne took the mechanized city.
His geography was exaggerated, but the direction was right. Verne imagined Paris bursting through its old limits and swallowing the surrounding communities into a metropolis more than a hundred kilometers across. The city never became that enormous; within its administrative boundaries it had about 2.79 million inhabitants in 1962. But the Paris region had grown to roughly 8.47 million people, spreading into the suburban landscape Verne foresaw. And in 1958, two years before his fictional 1960, the French state began the systematic development of La Défense, where the CNIT opened that same year as the first great structure in what would become Europe's largest purpose-built business district.
That corporate city arrived beside old Paris, not in place of it, and here Verne's Paris and the real one part ways. He assumed that modernity would erase what preceded it. Paris instead proved adept at accumulation. The Métro ran beneath medieval churches. Automobiles passed eighteenth-century façades. Modern offices rose beyond the Arc de Triomphe while Notre-Dame stood where it had stood for eight centuries.
Verne's failure to foresee that resilience is what dooms his young hero, Michel Dufrénoy. Michel is sixteen, orphaned, sensitive, impractical and devoted to literature. At the enormous Société générale de Crédit instructionnel, an educational establishment run with the logic of a corporation, he wins a prize for Latin verse. The announcement is greeted with laughter. Science, mathematics, engineering and commerce dominate the curriculum. Greek and Latin are disappearing. Literature survives as an embarrassment. Michel steps forward and snatches, rather than receives, his prize: the latest Factory Manual. He flings it to the ground.
The joke contains Verne's real anxiety. The danger he sees in the future is not that people will know too little but that they will recognize only one form of knowledge. The society of 1960 is thoroughly educated in everything that can be applied, calculated, manufactured or sold. What it has lost is confidence in anything whose usefulness cannot immediately be demonstrated. Education has become an industrial enterprise. Michel's uncle, the banker Stanislas Boutardin, embodies the principle. For him, Verne writes, "painting stopped with a tinted drawing, and drawing with a diagram, sculpture with a plaster cast, music with the whistle of locomotives, and literature with stock market quotations."
“The practical man has not defeated ignorance. He has defeated imagination.”
Michel goes looking for Victor Hugo, Balzac, Musset and Lamartine at an enormous bookstore, where the clerk has never heard of Hugo. He finds his way instead to his Uncle Huguenin, a librarian presiding over the library's deserted literary rooms. "Literature is dead, my boy," Huguenin tells him. "No one reads anymore; I am the guardian of a cemetery here, and exhumation is forbidden." Michel is then sent to work at the Casmodage bank, where he proves hopeless at the calculating machines. Transferred to a gigantic ledger, he meets Quinsonnas, a musician reduced to clerical work. Through Huguenin and Quinsonnas, Michel discovers a tiny remnant population of people who still remember poetry, music and books.
This is where Verne went most wrong. The actual Paris of 1960 was anything but a cemetery of culture. Jean-Paul Sartre was still one of the most famous public intellectuals in Europe and published his Critique of Dialectical Reason that year. Samuel Beckett, whose Waiting for Godot had first achieved major success in Paris in 1953, was producing some of the most radical drama of the century. And in 1960 Jean-Luc Godard released Breathless, shot on the streets and in the cafés of Paris, helping to turn the French New Wave into an international revolution in cinema. At the very moment Verne had imagined poetry, literature and art being suffocated by technology, Paris was showing the world how art could reinvent itself.
Verne was much better at predicting machines than people. He understood that technology would transform the means by which culture was produced and distributed, but he underestimated the human appetite for culture. Paris did not stop reading Hugo because it acquired automobiles. Calculating machines did not prevent Beckett from writing plays. Electricity did not extinguish painting, music or poetry. New technologies kept becoming instruments of new art. In Breathless, a young Godard used lighter cameras, faster film stocks and the streets of modern Paris to make a new kind of poetry out of the technological city.
Verne's larger prediction holds up better. What he foresaw, beneath the satire, was a civilization increasingly tempted to measure human activity by productivity and economic return. Quinsonnas's friend Jacques Aubanet sums up the history of Western thought in three questions: "With Montaigne and maybe Rabelais it was What Do I Know? In the nineteenth century it was What Does It Matter to Me? And nowadays we say: How Much Does It Earn?"
Michel tries to escape that arithmetic. He falls in love with Lucy, the granddaughter of his old rhetoric professor, and for a while love and literature create a refuge from the commercial city. But refuge requires money. Uncle Huguenin, who has noticed, offers the age's advice: "Love her like a madman, if you like, but marry her like a wise man," and only when his position in life allows it. Michel attempts to become a writer and discovers that culture has been industrialized. At the Grand Entrepôt Dramatique, plays are assembled like manufactured goods. One clerk handles expositions, another denouements, another entrances and exits. There is a clerk for rhyming couplets, a clerk for punch lines, a Department of Puns and a central office of jokes. Art has survived as an assembly line.
Michel cannot do it. Handed a scenario for a farce, he rips it to shreds. "I shall not stay another minute in this charnel house!" he decides. "I'd rather starve to death!" He retreats to a borrowed room and begins writing what he hopes will become "a book of useless but splendid poems." That phrase is the moral center of the novel. A cathedral is useless if shelter is the only measure of architecture. Human beings have repeatedly enlarged their world by pursuing things whose value could not initially be entered on a balance sheet.
“Civilizations reveal themselves partly by what they permit to be useless.”
Then winter closes around Michel. Paris freezes, money disappears, food becomes scarce, and the triumphant machinery of the century cannot rescue him. With his last twenty sous he does something wholly irrational. Instead of buying food, he buys Lucy a half-withered bunch of violets from a florist who sells them to him as charity. When he reaches her house, she and her grandfather are gone, evicted and lost somewhere in the city.
THE TOMB OF ALFRED DE MUSSET IN PÈRE-LACHAISE CEMETERY, PARIS. ADOBE STOCK.
Half-starved and delirious, Michel wanders through the electric Paris that had once seemed so marvelous. Electric signs write advertisements in letters of fire. At an electric concert, two hundred pianos wired together are played by a single pianist. Even execution has been modernized, criminals are now put to death by electricity. Michel comes to believe that the demon of electricity is pursuing him. Eventually he reaches Père-Lachaise cemetery, where Verne brings the living city of the future into confrontation with the dead artists of the past. Michel passes the graves of musicians and writers, finds the tomb of Alfred de Musset, and lays the violets on it, weeping. Then he climbs higher and, through a clearing in the cypresses, sees Paris: a hundred thousand houses, the smoking chimneys of ten thousand factories, the lighthouse of the Port de Grenelle and, floating above it all, the armored balloons that protect the city from lightning. He longs to cut their ropes and let Paris be destroyed under a rain of fire. "O Paris!" he cries. "O Lucy!" he murmurs, and falls unconscious in the snow.
Verne was wrong about much of the Paris he would never see. There was no Napoleon V. The Seine did not become an industrial power plant of the kind he imagined. Compressed-air trains did not sweep along concentric elevated railways. Literature did not vanish, and the Académie française did not empty itself of writers. Above all, the historic city proved far more durable than his future allowed. Yet more than 160 years after he wrote the book, those errors matter surprisingly little. He understood the automobile city, mass transportation, mechanized offices, instantaneous communication, suburban expansion, corporate finance and the growing authority of technical education. He saw that speed itself would become a social value and that efficiency, once liberated from the factory, might become a philosophy of life.
Paris in the Twentieth Century is finally a book about the danger of confusing technological progress with human progress. Verne imagined a city that could calculate almost everything except what a human being was worth. The actual Paris of 1960 proved him wrong in the most hopeful way. It accepted many of his machines and kept its poets.
Michel Dufrénoy crosses Verne's frozen Paris carrying almost nothing: a memory of books, a love of poetry, a handful of dying flowers and the name of someone he loves. None is useful in the language of the world that has rejected him. Yet Verne leaves us with the suspicion that without such useless things, all the machinery of the future may have very little reason to exist.
John Steele is the Publisher and Executive Editor of Blue Continuum.

title: Extremely brief history of PDP computers
content:
Extremely brief history of PDP computers
by kqr, published 2026-10-29
Tags: product_development organisations unix lisp
I don’t know why I started to put this together. These machines fascinate me, because so much of early computing/hacker type culture happened on them. I started writing a table, but realised a timeline would be more intuitive. In this graph, the price is for a minimal configuration and adjusted for inflation. The time is the memory cycle time, a decent proxy for speed.
Some notes:
The pdp-1 was created mostly as an experiment. At the time, industrial control systems used either humans or complicated contraptions of logic boards to make decisions. Some engineers at dec wanted to see if there was a customer base willing to use general-purpose computers instead.1
1 But it wasn’t called a computer then, because the word “computer” back then meant big mainframe systems that ran batch calculations.
The pdp-4 was a variant of pdp-1 that was a little slower and much cheaper. It was not compatible with the pdp-1. The pdp-4 was upgraded with new chip technology and became the pdp-7, which was then optimised further for cost and speed and became the pdp-9.
The pdp-5 was created when they realised the pdp-1 and pdp-4 machines were overkill for industrial control systems. By being smaller, it could be much cheaper, at the cost of compatibility with pdp-1 and pdp-4. It was still intended for roughly the same market. The chip upgrade turned it into the pdp-8.
The pdp-6 was a completely different beast, aimed at a different market. It supported having tonnes of directly-addressable memory, as well as memory protection, so it could be used as a time-sharing system. The amount of memory made it run Lisp well.2
2 The smaller machines could also run Lisp, but not large Lisp programs.
With the chip upgrade, it became the pdp-10.
The pdp-11 was a new architecture again, intended to subsume all the previous models, to avoid running three incompatible lines in parallel. There were many variants of the pdp-11, with various performance characteristics and corresponding price points. However, even its most powerful configuration wasn’t powerful enough to attract many pdp-10 users.
The vax came much later, but it’s included in the table anyway because it is what eventually subsumed the pdp-10. The vax was somewhat compatible with the pdp-11, but they served different markets.
There is a noticeable split in the hacker culture between users of the smaller (18 bit and less) and larger (32 bits and more) computers, exemplified by the contrast between Unix and Emacs. Unix was first created on pdp-7, then ported to pdp-11, then distributed to other pdp-11 users. The fact that it needed to run on these smaller machines, and still handle time sharing, shaped much of its implementation and interface. The same thing is true of the C language and standard library. Then we have something like Emacs, which was created on the massive pdp-10, and gained popularity with other pdp-10 users. It had plenty of hardware resources to use, and it did. The same thing is true of many Lisp variants.
What decided whether you became a small-computer hacker or large-computer hacker was what your employer could afford. Unix was created at Bell Labs, a private company that tried to do more with less. Emacs, in contrast, was built at mit, which at the time was flush with darpa money. This is why Richard Gabriel calls it “mit/Stanford style” and “New Jersey approach”.
Some other examples of things that were developed on the pdp-11 includes Usenet, vi, rsx-11 (another operating system whose lineage continues into Windows nt), make, the idea of a shell with composable commands, plus tiny programming languages like awk. Things that were made with the pdp-10 includes Scheme, TeX, Zork, email, and Microsoft basic.
What do I want to say with this? I don’t know.

title: Azure's Weakest Link - Five Full Cross-Tenant Compromises
Cisco is letting a 27-year-old refactor 98% of its legacy code with unlimited AI tokens: ‘Go nuts’ | Fortune
content:
Gen Z can’t catch a break. Entry-level jobs are vanishing; some 40% of bosses say they plan to hire fewer grads because AI can do the job cheaper, and young workers are routinely slammed for showing up late and refusing to put in overtime for free. Cisco’s president and chief product officer Jeetu Patel isn’t buying it—he’s just handed one of the company’s biggest jobs to a 27-year-old he found hidden in the org chart “five levels” below him.
“I’ve given him unlimited tokens because he’s going to refactor code,” Patel told Fortune at a small roundtable dinner. “So I’m like, you can go, you can go nuts.”
The “him” is Padmanabhan Krishnamurthy, or “Paddy,” as Patel affectionately calls him. He joined Cisco in 2025 after the $429 billion tech giant acquired EzDubs, the real-time translation startup Krishnamurthy cofounded in 2023. And despite coming in as a former founder with CEO experience, he was, in Patel’s words, “buried away in the organization doing something unstrategic.”
That changed when Patel dropped into Cisco’s San Francisco office, and the pair got talking. Krishnamurthy reckoned he could rewrite Cisco’s legacy code with a two-person team. Patel says even the most AI-forward people on his own team weren’t thinking that way.
So he has given himself four weeks to prove it, with the final goal of refactoring 98% of Cisco’s legacy code within 24 months.
Now, he’s on the hunt for more Paddys: young hires who will “challenge the system and the status quo,” or, as he puts it, be “an energizer bunny that just goes out and kind of revs everyone up.”
Cisco’s president says Gen Z should be teaching his veterans, not doing data entry—and he’s fine with the tension that causes
At most companies, only someone with decades of experience under their belt would be trusted with a project this size. Patel thinks that’s a problem.
“If you don’t hire the early-in-career [workers], and you just let your workforce continue the way that they were, where do fresh ideas get injected? How do you challenge the status quo?” he said.
Seasoned staff can still come up with new ideas, Patel added. What they can’t do is ask the questions that only someone with no experience would think to ask.
And getting the two to get along isn’t always smooth. Patel admits that putting a Gen Zer in a room with people who’ve been at Cisco for decades can create friction—but he says that’s the point.
“Tension is good,” he said. “I actually try to create tension in the teams because you want to have enough friction on the ideas. You don’t want to have friction with people and personalities.”
“What you have to do is establish enough trust with people to say you are going to be expected to create unreasonable goals for yourself,” he added. “And so, in order to go out and achieve those unreasonable goals, think outside of the box.”
And he’s not just pushing senior staff to take notes from twentysomethings. He said that he treats every intern as “kind of a reverse mentor,” and even does talks at colleges to find students who are “hungry.” 
His latest Gen Z bet came out of one of those talks, to 17- and 18-year-old Stanford scholarship students. While a line of students fired questions at him, one, Baya, stood off to the side, just listening. She waited until everyone else had finished before she opened up.
He told her to email him every month with what she’d learned about AI. It was a test of follow-through: “Everyone can go out and have one good conversation. But are they going to stick with their commitments?”
She never missed one, landed an internship at Cisco, and redesigned “something” that experienced staff hadn’t been able to crack. 
“I didn’t bring her in so that she can do grunt work and do data entry,” he said. “We brought her in so that she could actually teach our people how to think completely differently.” Now he wants to recruit her.
Patel isn’t the only one betting on Gen Z—OpenAI investor Josh Kushner and Will.i.am are hunting for young, hungry talent
Patel isn’t the only boss who sees Gen Z’s lack of experience as an asset.
Thrive Capital’s founder Josh Kushner told Fortune he specifically likes to hire people with less than four years of industry experience.
When he launched the venture capital firm at just 26, he faced pressure to bring in older, more seasoned hires. But, as he put it, “anyone who has experience that is talented will never want to work with a 26-year-old.” So, instead, he recruited the “smartest people that we knew who were our ages.”
And that bet paid off: His firm made early investments in startups worth billions, including OpenAI, which is currently raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation.
These days, Kushner could easily hire industry veterans with glowing résumés—but he’d still rather “find that young, hungry person.”
Alon Chen, founder and CEO of Tastewise—a generative AI platform trusted by PepsiCo, Nestlé, and Mars—is also actively looking for Gen Zers with zero experience.
“I’m hiring entry-level because they have no boundaries or limitations in how they think about the world,” Chen told Fortune. “They’re almost like AI natives themselves, having been born and raised in this new realm of opportunities. And I see some of the best ideas coming from the younger generation that have not yet been in the job market.”
And Will.i.am has reached a similar conclusion. The Grammy-winning Black Eyed Peas frontman might be best known for his chart-topping hits, but behind the scenes, he’s a serious investor too. He backed Tesla, OpenAI, and Pinterest before they became household names—and now, he’s betting on Gen Z for his next investment. 
Why? He believes the next big tech breakthroughs will come from young innovators at MIT and Stanford.  “They’re young kids, and they’re native to this,” Will.i.am told Fortune. “So you want to hunt for that. That’s the only thing I’m focused on.”
And Patel told Fortune that the trend toward hiring Gen Z will only continue, thanks to AI.
“The only way for us to keep accelerating is to make sure we’re surrounded by people with a broad range of experience,” he said. “Roughly one-third of my team is experienced, scaled operators who understand how the Cisco engine works. The second third are systems thinkers from the market who bring the outside-in perspective. And the final third is made of entrepreneurial founders, CEOs, and engineers who are AI-native who operate in founder mode.”
“Either of these groups by themselves aren’t nearly as potent as when all three work together. It’s what creates magic.”

title: trapped in the technologist factory
content:
The first time I was paid to use Clojure was only two years after the language was released. Needless to say, it was at an early-stage startup.
The idea behind Runa was that we’d do dynamic pricing for smaller online retailers, offering targeted discounts based on individual shopper behavior. In practice, we offered a fixed discount to anyone who abandoned their shopping cart. By treating a small percentage of customers as a control group, we could calculate our effect on the retailer’s sales, and take a cut. Our biggest problem was convincing retailers to let us control their prices, closely followed by convincing them the math behind our calculated “lift” was sound.
We told ourselves a big contract was always just about to close, permanently increasing our traffic by an order of magnitude. We used HBase as our primary data store, because it was designed to scale, just like us.1 In the future, we would power a loosely federated Amazon, composed of independent online retailers, knit together by our software. If we built it, they would come.
But they didn’t. The only thing that kept us afloat was a bespoke product we had built for eBay, because our CEO knew an executive there. Later, after I left, that same executive moved to Staples and convinced them to acquire the startup outright. Nothing we had built was useful to Staples, it was just evidence of our ability to “innovate”. The resulting “skunk works” team has since been disbanded.
My next job was at Factual, a more established startup that had built their product using Java and embedded Javascript, and were beginning to adopt Clojure. Their product was an index of all the places in the world, generated by applying hundreds of different heuristics to web crawl data. Each entry had a canonical id and various properties like name, address, and hours. More interestingly, it also had the equivalent ids from different platforms like Yelp and Foursquare, and we offered an API that could resolve an an incomplete (or even partially incorrect) set of properties to the corresponding entity in our index.
Our product could stitch together thousands of disparate datasets, so long as they had some geographic component; I liked to describe it as a “foreign key for the world”. Unfortunately, there’s not much money in ontologies. By the time I had joined, the dataset had already been used as the basis for Facebook Places and as part of Apple’s then-new map offering. These were large contracts, but there are only so many big tech firms in the world, and even fewer with a geographic component to their data. No matter how much we tried to make up the difference with our smaller customers, we didn’t have a path to a billion dollar valuation.
We began to offer services powered by our data. Internally, this was presented as less a pivot than a demonstration of the intrinsic value of our data; once people saw what we could do with our data, surely they’d have some ideas of their own. Our first customers were adtech firms, hoping to do better geographic targeting for mobile ads. We hired salespeople and marketing executives with a background in digital advertising, and when sales started to take off we hired more. Even as I built services to ingest billions of daily ad impressions and bespoke almost-databases to power on-premise services for our adtech partners, I told myself it was all incidental; our business was data, not ads.
I was wrong, of course. The advertising side of the company was where all the growth was happening, and our product direction was whatever helped them close deals. But I wasn’t the only person who was slow to acknowledge this fact. In my exit interview with the CEO, just after I had given notice, I told him that he should be more direct with everyone that Factual’s focus had permanently shifted. He told me what I had only just stopped telling myself: ads were a temporary diversion, and we’d return to the underlying data before too long. In the years that followed, however, Factual became increasingly focused on location-based advertising, until it finally merged with Foursquare.
When a startup takes venture funding, its singular goal becomes growth; it will either reach a billion dollar valuation or die trying. With that growth comes ever-greater technical challenges. Some of these are obvious: more users will not only require more machines, but a more complex infrastructure.2 Others are less obvious: as the userbase grows, each individual becomes increasingly abstracted in the business logic of our software. To deal with the first challenge, we must have technical acumen. To deal with the second, we must have a deep understanding of our business domain.
This means that as long as a startup continues to grow, its engineers can (and must) continue to improve their knowledge and acumen. But most startups fail. Some of those failures are because the company couldn’t keep up with their own growth, but these are the exception. The common, boring reason for failure is that the startup barely grew at all.
Confronted with stagnation, an engineering organization can have two reactions: they can try to help reinvent the company, or they can continue to prepare for the growth that must, inevitably, come. At Runa, we chose the latter.
At first, the engineering leadership adopted promising, poorly-understood technologies (Clojure! HBase!) which would give them the necessary leverage down the line. But once they launched, and the stagnation set in, that preparation became a need for constant readiness. Any early technical mistakes, however regrettable, were baked in. Trying to revisit them, to build something better, would just leave us flat-footed when the growth finally came.
I joined Runa only a few months before the engineering organization entered its defensive crouch. I was too inexperienced and too distracted3 to question it. Every day we played Jenga, trying to jostle the existing codebase as little as possible with each new commit. Later, as I realized I wasn’t proud of any of the work I had done so far, I began to energetically push for rebuilding key pieces of the system.
After a few months, I was told to either drop it or take three weeks severance. I took the severance.
Of course, even if I had gotten my way, nothing would have changed. All of us were carefully ignoring the actual problem, which is that our business model didn’t really work. Our product and pricing model both required unjustifiable levels of trust from our prospective customers, but none of us saw that as our problem to solve. We were downstream of the business model; our job was simply to wait and prepare for its eventual success.
I joined Factual because I found the problem space fascinating, but most of it had been solved by the time I joined. About six months later, the leadership began to acknowledge that our business model, while successful, wasn’t going to get us to a billion dollar valuation. So began my descent into adtech.
I wanted to prove that I had learned my lesson; if the current business model wasn’t working, I’d help them build a new one. I built services to consume the raw data, and on-premise servers to provide the processed result to our customers. I attended sales meetings, wrote design docs, and painstakingly analyzed packet dumps to prove to partners that latency spikes were occurring elsewhere in their system.
In the end, I learned that I didn’t like the advertising industry very much. When a brand wanted to run a digital ad campaign, they went to an agency, which is be responsible for spending their budget to the greatest effect. The agency then went to a demand-side platform (DSP), which was be responsible for making real-time bids on individual ad impressions on an exchange. To inform those decisions, the DSP went to a company like Factual, which could distill a phone’s current and past locations into binary features relevant to the campaign.
Crucially, when you’re not selling something online, it’s almost impossible to measure the efficacy of a digital ad campaign.4 This means that the agency could say almost anything, so long as it closed the deal. The DSP, in turn, sold whatever they thought would help agencies close their deals. And at the end of this chain was Factual, selling whatever we thought would entice the salespeople enticing the salespeople enticing the brands.
I thought I had become product-focused, ready to solve any problem that would help the company to succeed. In truth, I was only really paying attention to the technical problems. Once they were largely solved, it became harder to ignore my ambivalence for what the product actually did. Eventually, I left.
I learned two lessons from this time in my life. The first was personal: I am, at heart, a technologist. I like to generalize, to abstract. While I believe it’s crucial to understand the context around your software, I’m happiest when that context is other people’s software.
The second lesson was broader, and less obvious:5 our industry is designed to foster people like me.
This was surprising because it seems so clearly against our own interest. In almost every case, companies fail because they build the wrong thing. Unless your customers are themselves engineers, I’m the wrong person to help with that. You want someone comfortable at the periphery of your system, who wants to learn about the competitive landscape, who wants to talk to customers. You want a product engineer.
But consider our standard interview questions: data structures, recursion, and computational complexity. It always feels a little strange when I see someone arguing that these don’t reflect “real” day-to-day software tasks; I write recursive functions all the time. But that’s a consequence of the abstraction; what might be a simple nested lookup on any specific datatype becomes recursion when you try to generalize over a set of possible datatypes.
Likewise, I’ve seen it argued that the difference between, say, O(log N) and O(N) isn’t important, because in practice N tends to be small enough. That may be true for some domains, maybe even most of them, but if you’re building a general-purpose tool you have to focus on the pathological cases.
Of course, others will argue this first-year CS material is the essence of what we do. This was certainly the attitude when I was at Google;6 since their existing employees were going to any length to avoid writing Javascript, they decided that anyone with frontend experience would be held to a lower technical standard. These hires were widely viewed as second-class; people who were only allowed in because they were willing to do the work no one else wanted.
But if we want to hire product engineers, what questions should we ask instead? It’s impractical, given the sprawling scope of our industry, to only consider candidates with prior experience in our exact product space. Likewise, it’s unrealistic to expect that we’d have expertise in a candidate’s prior product spaces. We lack a common vocabulary, a common understanding of the nuances that separate good design choices from middling ones.
And so we continue to search for our keys under the streetlamp; they could be anywhere, but this is where the light is. If we’re lucky, the technologists we hire will also have all the other skills necessary to make humane, useful software.
This means that even if you’re not a technologist, you have to learn how to pretend.7 And this brings us back to the beginning, when it was obvious that my first Clojure job, only two years after the language was released, would have been at an early-stage startup.
Most new technologies, if they get adopted at all, follow a familiar path: first come the hobbyists, and then the companies which employ those hobbyists. This second step is easiest when the company has little to no process around adopting a new technology; in other words, an early-stage startup. The standard narrative around this phenomenon is that certain technologies are simply more powerful, but only startups are daring enough to hire from the niche pool of talent that knows how to wield them.
But new technologies8 don’t have power; for that they’d need a community, documentation, and a thriving ecosystem of ancillary technology. What they have is potential, which resonates with the potential within the startup and the early adopter; perhaps they can all, over time, grow together.
As many have pointed out, this is not a rational strategy for building a company. It is, however, a phenomenal way to train new technologists. Chesterton notwithstanding, the fastest way to learn why a fence exists is to tear it down and see what happens.
Seen from this perspective, it doesn’t seem so irrational; most startups fail before reaching a scale that has any existential technical risks. The only guaranteed benefit they can offer their engineers is the freedom to invent their own challenges, and learn through iterative failure.9 If the startup fails, there’s no harm done. If the startup gets traction, the engineers can apply their newfound wisdom.
This means startups don’t adopt new technologies despite their immaturity, they adopt them because of that immaturity. This drives a constant churn of novelty and obsolescence, which amplifies the importance of a technologist’s skillset, which drives startups to adopt new technologies.
This flywheel has been spinning for a long time, and won’t stop simply because I’ve pointed out that we’re conflating novelty with technological advancement. Hopefully we can slow it down, though, because I believe it’s causing real harm.
By introducing abstraction into every problem we solve, we distance ourselves from how our work is ultimately used. We tell ourselves we’re in the business of building sharp knives; if we made them safer, they’d be useless for everything except spreading butter. We float above the the effects of what we’ve created, treating them as inexorable consequences of progress.
It’s true we can’t encode our values into general-purpose software,10 but we’re not simply atomized technologists, and our worlds are not bounded by the interfaces we expose. We share a collective responsibility for what we create, and are capable of collectively acting on that responsibility.
But what does a belief in collective responsibility mean, in practical terms? What actions does it entail? Honestly, I don’t know. All I know is that we can’t stay under the streetlamp forever. At some point, we’ll have to see what’s out there in the dark.
In a twist that will surprise no one, the way we used it could never scale. To support ordered scans over keys, HBase partitions on contiguous ranges in the keyspace. Since we wanted to scan over the events for a given day, all of our keys began with a timestamp. This meant every write for a given time period was focused on a single shard, which would drive HBase to constantly repartition its shards in a futile attempt to equally distribute the load.

title: Sashank Gondala on X: "Building an AI-native engineering org" / X
content:
Sashank Gondala
@sgondala2
Building an AI-native engineering org
5 min read
Last week Will Larson (@Lethain) asked how leaders are evaluating engineering managers for AI skills. My reply, a list of questions to think about, got a lot of bookmarks.
More broadly, I've been thinking about how to build an AI-native engineering org for a while. Sharing some lessons from the last nine months of building at FurtherAI.
Part 1: What changed in how we ship
How much we ship per engineer
Since January, the number of code changes each engineer merges a day has grown about 5x, while our revert rate has stayed under half a percent.
But giving engineers coding agents didn't get us there on its own.
Every time we sped up one step, work piled up at the next.
So we started going through the entire process of shipping software, one step at a time, and figuring out what we could optimize.
Rebuilding the shipping process
Code (March) – Agents write the code and engineers steer them. We don’t have a clean number for where this started, as early on the tools only left a mark on a change once in a while. But it’s safe to say it’s now almost 100%.
Tests (April) – Agents write tests alongside code. 91% of changes now include tests, up from 15%.
Review (May) – AI reviews 99% of changes before a person does, up from 60%. Human reviewers can focus on the parts that need judgment.
CI (June) – We parallelized tests and run only those affected by a change. CI now runs 20× the tests in the same 17 minutes.
Bug reports (July) – We've started using ClaudeTag (@claudeai) to automate our bug intake process. Anyone can report a bug in Slack, and ClaudeTag figures out duplicates, files a ticket, and assigns it to the right person. It now files 60% of bug tickets.
Rules (August) – When a bug or a review comment exposed a rule only engineers knew, we turned it into a small Python check that runs on every commit and every PR, fails the build and prints the fix. This way, we convert tribal knowledge into rules. Agents hit these checks, fix their own code and move on. We went from zero to 21 rules. They're a big part of why low-risk changes can now merge without a person.
Merging (August) – Low-risk changes that pass tests, automated checks, and AI review merge on their own. Up to a third of our changes now merge without a person involved.
Code channels (September) – Anyone can open a Slack channel, describe a change to an agent, and have it open a PR. We don't have a clean number for this yet, but it's been great for collaboration: several people can work with the same agent in one channel, adding context and steering it as it goes. We also heavily use Devin's (@cognition) cloud sessions to collaborate as a team.
We also use our in-house Poirot and Sherlock agents to investigate and resolve issues across production and staging. They have all the tools and context they need across logs, metrics, trace and read-only database access
Some of the best moments are when agents work together. Claude Tag triages a request, Devin does the work, and Poirot pulls the internal data it needs. It's fun to watch them talk to each other and pass information along.
One interesting side effect is that non-engineers have started shipping code too. Our designer has merged about 50 changes since August, including the ones that built our design system. People in deployment and customer-facing roles can also make UI tweaks themselves right from slack
What it cost us
None of this was free. Through the summer, much of our engineering effort went into tests and tooling, and customer-facing changes per engineer stayed between 17 and 30 a month.
In September, that jumped to 45. October is on pace for 48.
Part 2: What's changing in the team
As engineering got faster, we started noticing a different problem.
The new bottleneck
We got much faster at writing code, but not nearly as fast at deciding what to build.
Here's a simplified example.
Say a feature used to take ten days: three to plan, six to build, and one to review.
If agents make building 3.5× faster, but planning and review stay the same, the overall feature only gets 1.75× faster.
Planning and review now account for 70% of the time, up from 40%.
Traditionally, a lot of these decisions flow through engineering managers, PMs, and designers. That becomes increasingly difficult as engineers get faster.
How do you organize a team where engineers can build much faster, without creating bottlenecks around decisions and reviews?
Our bet is to push more ownership to engineers. Rather than adding more layers of management, we want engineers to handle more of the planning, execution, and review themselves.
That changes what we expect from engineers and managers.
What it means for engineers
I'm starting to think of engineering seniority in terms of how much of a problem someone can own end to end. Roughly:
Junior engineer – Builds with an agent and can tell when it's wrong.
Senior engineer – Plans and reviews their own work.
Staff engineer – Takes a vague problem, makes the tradeoffs, and owns the number that says whether it worked.
It also means engineers need to be closer to customers.
We're empowering engineers to own more of the process end-end, from understanding the customer problem to shipping a solution to verifying success and owning regressions in production.
What it means for managers
This also changes what we expect from engineering managers.
1. Be in the work.
Managers need to understand what's being built, why, and whether it's the right solution.
I want managers trying features on staging as an end user would, not just checking that the code was reviewed. You catch a different class of problems when you actually use the product.
But the goal isn't just to review more. As always, it's to develop engineers who can make the right decisions themselves, so managers only step in on the ones that need their judgment.
2. Be more product-savvy.
When writing code becomes cheaper, deciding what to build matters a lot more.
I want engineering managers who understand customers, have strong product opinions, and are comfortable making product decisions, not just technical ones.
They should also help engineers develop that judgment. We shouldn't need a PM or designer to make every small product decision.
Where this leaves us
We spent most of this year figuring out how to make engineers faster. Now we're trying to figure out how to make the entire organization move at that speed.
I suspect this will be a harder problem than automating code, tests, and reviews.
We're still early, and there's a lot we haven't figured out. But it's one of the most interesting engineering challenges I've worked on.
I'm curious what other teams are seeing. What broke first as your engineers started shipping faster?
We're hiring Engineering Manager / Director at @furtheraicom to solve the next wave of challenges. If this sounds interesting, reach out!

title: Turning a solar power system into its own backup - Ars Technica
content:
HEAT EXCHANGER
Turning a solar power system into its own backup
Plant design allows it to run on either stored solar heat or combustion.
JOHN TIMMER – OCT 29, 2026 6:02 PM | 42
The company plans on a modular design, with more capacity added through additional modules. Credit: 247Solar

Rather than directly converting photons into electricity, concentrated solar energy uses mirrors to turn sunlight into heat, which can then be used to drive traditional generating turbines. Up to about a decade ago, there was a case to be made that concentrated solar energy had a bright future, as improvements in heat storage had turned it into a way to generate power around the clock.
It wasn’t to be. While concentrated solar costs fell enough to compete with nuclear power, the price of photovoltaics plunged, making solar panels the cheapest source of power in most locations. Currently, if you have a good site to generate solar power, then the economics of PV panels are hard to beat.
That has left us needing to build a mixture of other facilities—typically batteries and natural gas facilities—to handle overnight needs or weather-driven shortfalls. But a small company is promising that it can help avoid the need to build a separate facility. Its version of concentrated solar is designed so that a fossil-fueled backup system shares most of the generating hardware with the solar side.
Back to the future?
Concentrated solar, also called solar thermal, is pretty simple in principle. Most of the site is covered with heliostats, devices that incorporate mirrors and a motorized tracking system that can keep their focus on a single point as the Sun moves across the sky. The point of focus is in a tower, where sunlight heats a working fluid. The hot fluid can then be used to power a traditional steam turbine, or its heat can be stored and used to generate power overnight.
ARS VIDEO
How Scientists Respond to Science Deniers
There are many potential variations, however: different working fluids and methods of heat storage, trough-shaped mirrors that eliminate the need for a tower, and so on. All of those variants are meant to reduce some of the issues inherent to solar thermal: lots of moving parts, potentially corrosive fluids, and so on. Those issues and the lack of standardization have helped ensure that the costs of these plants haven’t come close to keeping pace with photovoltaics.
Without any incentive to generate renewable power overnight, there hasn’t been any way for concentrated solar to compete. Construction of new plants has largely stopped, and a number of sources have simply stopped tracking the economics of it.
So it was a bit of a surprise to hear that India had contracted with a US-based startup called 247Solar to build and operate a small concentrated solar plant. While the plant will be extremely small (1 megawatt) and mix in photovoltaics, the company had a unique angle: The same hardware that is handling the solar thermal output can simply be run using fossil fuels if there is a significant shortfall in renewable generation.
“Our systems are their own backup,” said 247Solar’s Mark von Keszycki. “During times of low solar resource—long duration, bad weather, whatever the case may be—they’re able to burn a variety of fuels.”
To understand how this works, it’s best to step back and understand the entire system being built, which includes details about how the 247Solar team hopes to avoid some of the problems faced by other solar thermal systems and provide a great deal of flexibility in terms of how its systems get put to use.
Hot air
Like other concentrated solar systems, 247Solar’s will be using a field of heliostats. But the receiver—the hardware that they focus the sunlight on—is distinctive, in that it works with ambient-pressure air. (It’s an updated version of hardware developed by a German company.) Air exits this hardware at approximately 970° C. That air can potentially be used directly for industrial process heat or sent on to the hardware that generates electricity. But in most cases, it will be directed to heat storage.
Rather than dealing with molten salts and potential phase transition, 247Solar heats up ceramic pellets roughly the size of a golf ball. Depending on the details of the storage configuration, von Keszycki says that the heat from the storage could be used to generate power for anywhere from nine to 20 hours after the Sun sets. Hours will obviously be shorter if some of the heat is used to generate power during the day, but 247Solar plans to pair its system with photovoltaic installations for daytime generation.
Wherever the hot air comes from, it will be sent to a heat exchanger. This is designed as a drop-in replacement for a combustion unit on a traditional turbine to heat up compressed air to drive generation. “The heat exchanger does the same job as the combustor did,” 247Solar’s Bruce Anderson told Ars. “It’s in the same place in the turbine assembly as the combustor was: after the compression stage and before the expander.” The initial installation will pair two 200 kW generators; aside from the heat exchanger, everything else is part of a standard off-the-shelf package.
This is the point where the system’s flexibility comes in: It doesn’t care how the air in the exchanger gets heated. So, any of a variety of fuels can be burned to provide the equivalent heat. von Keszycki suggested that adding the capability to the system to burn fossil fuels tacks on less than 10 percent of its total cost.
The air coming out of the heat exchanger is still quite hot, in the neighborhood of 250° C, and von Keszycki called it “a separate usable resource” that could be directed to a variety of applications, including industrial processes and absorption cooling. Again, if intermediate temperatures are needed, it could potentially be mixed with some hot air coming directly from the storage medium, albeit at the cost of generation.
Scaling up
The first installation will be small, with a pair of 200 kW generators, and so will mostly serve to validate the system’s engineering—Anderson said the biggest worries are “unknown unknowns.” But the system is designed to be modular, and the company is already working through the engineering of a 3 megawatt facility that combines multiple units that share a single tower that holds multiple receivers and heat storage.
The installation will also give the company a sense of how the system actually works out financially. On a typical grid, there are few incentives for providing around-the-clock renewable energy. And the cost of ensuring that there is enough generation to back up solar plants is often absorbed by other parties. The ability to generate fossil-fuel-based backup power without having to build a dedicated facility can definitely save someone money, but markets aren’t always set up so that it’s easy to extract those savings.
So, it’s not surprising that 247Solar has other markets in mind. It’s especially excited about remote mining sites, which typically require diesel to be shipped in, often at considerable expense. The 247Solar system would avoid that expense, while potentially providing process heat that could be useful for some of the ore processing. And powering mining operations without emissions would work well for companies that are required to account for the carbon emissions of their supply chain.
Still, there might be a space for this sort of facility on the grid, if it does successfully avoid the need for dedicated fossil fuel plants that only ever run for a small fraction of the night—provided the price and incentives line up.
JOHN TIMMER SENIOR SCIENCE EDITOR
John is Ars Technica's science editor. He has a Bachelor of Arts in Biochemistry from Columbia University, and a Ph.D. in Molecular and Cell Biology from the University of California, Berkeley. When physically separated from his keyboard, he tends to seek out a bicycle, or a scenic location for communing with his hiking boots.

title: The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning
content:
Home Blog
The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning
October 27, 2026
Ali Behrouz and Vahab Mirrokni, Google Research
We introduce a sleep phase in continual learning, enabling large language models to continuously integrate new facts and enhance reasoning while mitigating catastrophic forgetting or static knowledge cutoffs.
Modern LLMs achieve impressive performance via pre-training and in-context learning (ICL). However, once deployed, they remain largely static, operating with a fixed knowledge cutoff date that leaves them unable to acquire long-term capabilities or adapt to new information.
While updating models with new data seems like the obvious solution, continual parameter updates often trigger catastrophic forgetting, a fundamental issue where learning new tasks severely degrades performance on previously learned ones. Alternatively, relying strictly on ICL limits knowledge retention to the immediate context window: once the context session ends, the acquired short-term information is forgotten.
Inspired by how the human brain processes and stabilizes memory during rest, we introduce a sleep framework in continual learning: a learning paradigm that equips large language models (LLMs) with a continuous periodic lifecycle, enabling them to continually learn, consolidate fragile short-term context into stable long-term parameters. With this framework, we demonstrate that alternating between active interaction and offline memory consolidation allows LLMs to continuously acquire new facts, retain long-context knowledge up to 10M tokens, and improve complex reasoning.
Rethinking machine learning: Active (wake) vs. sleep phases
Traditional machine learning relies on a strict separation between training and inference. In a continual learning framework, this distinction becomes artificial; an intelligent agent must constantly learn, adapt, and process information.
Under the sleep paradigm, an LLM operates across two primary states:
Active (wake) phase: The model actively receives, processes, and interacts with inputs, storing temporary information in fast, short-term memory components.
Sleep phase: The model pauses processing new inputs and redirects its internal computations toward memory consolidation and self-improvement.
While terms like "sleep," "dreaming," and "self-improvement" borrow from neuroscience, our framework operates entirely within a fixed model architecture and human-defined training rules. During the offline sleep phase, the model unlocks pre-allocated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) memory blocks and updates its numerical weights using self-generated practice examples. This automated post-training cycle helps a deployed model absorb new facts and sharpen its reasoning accuracy while keeping its core codebase and design unchanged.
Key components of the sleep process
The sleep paradigm addresses catastrophic forgetting and continuous adaptation through two stages: memory consolidation and dreaming.
1. Memory consolidation
In the human brain, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) slow-wave sleep consolidates fragile memories into long-term structures via abstraction and distillation. Our proposed sleep framework mirrors this natural phenomenon through two key technical mechanisms:
Parameter expansion & continuum memory hierarchy: To prevent catastrophic forgetting, the model dynamically scales its capacity during sleep. Using a Mixture of Experts (MoE) and Hope architecture , newly unlocked, low-rank experts are integrated into stable, lower-frequency memory blocks to store incoming knowledge without disrupting older parameters.
Knowledge seeding (upward distillation): Fragile short-term memories stored in high-frequency layers (e.g., in-context memory) are transferred into the newly expanded long-term parameters. This is achieved through Generalized Knowledge Distillation (GKD) combined with reinforcement learning (RL)-based imitation learning:
On-policy distillation: The expanded student model learns token-specific feedback from teacher distributions generated on self-sampled sequences.
Learning to imitate (LTI): The student model is rewarded based on semantic and absolute similarity (Levenshtein distance) when completing prefixes of teacher-generated text.
Synaptic pruning: Once the memory consolidation into lower-frequency modules is complete, the high-frequency temporary parameters are reset, freeing up capacity for future active sessions.
Overview of our sleep framework: Input streams from the active phase are stored in short-term memory before entering the sleep cycle, which bifurcates into Consolidation (transferring fragile short-term tokens into expanded long-term parametric memory using low-rank structures and MoE) and Dreaming (autonomous self-improvement via synthetic routing with random experts and RL refinement).
2. Dreaming for self-improvement
During REM sleep, the human brain actively simulates scenarios, consolidates emotional/semantic connections, and explores novel neural pathways. Mirroring this, during the “dreaming stage”, the sleep framework implements an autonomous self-improvement loop:
Random expert selection: During synthetic data generation, the MoE router randomly activates non-standard experts. This forces the model to mix disparate domains of knowledge and uncover latent patterns.
Curated rehearsal: The model generates synthetic training samples ("dreams") and filters them using gradient-based data selection to prioritize samples with the highest potential to boost overall model capability.
RL refinement: The model performs supervised fine-tuning on top-rated dream samples and evaluates whether the generation improves performance on downstream tasks.
Theoretical foundations
Beyond the empirical results, our sleep paradigm is grounded in a theory that clarifies why its two stages (memory consolidation and dreaming) can support continual learning without simply trading new knowledge for old capabilities.
For memory consolidation, the analysis shows that knowledge seeding can be understood as a structured, low-rank compression problem. The model is not asked to copy every detail of its short-term traces into its parameters. Instead, it identifies a compact set of directions that best preserve both the model’s own on-policy behavior and the semantic qualities rewarded by the learning objective.
This perspective explains the complementary roles of the two signals: on-policy distillation aligns consolidation with the trajectories the model will actually produce at inference time, reducing the mismatch that can arise when training only on teacher-generated distributions; meanwhile, the semantic reward changes what is worth retaining, prioritizing directions that preserve meaning and task-relevant behavior rather than merely matching token probabilities. Parameter expansion then provides the capacity needed to write these selected memories without overwriting previously consolidated knowledge.
For dreaming, the theory characterizes random expert activation and reward-based sample selection as mechanisms for improving the geometry of learning. Injecting different MoEs broadens the set of gradient directions explored during synthetic generation, exposing the model to a richer collection of updates than those induced by its ordinary wake-time data alone. Gradient-based filtering then emphasizes the synthetic experiences that carry the most useful learning signal, strengthening informative directions while preserving the structure of the underlying gradient space.
Together, these steps yield a more balanced optimization landscape: learning is less dominated by a small number of directions, gradients are better conditioned, and the model can make more stable progress when refining its capabilities. In this view, dreaming is not simply self-generated data augmentation; it is a deliberate process for diversifying, selecting, and consolidating the updates through which the model improves itself.
Comparative performance of our sleep framework against baseline approaches (such as in-context learning and supervised fine-tuning) across major evaluation axes, including Class-Incremental Learning, continual translation, long-context scaling up to 10M tokens, factual knowledge incorporation, and mathematical reasoning.
For continual translation, in unseen languages, such as Manchu and Kalamang, the sleep framework maintained a near-zero performance drop in multi-stage evaluations, whereas standard baselines like ICL, Cartridges, and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) suffered severe catastrophic forgetting during sequential learning.
In long-context understanding on the BABILong benchmark, our sleep method demonstrated near-perfect scaling up to 10M tokens, outperforming strong baselines like GPT-4, and Titans by using sleep-time consolidation to compress long-context information directly into parametric memory.
For factual knowledge incorporation evaluated on SQuAD and continued pre-training (CPT), our sleep method achieved 48.9% on single-task and 46.2% on CPT evaluations, outperforming baseline methods including the base model, SFT, and Self-Adapting Language Models (SEAL) by successfully integrating new factual information without degrading existing model representations.
Finally, on mathematical reasoning benchmarks including AIME 24/25 and HMMT 25, sleep-enhanced base-model achieved accuracy scores of 79.2%, 69.0%, and 46.1%, respectively. This outperformed baselines like SFT, group relative policy optimization (GRPO), and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), showing that pairing memory consolidation with imitation learning drives superior reasoning performance.
Conclusion
Our sleep paradigm provides a path toward autonomous, continually learning AI systems. By moving beyond static pre-training and fragile context windows, alternating between active learning and offline rest empowers LLMs to retain short-term memories, abstract new skills into long-term parameter structures, and continuously self-improve without catastrophic forgetting.
Acknowledgements
This research was conducted by Ali Behrouz (Google and Cornell University), Farnoosh Hashemi (Cornell University), Adel Javanmard (Google and University of Southern California), and Vahab Mirrokni. We thank Yuan Deng and Corinna Cortes for reviewing the work and their valuable suggestions. We also thank Mark Simborg, Kimberly Schwede, and Tim Herrmann for their help in crafting this blog post.

 Knock On Wood is an internet-connected device that performs the familiar gesture of knocking on wood, allowing users to follow the superstition remotely when no wood is nearby. Through a web app, users press a digital button to trigger a physical device that knocks on wood in real time.
 The project is part of an ongoing series, Machines Responding to Superstitions, by designers Shashwath Santosh and Nithin Eluvathingal. Drawing on industrial design, engineering, manufacturing, critical thought, and world-building, the series uses machines to examine everyday beliefs and rituals.
Knocker strapped to a tree, about to knock on wood | all images ©Shashwath Santosh and Nithin Eluvathingal

 Each knocker connects to the internet and communicates with a central server, allowing multiple devices to respond to users around the world. Someone in a Tokyo café, for example, can trigger a knocker in New York’s Central Park using only a web browser, while the device requires a Wi-Fi connection. For the woodland setup shown in the project visuals, the designers Shashwath Santosh and Nithin Eluvathingal used a portable Wi-Fi hotspot to connect the machines.

title: How Do You Take a Picture of a Black Hole? | Quanta Magazine
content:
THE JOY OF WHY
How Do You Take a Picture of a Black Hole?
Astrophysicist Shep Doeleman explains how capturing the first image of a black hole required a telescope the size of the world, and why the next goal is to create a movie.
Add as Preferred Source
(opens in a new tab)

Chanelle Nibbelink for Quanta Magazine
Introduction
AUTHORS
Janna Levin
Contributing Columnist

Podcast Host

astronomy

All topics
Black holes are one of the universe’s most exotic and elusive objects. When nothing, not even light, can escape their powerful gravitational grasp, taking a picture of one seems unimaginable. But an image of a black hole, or more accurately its shadow, could offer insights that theory alone may not provide when testing predictions. So how can it be done?
Harvard astrophysicist Shep Doeleman
(opens a new tab)
and a team of 250 researchers achieved this extraordinary feat by linking a group of radio telescopes around the world. This network, called the Event Horizon Telescope
(opens a new tab)
, produced the first image of a supermassive black hole in the galaxy M87, around 55 million light-years away, and the first image of the black hole at the heart of our galaxy. In this episode, Doeleman tells co-host Janna Levin how he turned the Earth into a telescope capable of seeing a black hole, the incredible level of science and collaboration that was required to achieve this, how the images have furthered our understanding of these exotic objects, and how movies of black holes may be possible by the early 2030s.
