title: Digital minimalism
content:
Dark Mode Toggle

Digital minimalism
2026 Oct 31
See all posts



For a long time I have been a fan of minimalism in my physical life: have few physical possessions, and try to do more with less. Four years ago, I wrote this blog post describing what I had in the 40-liter backpack that I travel around with.
Physical minimalism, however, was an idea that came of age in the 2000s and 2010s and was responding to the challenges and the opportunities of the 2000s and 2010s. I continue to believe that it is valuable - though I recognize some arguments in the other direction, notably that having the right kinds of physical things can make more practical to have more self-sovereignty over your life. But I also think that in the modern era, we need a new kind of minimalism: digital minimalism.
Digital minimalism is about being intentional about ways that you access digital technology, making each use a conscious choice rather than something that you get sucked into by default. In this post, I will describe some experiments that I've done in this direction.
Social media minimalism
Twitter (aka X) has always had a strain of toxicity to it, that has been increasing in recent years. The platform is definitely engaging, but it's often far from informative, and the ways in which it engages often do not make you feel good. But this all seemed to hit a particular crescendo for me around the end of 2024 and beginning of 2025. Many things were happening at that moment, but if you spent a lot of time on X you will likely remember a particular one: everyone seemed to be suddenly becoming fans of Adolf Hitler.

This is not even mentioning the time that Grok itself briefly turned into "MechaHitler".

Around the same time, "Crypto Twitter" was spiraling into a mood that I saw described as "financial nihilism": roughly, that the natural end state of blockchains is gambling, this is good, and if you dislike this and wish for something better then you are a stuck-up elitist prick.
Naturally, I had (and continue to have) my intellectual disagreements with both of these trends. But on top of that, I also started to more seriously pay attention to the fact that while the style of discourse on the platform was engaging, it was not enlightening and not making me feel good. And so for much of this year, I have been doing an experiment in distancing myself somewhat from this chaos. I did not leave X the platform, but I did leave X the interface. Instead, I have been doing most of my tweeting through Firefly:


Firefly is a multi-client that combines together X, BlueSky as well as Farcaster and Lens (both partially-Ethereum-based decentralized social media platforms). You can see tweets from all four platforms, and you can make a tweet that gets auto-posted to all four platforms.
My primary goal in doing this was to support decentralized social media, and to continue to engage with X but in a way that distributes network effect rather than locking it in. But in my months of using Firefly, I found that it also has a different effect: I feel much better using it.
I suspect the primary reason is that while Firefly allows you to tweet, and see other people's tweets, it is missing one central part of the X interface: The Algorithm™.
In particular, I suspect that in my time using the X interface, I fell into the following trap:
See someone making a tweet supportive of Adolf Hitler.
Click on the tweet and look around its quotes and responses, the same way that someone would morbidly stare at a car accident.
The Algorithm™ thinks: "This user seems to be a fan of Adolf Hitler. Let me mark that down as one of his interests."
See ten tweets supportive of Adolf Hitler.
Click and look around with morbid curiosity, the same way that someone would morbidly stare if they saw for the first time a car accident where ten cars were crashed and burning at the same time.
The Algorithm™ thinks: ... well, you get the idea.
See a hundred tweets supportive of Adolf Hitler.
Now, in fairness to X and Elon and its hard-working employees, the Adolf Hitler fandom does seem to have greatly wound down in the one and a half years since then. I suspect part of this is because such movements inevitably burn out once people realize how immoral and stupid they are. But another part is undoubtedly genuine improvements in how The Algorithm™ works.
But even still, in those moments when I go back into the X interface, I find myself logging back out and going back to Firefly. I also find that my mind has changed. I find myself less interested in the various battles that the intellectual titans on the platform seem to be sucking every day of their lives into. Recently, I logged back in, and I learned that the culture war issue du jour was that people were stridently arguing about whether or not Mao was evil. When I saw this, I had an emotional response that was sort of similar to what I think is the common experience of being an adult, seeing some food or TV show or game that you used to love as a kid, and realizing that you now find no interest in it at all. I smiled, and immediately went back to enjoying my day.
My verdict: I recommend more people try this. Explore ways of greatly decreasing or scoping your social media use: use something like Firefly, access X only on Tuesdays, whatever works for you. Get the information benefits of the platform without getting sucked in to the vortex, which does operate on you in powerful subconscious ways that you may not realize.
Cell data minimalism
For a period of 100 days, I embarked upon a second experiment: I lived my life with my phone always on airplane mode. I still used wifi, but not my cell connection.
I had two goals in doing this:
Privacy. A phone connected to cell is an always-on tracking device. Cell companies are notoriously bad at keeping that data secure, and sometimes they themselves sell it. So there is a large chance that a trail of your location will end up in the hands of intelligence agencies, military contractors, advertising companies, and more.

Anonymous SIM cards are not a sufficient solution, for two reasons: (i) your phone can still be linked across its entire usage lifetime through its IMEI number, and (ii) you leak all kinds of data that can be used to reconstruct who you are from your fine-grained movement patterns, internet access patterns, and modern AI makes it very practical to uncover these patterns.

Hence, the best location privacy solution is not having a cell connection at all (also, use GrapheneOS, and be very limited in what apps you give location permissions to; I had already been doing both).

Mental health. Not having the internet at all for significant periods of time (when I'm outside) has been a good way of (re-)building the habit of surviving without it, and getting more mental peace and the space to think about other more healthy and productive things.
On the whole, I consider the experiment to have been a success. During those 100 days, I violated the "no cell data" rule once literally but not spiritually - I turned it on briefly to receive a confirmation code that I needed in order to maintain that phone plan itself, and once spiritually but not literally - when going on a remote and slightly dangerous hike, friends insisted that I bring along a few communication devices that they had for emergency comms and use them to check in once every few hours.
My largest inconvenience was a stretch of time I was in Singapore, when my inability to receive SMS confirmation codes meant that I could not log into Grab (the regional Uber equivalent). As a result, my food options were more limited, and I had to take the subway instead of a car even in situations where that was much more inconvenient.
Since those 100 days, I have opened the cell connection occasionally, but so far I have broadly continued an "airplane mode by default" lifestyle.
For navigation, I used CoMaps, a local-first mapping application that downloads OpenStreetMap data and then shows you a map, gives you directions to get where you need, etc locally. My general review of CoMaps is that I find it worse than Google Maps for navigating the human world (restaurants, stores, opening hours...) but better for navigating the natural-ish world (it knows about many trails that Google Maps does not, though it does occasionally fail by claiming trails that do not actually exist, leaving me on one occasion pushing through hundreds of meters of shrubbery to get back to civilization).
I also became interested in the concept of local world knowledge apps. In principle, the data size of meaningful packs of information about the whole world is not that large. Compressed English wikipedia (without media) is only 27 GB. OpenStreetMap's planet.asm is 2.2 TB, though you can doubtlessly prune that down to 1-10% of its size and have everything you might conceivably need.
This month there was a bounty (organized by Statuette; I contributed as one of the donors) to create local phone apps that try to make useful knowledge easily accessible offline.
Here are two of the apps:

Left: FieldAtlas. Right: Commonplace

My general impression is: right now, we are exactly on the cusp of these kinds of apps starting to make sense. Most of the participants in the competition were trying to use on-device text LLMs to think for a long time before coming up with an answer. My impression is that this approach was too slow: answering a single question would take anywhere from 1 to 22 minutes. The best apps, on the other hand, used some kind of semantic search to show the user a search result from the local database immediately, and then followed that up with a very small LLM writing a text answer. This gives actually-good answers in a very reasonable timeframe.
Finally, when you're out and about, especially if you have meetings, sometimes you do need to have internet when you're on the go. When you arrive at a place, you often need to contact a person you're meeting to confirm their exact location or to get them to open the door. When you're at one meeting, you often need to re-confirm details about the next. If you don't have cell data, your only option is public wifi - and importantly, the public wifi hotspot must allow you to connect without providing an SMS confirmation code.
Different places are very different in terms of how friendly they are. Here is a quick tier list, taken from places I've traveled to while I was paying attention to public wifi availability:
Taiwan (or at least, the Taipei area)

Taipei has a huge number of public wifi hotspots. When I opened my phone to check when walking outside (or even when inside an Uber), there was literally an over 25% chance that there was a hotspot I could connect to that was in range at that moment. Usually, these were either municipal government wifi, or public wifi run by local convenience store chains.

Ukraine, USA, Canada, Singapore

Ukraine was the most surprising for me. In a surprisingly large number of places, across multiple cities, there were open hotspots available, some of which did not even require a clickthrough. (If you're wondering if it's responsible for them to do this, given Ukraine's security needs, I suspect the answer is that they are primarily concerned about decreasing the enemy's internet access near the frontline and on drones flying at high speed through the air toward their cities, and street-level wifi is not really useful for either of those)

USA, Canada and Singapore were all similar: they had a very high number of theoretically-public wifi hotspots in general, but a large portion of those hotspots were gated behind either SMS or some kind of login. But even still, a very significant number of open wifi hotspots were available.


Also, I learned that Toronto has a fraternity (or sorority) that seems to be named after SBF.


Austria, Hungary

Both halves of Charles I's old empire are similar. There are many hotspots, but the great majority of the public ones require an SMS confirmation code to log in. I could find properly open wifi, but on several occasions it took trying quite a few hotspots and walking around for a while.

Switzerland

Despite its general reputation for privacy, Switzerland ranked at the bottom for me. Almost all public wifi hotspots require an SMS confirmation code. In my first 1.5 kilometers walking through the downtown, I found only two that do not: a random shoe store, and Starbucks, which lets you connect for 10 minutes, and then longer if you enter a confirmation code that you receive by email.
Web minimalism
Recently, I have been starting to do more and more things without relying on user interfaces inside of websites at all. The last few times I updated my IPFS hash on ENS, I did so through a command-line tool that an AI wrote for me. Many of the payments that I make through privacy protocols, I now make through the kohaku-cli tool.

Sending through kohaku-cli. Today, the CLI is even cleaner and easier to use; no need to specify the value twice and know what a tail call is.

Websites and web applications, especially web applications for doing crypto things, are dangerous for several reasons:
If you access a web application, you end up re-downloading the application from the server thousands of times, and you are fully trusting the server each time. If the server gets hacked even one of the thousands of times that you open the site, you might be screwed. Regular old-fashioned applications (where you explicitly click "download") are better than this: you only need to trust the server to not be malicious or hacked at that exact moment once.
Websites and web applications are by default very bad for privacy. When you access a website, it can see your browser (including version number), your operating system, your screen size, and once you start acting hundreds of other data points (eg. mouse movements, button click patterns) that quickly identify you. Websites often send user data (and metadata) to all kinds of third-party providers, from CDNs serving scripts to analytics companies, and this all happens by default.
As we've seen with social media, web applications crafted by third parties with commercial interests may not have your interests at heart. Fine-grained UI decisions may be dark patterns optimized to extract, whereas what you want is bright patterns that are optimized to enlighten and educate and protect you.
So what's the alternative? Basically, bring back the Unix Philosophy, but make it better and much more user-friendly with local AI: speak English to tell your computer what to do rather than Bash.
At its core, the Unix philosophy was simple: make simple, modular tools that each do one thing and one thing well, and that are designed to talk to each other through the most universal interface (text). You as a user have extremely fine-grained choice about how to make the different programs fit together. UIs, on the other hand, combine many functionalities into one

title: The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning
content:
Home Blog
The sleep framework: A new way for LLMs to retain knowledge in continual learning
October 27, 2026
Ali Behrouz and Vahab Mirrokni, Google Research
We introduce a sleep phase in continual learning, enabling large language models to continuously integrate new facts and enhance reasoning while mitigating catastrophic forgetting or static knowledge cutoffs.
Modern LLMs achieve impressive performance via pre-training and in-context learning (ICL). However, once deployed, they remain largely static, operating with a fixed knowledge cutoff date that leaves them unable to acquire long-term capabilities or adapt to new information.
While updating models with new data seems like the obvious solution, continual parameter updates often trigger catastrophic forgetting, a fundamental issue where learning new tasks severely degrades performance on previously learned ones. Alternatively, relying strictly on ICL limits knowledge retention to the immediate context window: once the context session ends, the acquired short-term information is forgotten.
Inspired by how the human brain processes and stabilizes memory during rest, we introduce a sleep framework in continual learning: a learning paradigm that equips large language models (LLMs) with a continuous periodic lifecycle, enabling them to continually learn, consolidate fragile short-term context into stable long-term parameters. With this framework, we demonstrate that alternating between active interaction and offline memory consolidation allows LLMs to continuously acquire new facts, retain long-context knowledge up to 10M tokens, and improve complex reasoning.
Rethinking machine learning: Active (wake) vs. sleep phases
Traditional machine learning relies on a strict separation between training and inference. In a continual learning framework, this distinction becomes artificial; an intelligent agent must constantly learn, adapt, and process information.
Under the sleep paradigm, an LLM operates across two primary states:
Active (wake) phase: The model actively receives, processes, and interacts with inputs, storing temporary information in fast, short-term memory components.
Sleep phase: The model pauses processing new inputs and redirects its internal computations toward memory consolidation and self-improvement.
While terms like "sleep," "dreaming," and "self-improvement" borrow from neuroscience, our framework operates entirely within a fixed model architecture and human-defined training rules. During the offline sleep phase, the model unlocks pre-allocated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) memory blocks and updates its numerical weights using self-generated practice examples. This automated post-training cycle helps a deployed model absorb new facts and sharpen its reasoning accuracy while keeping its core codebase and design unchanged.
Key components of the sleep process
The sleep paradigm addresses catastrophic forgetting and continuous adaptation through two stages: memory consolidation and dreaming.
1. Memory consolidation
In the human brain, non-rapid eye movement (NREM) slow-wave sleep consolidates fragile memories into long-term structures via abstraction and distillation. Our proposed sleep framework mirrors this natural phenomenon through two key technical mechanisms:
Parameter expansion & continuum memory hierarchy: To prevent catastrophic forgetting, the model dynamically scales its capacity during sleep. Using a Mixture of Experts (MoE) and Hope architecture , newly unlocked, low-rank experts are integrated into stable, lower-frequency memory blocks to store incoming knowledge without disrupting older parameters.
Knowledge seeding (upward distillation): Fragile short-term memories stored in high-frequency layers (e.g., in-context memory) are transferred into the newly expanded long-term parameters. This is achieved through Generalized Knowledge Distillation (GKD) combined with reinforcement learning (RL)-based imitation learning:
On-policy distillation: The expanded student model learns token-specific feedback from teacher distributions generated on self-sampled sequences.
Learning to imitate (LTI): The student model is rewarded based on semantic and absolute similarity (Levenshtein distance) when completing prefixes of teacher-generated text.
Synaptic pruning: Once the memory consolidation into lower-frequency modules is complete, the high-frequency temporary parameters are reset, freeing up capacity for future active sessions.
Overview of our sleep framework: Input streams from the active phase are stored in short-term memory before entering the sleep cycle, which bifurcates into Consolidation (transferring fragile short-term tokens into expanded long-term parametric memory using low-rank structures and MoE) and Dreaming (autonomous self-improvement via synthetic routing with random experts and RL refinement).
2. Dreaming for self-improvement
During REM sleep, the human brain actively simulates scenarios, consolidates emotional/semantic connections, and explores novel neural pathways. Mirroring this, during the “dreaming stage”, the sleep framework implements an autonomous self-improvement loop:
Random expert selection: During synthetic data generation, the MoE router randomly activates non-standard experts. This forces the model to mix disparate domains of knowledge and uncover latent patterns.
Curated rehearsal: The model generates synthetic training samples ("dreams") and filters them using gradient-based data selection to prioritize samples with the highest potential to boost overall model capability.
RL refinement: The model performs supervised fine-tuning on top-rated dream samples and evaluates whether the generation improves performance on downstream tasks.
Theoretical foundations
Beyond the empirical results, our sleep paradigm is grounded in a theory that clarifies why its two stages (memory consolidation and dreaming) can support continual learning without simply trading new knowledge for old capabilities.
For memory consolidation, the analysis shows that knowledge seeding can be understood as a structured, low-rank compression problem. The model is not asked to copy every detail of its short-term traces into its parameters. Instead, it identifies a compact set of directions that best preserve both the model’s own on-policy behavior and the semantic qualities rewarded by the learning objective.
This perspective explains the complementary roles of the two signals: on-policy distillation aligns consolidation with the trajectories the model will actually produce at inference time, reducing the mismatch that can arise when training only on teacher-generated distributions; meanwhile, the semantic reward changes what is worth retaining, prioritizing directions that preserve meaning and task-relevant behavior rather than merely matching token probabilities. Parameter expansion then provides the capacity needed to write these selected memories without overwriting previously consolidated knowledge.
For dreaming, the theory characterizes random expert activation and reward-based sample selection as mechanisms for improving the geometry of learning. Injecting different MoEs broadens the set of gradient directions explored during synthetic generation, exposing the model to a richer collection of updates than those induced by its ordinary wake-time data alone. Gradient-based filtering then emphasizes the synthetic experiences that carry the most useful learning signal, strengthening informative directions while preserving the structure of the underlying gradient space.
Together, these steps yield a more balanced optimization landscape: learning is less dominated by a small number of directions, gradients are better conditioned, and the model can make more stable progress when refining its capabilities. In this view, dreaming is not simply self-generated data augmentation; it is a deliberate process for diversifying, selecting, and consolidating the updates through which the model improves itself.
Comparative performance of our sleep framework against baseline approaches (such as in-context learning and supervised fine-tuning) across major evaluation axes, including Class-Incremental Learning, continual translation, long-context scaling up to 10M tokens, factual knowledge incorporation, and mathematical reasoning.
For continual translation, in unseen languages, such as Manchu and Kalamang, the sleep framework maintained a near-zero performance drop in multi-stage evaluations, whereas standard baselines like ICL, Cartridges, and supervised fine-tuning (SFT) suffered severe catastrophic forgetting during sequential learning.
In long-context understanding on the BABILong benchmark, our sleep method demonstrated near-perfect scaling up to 10M tokens, outperforming strong baselines like GPT-4, and Titans by using sleep-time consolidation to compress long-context information directly into parametric memory.
For factual knowledge incorporation evaluated on SQuAD and continued pre-training (CPT), our sleep method achieved 48.9% on single-task and 46.2% on CPT evaluations, outperforming baseline methods including the base model, SFT, and Self-Adapting Language Models (SEAL) by successfully integrating new factual information without degrading existing model representations.
Finally, on mathematical reasoning benchmarks including AIME 24/25 and HMMT 25, sleep-enhanced base-model achieved accuracy scores of 79.2%, 69.0%, and 46.1%, respectively. This outperformed baselines like SFT, group relative policy optimization (GRPO), and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD), showing that pairing memory consolidation with imitation learning drives superior reasoning performance.
Conclusion
Our sleep paradigm provides a path toward autonomous, continually learning AI systems. By moving beyond static pre-training and fragile context windows, alternating between active learning and offline rest empowers LLMs to retain short-term memories, abstract new skills into long-term parameter structures, and continuously self-improve without catastrophic forgetting.
Acknowledgements
This research was conducted by Ali Behrouz (Google and Cornell University), Farnoosh Hashemi (Cornell University), Adel Javanmard (Google and University of Southern California), and Vahab Mirrokni. We thank Yuan Deng and Corinna Cortes for reviewing the work and their valuable suggestions. We also thank Mark Simborg, Kimberly Schwede, and Tim Herrmann for their help in crafting this blog post.

title: tree-mounted machines connect to web app to let users knock on wood remotely
content:

tree-mounted machines connect to web app to let users knock on wood remotely
knock on wood is an internet-connected device that performs the familiar gesture of knocking on wood, allowing users to follow the superstition remotely when no wood is nearby.
Shashwath
edited by Christina Vergopoulou
October 11, 2026
3 min
PREFER DESIGNBOOM ON GOOGLE
[FEATURED]
WEB APP TURNS SUPERSTITION INTO REMOTE-CONTROLLED DEVICE
 Knock On Wood is an internet-connected device that performs the familiar gesture of knocking on wood, allowing users to follow the superstition remotely when no wood is nearby. Through a web app, users press a digital button to trigger a physical device that knocks on wood in real time.
 The project is part of an ongoing series, Machines Responding to Superstitions, by designers Shashwath Santosh and Nithin Eluvathingal. Drawing on industrial design, engineering, manufacturing, critical thought, and world-building, the series uses machines to examine everyday beliefs and rituals.
Knocker strapped to a tree, about to knock on wood | all images ©Shashwath Santosh and Nithin Eluvathingal
  NETWORK OF MACHINES MAKES REMOTE KNOCKING ON WOOD POSSIBLE
 Each knocker connects to the internet and communicates with a central server, allowing multiple devices to respond to users around the world. Someone in a Tokyo café, for example, can trigger a knocker in New York’s Central Park using only a web browser, while the device requires a Wi-Fi connection. For the woodland setup shown in the project visuals, the designers Shashwath Santosh and Nithin Eluvathingal used a portable Wi-Fi hotspot to connect the machines.

title: How Do You Take a Picture of a Black Hole? | Quanta Magazine
content:
THE JOY OF WHY
How Do You Take a Picture of a Black Hole?
Astrophysicist Shep Doeleman explains how capturing the first image of a black hole required a telescope the size of the world, and why the next goal is to create a movie.
Add as Preferred Source
(opens in a new tab)
i
Chanelle Nibbelink for Quanta Magazine
Introduction
AUTHORS
Janna Levin
Contributing Columnist
Steven Strogatz
Podcast Host
October 29, 2026
VIEW PDF/PRINT MODE
astronomy
astrophysics
black holes
cosmology
galaxies
telescopes
The Joy of Why
All topics
Black holes are one of the universe’s most exotic and elusive objects. When nothing, not even light, can escape their powerful gravitational grasp, taking a picture of one seems unimaginable. But an image of a black hole, or more accurately its shadow, could offer insights that theory alone may not provide when testing predictions. So how can it be done?
Harvard astrophysicist Shep Doeleman
(opens a new tab)
and a team of 250 researchers achieved this extraordinary feat by linking a group of radio telescopes around the world. This network, called the Event Horizon Telescope
(opens a new tab)
, produced the first image of a supermassive black hole in the galaxy M87, around 55 million light-years away, and the first image of the black hole at the heart of our galaxy. In this episode, Doeleman tells co-host Janna Levin how he turned the Earth into a telescope capable of seeing a black hole, the incredible level of science and collaboration that was required to achieve this, how the images have furthered our understanding of these exotic objects, and how movies of black holes may be possible by the early 2030s.

Transcript
 JANNA LEVIN: Okay. I’m Janna Levin
STEVE STROGATZ: And I’m Steve Strogatz.
LEVIN: And this is The Joy of Why
STROGATZ: A podcast from Quanta Magazine where we look at some of the biggest unanswered questions in math and science today.
LEVIN: Welcome to another episode.
STROGATZ: Great to see you.
LEVIN: Great to see you. I’m pretty excited about this one. I cannot deny or hide it. We’re talking about not only an area where I’ve spent a lot of my life black holes — the greatest, strangest topic out there — but also I had a chance to talk to an old friend. So it’s a fun episode, I hope.
STROGATZ: I’m really looking forward to hearing it. I know you’ve always had a special affection for black holes. I’ve had a chance to interview you in some earlier version of this.
LEVIN: That’s right.
STROGATZ: And you blew my mind over and over about black holes.
LEVIN: Yeah, they require some defense. They’ve got a bad reputation, not entirely earned.
STROGATZ: What’s the bad reputation? Because they like to eat things?
LEVIN: Yeah. You know, black holes, kind of this monster truck language around black holes all the time. You know, they’re like… But actually, black holes are remarkably elegant, clean, simple systems. They leave you alone if you leave them alone. They’re actually quite small for their heft. That’s kind of their whole gestalt, that they’re actually tiny for their heft.
And, uh, you know, though they’re the darkest phenomenon in the universe, they figure out a way to become the brightest beacons that we see on the edge of what’s observable.
STROGATZ: Wow.
LEVIN: So, they’re, they’re pretty awesome. I also think that they’re fundamental to physics, unlike any other macroscopic object you can think of.
STROGATZ: Hmmm. When I think of black holes, I tend to focus on what they do to spacetime. You know, that they cause singularities. It’s their geometry that always grabs me. But that’s not really necessarily the only way to think about black holes. They’re really objects. Real players.
LEVIN: Yeah. I think after people got over the thrill that they actually existed out there and that they could indirectly be detected, there was a sense that they’re not major players in the universe. “Eh, so there’s some black holes out there.”
Quite to the contrary, I think we’ve come to understand that they sculpt our history and our past, that they have a very regulating and important role in determining the shape and size of galaxies and where there might be habitable regions even. And ultimately, we’re kinda doomed to fall into black holes eventually. So, they’re kind of our past and our future.
But, it might surprise people that we had never actually taken a picture of a black hole. All of our evidence had been indirect until about 10 years ago, and that group worked for well over a decade, for some people up to two decades, to try to capture the first picture of a black hole.
STROGATZ: Huh. Wild.
LEVIN: It was a tremendous accomplishment, led by Shep Doeleman, who is our guest. So let me tell you about Shep. Shep is a senior research fellow at Harvard University, the assistant director of Harvard’s Black Hole Initiative, also an astrophysicist at the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory.
And he was the founding director of the Event Horizon Telescope Consortium, which is a network of observatories around the world which gave us the first and only images humanity has ever captured of black holes.
STROGATZ: Hmm. This sounds like it’s gonna be a great discussion of science at its best.
LEVIN: Yeah, it’s an epic story. Let’s hear from Shep himself.
[Music plays]
LEVIN: Shep, welcome to The Joy of Why.
Shep Doeleman
SHEP DOELEMAN: It’s good to be here, Janna.
LEVIN: It’s a pleasure to have you on the show. I’m really curious if you remember not just your way into black holes, but your way into the entire idea of thinking about the universe?
DOELEMAN: Wow. Well, everybody falls in love with astronomy at some point. I don’t care who you are, you fall in love with astronomy. And whether it’s staring up at the night sky, you know, at summer camp or seeing a meteorite, for me, it was seeing a total solar eclipse. I was 13, 1980. And my parents took me out to the middle of the desert in Oregon and at first we thought we weren’t gonna see totality, the clouds were moving in, and then the clouds just parted and we saw this amazing eclipse. It was just tremendous.
LEVIN: Did you think at that moment, “Well, this is what I’m gonna do for the rest of my life”? Or is it that the memory comes back and we reconstruct the story, you know?
DOELEMAN: That’s a great question. I think it mostly, it just comes back. Life isn’t linear like that. But I will say the idea that there would be these huge objects that were moving and they could align perfectly and allow you to see what would normally be hidden, like the corona of the sun, was startling to me. I mean, it didn’t have to be that way. Like, the angular diameter of the moon doesn’t have to be the same as the sun so they totally block each other out. But these coincidences sometimes give you a special view into nature.
LEVIN: Yeah. I, I love that there’s just this idea that we’re inspired by the firmament, science’s oldest instrument, and that we all have it in common.
Um, so I really feel we have to make a confession ’cause we’ve known each other a really long time. I feel like we met maybe the first week of graduate school at MIT. I think over a cookie table.
DOELEMAN: I think so.
LEVIN: So I remember just you were always trying these crazy ideas in graduate school. You were like a creative curiosity in search of a problem. Tell me a little bit first about how you landed on this idea of pursuing a portrait of a black hole?
The idea that there would be these huge objects that were moving and they could align perfectly and allow you to see what would normally be hidden, like the corona of the sun, was startling to me.
DOELEMAN: Portrait of a black hole, I love that. So I graduated high school pretty early. I was 15 years old. And went to college, and then after that I was pretty burned out, and I saw an advertisement that said, “Go to Antarctica and run all these experiments down there.” And I said, “That’s for me.” I interviewed for the position, and somehow they gave it to this 19-year-old kid. They needed some warm body down there to look after the cosmic ray experiments, the aerophotometry experiments, the electromagnetic experiments, and I got a real taste for doing experimental research in difficult circumstances. I just loved it. And then came back to MIT, where I met you in 1988.
LEVIN: Oh, you didn’t have to say the year, man. That was unnecessary [laughs].
DOELEMAN: I know, when the Earth was cooling. But, I cast around a bit. I started in the X-ray group there, and then I did a little bit of neuroscience looking at biophysics. And then I was introduced to this idea of turning the Earth into a telescope, and this experiment that we use to image black holes and that immediately drew me in.
LEVIN: Yeah. So we’re gonna talk about this project, but when you were in graduate school, what was the status of black holes scientifically? Were they detected? Did everyone believe that they were real astrophysical phenomena?
DOELEMAN: There was really a sense that black holes existed or strong evidence for them. And of course, there are two flavors of black holes. There are stellar-mass black holes which form during star death. So when a star goes supernova, it will explode the outer shells off, and then the interior part will collapse and if the star is massive enough, it will turn into a black hole, and that black hole could be tens of solar masses.
But then there are these behemoths, these supermassive black holes that live in the centers of galaxies. And while there can be many stellar-mass black holes in a galaxy, there’s probably just one, maybe two, supermassive black holes at the core of any given galaxy.
And for the stellar-mass black holes, people had seen these X-ray binaries, and they were seeing very fast fluctuations in X-rays and even in the radio from these stellar-sized sources. And everything fit with this idea that there was a black hole eating another star that goes an X-ray binary.
LEVIN: And that was Cygnus X-1, a first X-ray object in the direction of the constellation Cygnus, right?
DOELEMAN: Exactly, it was those kinds of sources. And then the radio people predominantly had seen some very high-resolution images that were very troubling. So you would see in the optical, a galaxy would look like a normal run-of-the-mill galaxy with a lot of optical light coming from stars.
But then if you looked at it in the radio, you would see these oppositely directed jets of material all tracing to the center of the galaxy. What is causing that?
And the best idea that people had for that was a spinning supermassive black hole that was energizing jets that moved at near light speed from the north and south pole of that black hole, and it was piercing the entire galaxy.
So from two completely different lines of inquiry you had one flavor of black holes being suspected from the X-ray, and you had another suspected predominantly by the radio.
LEVIN: So even though people started to theorize that these must be black holes, nobody had taken a picture of a black hole, not in the ’70s, ’80s, ’90s, the noughts. I think that was a surprise to people because we talked about them as being such compelling inhabitants of the universe, death states of stars, but we had actually technically never seen one directly. Never taken a portrait. And that’s really what you set out to do in many ways.
I saw an advertisement that said, “Go to Antarctica and run all these experiments down there.” And I said, “That’s for me.”
DOELEMAN: Yeah. I think the simplest way of saying it is that seeing is believing in a certain way. I mean, you can theorize something, but actually seeing it confers a reality on things that you don’t get otherwise. And there were some really important signatures, too. It wasn’t just seeing it. It was measuring it. Taking the measure of the thing not only gives you confidence in its reality, but you can test predictions.
So in 1915, when Einstein came with his theory of general relativity, which governs the space time around a black hole, and then the year after that Schwarzschild solved it in the trenches of World War I, a story that we know well, even after that, it was pretty clear that if you went to the conclusion of that solution, you would wind up seeing a ring of light around the black hole.
That if a bunch of gas was drawn to the black hole, it heated up to hundreds of billions of degrees because you’re confining it to a small volume, and it emits light. That light would be curved by the gravitational force of the black hole. And from any direction that you look at the black hole, you would see a ring of light. Basically, the emission from behind the black hole lensed around into a ring. And the size of that ring you can derive from Einstein’s equations.
And so we theorized that if we could make a photo, if we could see this ring, we’d be able to measure the mass of the black hole. But also just the ring itself would be like the best evidence for the existence of supermassive black holes at that scale. So it wasn’t just a coffee table book we were after. We were after the real measurement of the fundamental nature of the universe.
LEVIN: Now, when people hear this idea that you’re gonna try to turn the Earth into a telescope or a telescope the size of the world, it sounds like such a crazy lark. What made you think it was viable? It was no mean feat.
DOELEMAN: Yeah. Well, so, so this idea of turning the Earth into a telescope had been around for a long time, since the ‘60s. And the key is that the angular resolution of a telescope or the ability to magnify things on the sky, it scales as the wavelength of light you’re observing, lambda, divided by the size of your telescope.
So if you wanna see things that are really small in the sky, you either reduce your wavelength of light or you expand the size of your telescope. So you’ll often see these huge blocks of glass on top of mountaintops. These huge optical dishes, and they’re big for a reason. They collect a lot of light, but also the bigger they are, the smaller the objects they can see.
LEVIN: The better the resolution.
DOELEMAN: The better the resolution, precisely. And so there are some objects that are so small, and black holes are the smallest objects predicted by Einstein’s theory of gravity, that you need extremely big telescopes, extremely fine angular resolution to see them, and you’ve gotta take this idea of turning the Earth into a telescope to the utmost extremes.
You have to operate it at wavelengths that had never been operated before ’cause you have to really go to smaller and smaller wavelengths to get the angular resolution you need. And that’s what took us 20 years, to push the technique to the absolute limit.

Marelleo, a story box I built for my kids | Zebra Rodeo
content:
BUILD NOTES
Marelleo
A box that plays a story when a child puts a figurine on top. I built it for my three kids knowing nothing about electronics, and learned the whole thing by breaking things.
October 15, 2026
It started as an irritation on holiday
Last summer, on holiday with friends and a small tribe of children, I came across the Toniebox. And honestly, I thought it was great. The child puts a figurine on the box, the story starts. They take it off, it stops. No screen, no menu, no parent to go and fetch. A two year old gets it in one second, which is roughly the highest level of usability anyone can reach.
The gesture is perfect. The business model, much less so. All these boxes work the same way: the object sells for a more or less reasonable price, and the money is made afterwards, on the content. Whether it’s the Lunii and its closed catalogue, the Yoto and its card packs, or the Toniebox and its figurines, every new story is a purchase, from a catalogue I don’t choose, on an object I don’t control. You’re not buying a player, you’re buying a subscription dressed up as a wooden toy. And that genuinely annoys me.
Meanwhile, I had been telling myself for years that I wanted to do electronics. Not as a dabbler: actually understand it. Except I knew nothing about it. I own a soldering iron that comes out every three years to reattach a headphone wire, never to build anything. The kind of guy who knows what a resistor is without ever having had to choose one.
The two urges met in the car on the way home. That would be my project. An RFID reader, a tag, a box that plays an audio track depending on what you put on it. Not to make a product. Just for my kids, and to learn.
TWO DISCOVERIES
V0
The breadboard, or the right to get it wrong
I already knew what I didn’t want. A Raspberry Pi is a full computer just to play an MP3: too big, too hungry, and it takes twenty seconds to boot. A child putting a figurine down does not wait twenty seconds, they wander off and play. At the other end, the genuinely low level chips, the ones you program in C with a 400 page datasheet, are far too steep for a beginner who would like to hear a story that same evening.
While reading around, I came across the two things that made the project possible. First the ESP32 development board: a microcontroller with WiFi built in, beefy enough to decode MP3, simple enough to program like an Arduino, and sold for a handful of euros. Then the breadboard, that perforated plate where you push components in without soldering anything.
It sounds like a detail. It is the whole project tipping over. On a breadboard, getting it wrong costs nothing: you unplug, you start again, nothing is damaged. When you’re learning, that is exactly the property you need.
So I read documentation, I talked it through with Claude, I drew wiring diagrams in a notebook. And very quickly, far too quickly to feel earned, I had a circuit that played an audio track when you put a tag on it. It was ugly, a plate of copper spaghetti, the speaker lying bare on the table. But it worked. A few hours, and I had a thing that told stories. I don’t think I had been that pleased with something made by my own hands since childhood.
The first circuit. An ESP32 on the breadboard, the NFC reader at the end of a few wires, a red LED saying it's alive. Not a single solder joint.
WHAT CAUGHT FIRE
The potentiometer, the smoke, and the smell of ski wax
What came next is less glorious. To set the volume I added a potentiometer, that little rotary knob which is nothing more than a variable resistor. Except that wired wrong, it no longer sets anything at all: it becomes a plain wire between plus and minus. That has a name, it’s called a short circuit, and it heats up terrifyingly fast.
It smoked. And it gave off a very particular smell, which took me a good while to place before it hit me all at once: ski wax. Burning wax. I recognise it instantly now, and it is never good news.
The battery was the other piece of work, and the one that made me think. You don’t connect a lithium cell to two wires and move on. You need a charge controller, a dedicated chip that decides when and how to fill it, that stops at the right moment and cuts out before anything stupid happens. You also need to fasten it down properly, because a lithium battery rattling around inside an enclosure and getting pinched is precisely the scenario in those videos nobody wants to watch.
3000 mAh, 3.7 V. Flat, light, and not remotely harmless.
The charging board, and its white connector which was not the same as mine.
And then a stupid detail: my battery’s connector did not match the one on the charging board. Two little white plugs that look alike, two different pitches, incompatible. So I did what you do at eleven at night on a Tuesday when you’re nearly there: I cut the connector off and soldered the battery straight on.
Immediate consequence, which I had not seen coming: no connector any more, therefore no way to unplug anything, and no switch anywhere in the circuit. The box was permanently on. Twenty four hours a day. A lithium cell hastily soldered into an object that never turns off, sitting in a child’s bedroom. Written down like that, it needs no comment.
That is the moment I stopped treating this lightly. Not out of fear, but because I understood that I was no longer tinkering with a gadget on the corner of a table: I was placing an electrical object into my children’s daily life. Everything else in the project follows from that realisation.
WORKSHOP NOTE
V1
From breadboard to perfboard
The first consequence was leaving the breadboard, and it wasn’t only about safety.
A breadboard holds by friction. Every wire is held by a tiny spring, which is wonderful for trying things and disastrous for lasting. Move the circuit and a contact is lost, and the fault that follows is far worse than a clean failure: it is intermittent. You hunt a bug in your code for an hour and a half, you reread the same function twenty times, and it’s a wire that no longer touches.
The same circuit as on the breadboard, but soldered. It survives being moved across the table, which is already a lot.
The next step is perfboard: the same grid of holes, but on a printed circuit, with every component soldered in. You lose the right to be wrong, you gain a circuit that holds together. That’s where I really learned to solder, and above all where I understood that my repair soldering had nothing to do with manufacturing soldering. Repairing is remaking a joint that existed. Building is making a hundred in a row, all clean, all identical, knowing that the hundred and first is the one that will fail.
THE ENCLOSURE
My kids unscrewed the knob until the wires tore off
For the enclosure I got very lucky: François Lagunas lent me his 3D printer and helped me through the first attempts. Without him I would still be cutting cardboard with a ruler. I drew my models in Fusion 360 on the free hobbyist licence, and printed.
The enclosure in Fusion 360. The circle on top marks where the figurine goes, the hole beside it takes the button, and the slot on the side lets the USB-C through.
The first version was too big and too fragile. And quality control arrived faster than expected, in the shape of three children aged 21 months, 5 and 7.
They broke the knob by turning it like animals. The volume knob ended up spinning with no end stop, round and round, and as it turned it wound the wires around themselves until it tore every one of them off. I opened the box onto a little nest of twisted copper. That’s where I learned the most important rule of the entire project: a five year old does not turn a knob, they unscrew it. And they don’t stop when it resists. They stop when it gives.
The potentiometer and its five tabs: three for the volume, two for the switch that turns the box off at the end of travel. Those are the wires that wound themselves up.
So I started over. I took every measurement again with callipers, component by component, so that each hole would land exactly where it should and each part would be held by plastic rather than by its wires. I thickened the walls, added pockets, lowered the height. Version after version, the object stopped looking like a prototype and started looking like an object.
Still in the spirit of nothing being allowed to give, I also abandoned self tapping screws. Screwing straight into printed plastic holds once, twice, and on the third go the material splits along the layers: the hole holds nothing any more and the part is fit for reprinting. The real answer is called a brass insert. You set it on the hole, come down on it with the tip of the soldering iron, the brass heats up, melts the plastic around itself and sinks in. As it cools you have a metal thread captured in the part, which you can screw and unscrew a hundred times.
The brass inserts sunk in with the soldering iron. Four minutes of work, and screws you can undo as often as you like.
And then came the only test that no technical argument passes on my behalf: my wife liked the box. Not politely: she put it on the living room shelf, among the objects you don’t tidy away when someone rings the doorbell. That also settles the cube shape, which I wasn’t sure about. An object for children that you don’t need to hide is an object that ends up being used.
In the opening photo, all of that is still visible: a circle engraved on the top, which says where to put the figurine because the antenna sits right underneath, the volume knob beside it, the play button, and the name raised in the front wall. The figurines are painted wooden people with an NFC sticker glued under their feet. Any object would do: a toy car, a token, a flat pebble. The child decides what tells what, and that is exactly what I wanted.
THE BOARD
V2
I wanted nothing left dangling
At that point I had a version that worked pretty well. But a wired circuit, however well soldered, is still a wired circuit. There is always a cable pulling on a joint, a module hanging off its legs, a connector that works loose when you shake it. And I had just spent a few weeks measuring, very empirically, how much my children shake things.
So I changed category and set about designing a printed circuit board. Everything that was scattered, brought together on a single board: the power supply, the charger, the amplifier, the SD card reader, the connectors. Every part in its place, nothing moving, nothing sticking out.
I used Claude to go from my wired circuit to a clean schematic, and that is where the division of labour became interesting. It reads a datasheet very well, spots that a pin needs a pull-up, works out a value, fetches a footprint from the library rather than copying it from memory. But it cannot route. Routing, that is to say physically drawing the path of every copper track between components without ever crossing another, is something I did by hand, in KiCad. 491 tracks. Entire evenings spent moving lines by a tenth of a millimetre to squeeze a connection between two pads eight tenths apart.
The routing file. Every red line is a copper track placed by hand. At the top, the hatched area under the WiFi module's antenna: no copper is allowed through there, or the range collapses.
That file has to be gone over with a magnifying glass before you send it, for a very concrete reason: you don’t order a single board. The minimum is five, manufactured and assembled in one go. One mistake in there isn’t a touch-up job, it is five boards for the bin and the whole invoice.
So I had it reread the entire schematic, line by line. It found three things I would never have seen, and each one would have cost the order.
WORKSHOP NOTE
The three mistakes caught before the order
The resistor that would have killed everything. To produce the 3.3 V the processor needs, I use a step-down converter, and I had put two resistors around it forming a divider. That is the normal way to set the output voltage. Except the chip I had picked comes in two families: an adjustable one, and a fixed output one. I had taken the fixed one. With my divider, the regulation would have read a voltage far lower than reality, concluded the output was too weak, and pushed. The arithmetic gives 13.7 V on a rail meant for 3.3. The WiFi module, the SD card, the NFC reader: all dead within a second of power-up.
The diode the wrong way round. In KiCad, pad number 1 of a diode is the cathode, and my file placed it the other way round. A reversed diode at that spot means the 5 V doesn’t come out, so the 3.3 V doesn’t exist, so the board doesn’t start at all. Five mute boards in one go, with no way of noticing without having them made.
And the checker that checked nothing. KiCad automatically verifies that tracks respect minimum clearances. Mine was configured with a minimum clearance of zero. It ran, it reported zero errors, and it approved absolutely anything, silently. That is the worst kind of bug: the tool that reassures you.
Once, the roles reversed and it gave me a silly amount of pleasure: I was the one who spotted that two components in my bill of materials were out of stock, before it did. We turned that into a small program that queries the manufacturer’s catalogue and returns the stock and price of each part number, so that it never happens blind again. A part number is not a given: you recheck it on the day of the order, not the day before.
DELIVERY
160 euros of boards, and nothing happens
I ordered from JLCPCB, who manufacture the board and populate it. For 160 euros I got five, already assembled, enough to keep one and give the rest to cousins and friends. Opening that parcel was one of the very good moments of the project. Green boards, crisp, components perfectly aligned, my name written on them, out of a file I had drawn on my sofa.
The board as received from JLCPCB, components placed. My name in silkscreen, and 491 hand-drawn tracks underneath.
First contact with the manufactured object: I can’t plug the USB in. The factory had added a small strip of material under the socket, a breakaway tab used to hold the board during assembly, which you’re meant to snap off on arrival. I had to work up the nerve to break it by hand on a thirty euro board. That took me a good ten minutes of contemplation.
Then I plug it in and test. And nothing happens. The NFC reader’s LED blinks, but no figurine is recognised, nothing plays, nothing appears on the network. Nothing.
I spent a quarter of an hour telling myself I was an old fool who had just burned 160 euros on useless boards, and that it served me right. A genuinely bad moment. Then I went looking, methodically, unplugging the harnesses one by one.
The culprit came down to two wires. I had swapped the two middle conductors on the NFC reader’s ribbon, the ones carrying the serial link. That link always crosses over: what one transmits, the other has to listen to. Wired straight, both ends talk at the same time and nobody listens.

title: Breaking the Open Web Won’t Stop the Bad Bots | TechPolicy.Press
content:
PERSPECTIVE
Breaking the Open Web Won’t Stop the Bad Bots
LILA BAILEY, TESS VARTANIAN / OCT 27, 2026
A close up of a spider in its web. Valeriia Neganova/Unsplash
Republish
Share
Late last month, more than 300 representatives from major media outlets were on Capitol Hill to advocate for the Stealth Bot Prohibition Act. They came with a legitimate grievance. Newsrooms are being hit by a surge of automated traffic, mostly from AI developers. AI developers extract enormous volumes of online content and then potentially deprive website owners of referral traffic and ad revenue with generative AI features and chatbots trained on that content. It is a real problem that deserves a real solution. But this bill doesn’t directly target the harms caused by abusive crawling. Instead, it would force anyone accessing a website automatically to identify themselves and their purposes for collecting public information. Rather than protect journalists, the bill threatens a basic tool they, and many others, rely on to gather information online.
Cutting-edge investigative journalism relies on automated data collection. In 2022, a Pulitzer-winning Wall Street Journal investigation analyzed over 31,000 financial disclosures from 12,000 senior government employees, revealing that nearly a quarter of federal officials traded stock in industries their agencies regulated. To conduct an investigation at that scale, the Journal relied on web scraping: an automated process where a software bot, known as a crawler, browses the internet and collects information. This fundamental tool of the open web is now under threat from bills that purport to target “stealth crawling,” but in reality would hamper legitimate public-interest activities, including preservation, journalism, research, and security.
Again, aggressive, large-scale scraping is a real problem — particularly as demand for AI training and content has exploded. It can overwhelm websites, increase costs, and threaten institutions that produce and preserve knowledge, including commercial publishers, Wikipedia, libraries, and the Internet Archive, where one of the authors of this piece works.
In an apparent attempt to reduce or eliminate problematic scraping practices, proposed bills, like the federal Stealth Bot Prohibition Act and New York’s Stealth Crawler Prohibition Act, would impose sweeping prohibitions on anonymous scraping without addressing the real harms.
Both bills define a “bot” or “crawler” as software that “retrieves, scans, indexes, scrapes, or otherwise accesses a website or other internet source.” A bot is “stealth” if it fails to disclose its identity and the “specific nature and purpose of the bot.” Under the federal bill, the FTC can pursue penalties of up to $53,000 if a person uses a stealth bot in a way that is “reasonably likely to damage, impair, or burden” a website’s “technical or commercial operation.” The bill provides no definition or standard of what is reasonably likely to impair a website. Under the New York bill, which only applies to covered news sites, a publisher can obtain a subpoena to unmask a crawler’s identity without requiring a showing of any harm.
Knowing the identity behind a crawler tells us relatively little about whether its behavior is harmful. Under the New York bill, a company that discloses its identity and then accesses the website 10,000 times a minute complies with the law even though it is still imposing enormous and likely unjustified costs on the site. But a journalist anonymously using a crawler to investigate potentially anti-competitive practices by tech companies does not. Many of the most socially valuable uses of crawling require anonymity. Revealing a crawler’s identity and purposes can change the very nature of the information that is collected; if the subject of the study knows it is being observed and by whom, its behavior will change. That is the point of studying it anonymously.
Moreover, not all automated data collection is abusive, and not all of it is used to train AI, but these proposed bills risk deterring archivists, researchers, and civic technologists from using automated data collection tools out of fear of liability. Journalists use scraping to analyze public records, as in the WSJ story. Researchers use it to study online discrimination and misinformation.
The Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine has used crawlers to archive more than one trillion webpages, creating a historical record of the internet that would otherwise constantly change or disappear. That archival record has helped provide the factual background for thousands of news stories, evidence in hundreds of court cases across the country, and often simply a backup for when things go wrong.
It is not just archivists who rely on scraping to advance the public good. Disability advocates have used scraping to automatically evaluate over one million websites to detect accessibility problems. Public health researchers use scraping to track the opioid epidemic as well as misinformation surrounding addiction and treatment. The federal government relies on crawlers to scan for threat detection, offering free cybersecurity services to organizations across the country. And for some of these users, anonymity is essential to the integrity and safety of their work. For example, environmental researchers gathering information from public corporate disclosures or satellite image portals may fear retaliation from the companies they are investigating.
Our content delivered to your inbox.
Join our newsletter on issues and ideas at the intersection of tech & democracy
SUBSCRIBE
The First Amendment has historically protected us from government-imposed identification requirements tied to receiving information. In Lamont v. Postmaster General, the Supreme Court struck down a law requiring recipients to affirmatively identify themselves before receiving certain political publications. The same principle applies to web crawling: requiring people to identify themselves as a condition of accessing publicly available information burdens the freedom to receive information.
That concern is heightened when laws use vague language. If researchers cannot easily understand what it means to “deploy” a crawler in a prohibited way, or what activity is “reasonably likely to burden or impair a website,” they may refrain from scraping rather than risk violating the law.
As we wrote in our letter to New York Governor Kathy Hochul, “deanonymization threatens the core of the open web without actually addressing these technological and potential economic harms of AI-related crawling.” Unmasking a crawler does not reduce the number of requests it sends to a server. It does not compensate a publisher whose content is used to build an AI product. And it does not restore referral traffic that publishers may lose when users turn to an AI chatbot for information.
Indeed, existing laws can be used to address many harmful uses of scraped data. For example, privacy laws can restrict how sensitive data is processed. Copyright law can respond to infringing AI-generated outputs. Consumer protection law can address deceptive data collection or use.
To tackle the specific issues raised by aggressive AI scraping, policymakers could support the development of standardized, interoperable technical solutions to help websites better manage automated traffic. Standards bodies such as the Internet Engineering Task Force are exploring new protocols for managing machine access to online content and developing mechanisms for anonymous attestation of good crawler behavior. Policymakers should allow that work to develop rather than prematurely imposing legal and technical measures that harm “good” bots and that “bad” bots will quickly learn to evade.
And if policymakers conclude that new legislation is necessary, liability should turn on conduct that causes identifiable harms like overwhelming servers with excessive requests, engaging in fraud, or collecting data for prohibited uses.
The spread of AI crawling has created legitimate challenges for publishers and website operators requiring thoughtful policy responses. But policymakers should resist treating anonymity as something wrong in and of itself. The open web depends on the ability to access, analyze, and preserve publicly available information without revealing our identity and seeking permission from every website owner first.
Policymakers who want to curb abusive crawling while preserving a healthy information ecosystem have better options, and we are eager to help them. We invite legislators at the state and federal levels to reach out to us about how alternative proposals could target harmful conduct while protecting the tools that journalists, researchers, archivists, and citizens have long used to navigate the digital world.

title: 6,000-year-old Stone Age arrows emerge from melting ice in Norway
content:
The oldest ice is disappearing: The Stone Age is emerging from the melting ice
'We have been at the edge of the ice. We have seen it happening. And we are witnesses to a rapidly changing archaeological landscape,' write the glacial archaeologists. Finds from the Viking Age are becoming scarce, while 6,000-year-old arrowheads are now emerging from the melting ice.
A 5,000-year-old arrowhead made of slate, found together with parts of its shaft right at the edge of the ice. Domesticated reindeer can be seen on the ice patch in the background. (Photo: Åsa Rommetveit Celius / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice)
Ida Irene Bergstrøm
JOURNALIST
PUBLISHED 26 September 2026 - 00:01
For exactly 20 years, archaeologists working with Secrets of the Ice have been recovering and preserving artefacts emerging from the ice in the mountains of Innlandet, eastern Norway.
Until now, most of the objects have been up to 2,000 years old. Many date from the Viking Age.
But the ancient ice is now beginning to melt.
And within this oldest ice lie the oldest finds: large quantities of arrow shafts and arrowheads from the Bronze Age and the Stone Age.
A bone arrowhead found together with parts of its shaft right beside the ice. Approximately 5,000 years old. (Photo: Frys Film / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice)
An arrowhead made from a freshwater mussel shell, dating from the Bronze Age, approximately 3,600 years old. The arrowhead is fragile and has begun to split apart. (Photo: Frys film / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice)
Here comes the Stone Age
ANNONSE
One of the oldest finds from this year's first field expedition is an arrow with an arrowhead and shaft made of slate.
By comparing it with previously discovered arrows, archaeologists estimate that it is between 5,000 and 6,000 years old.
The fact that arrows are emerging from the melting ice is not surprising. Over the 20 years they have been working here, the archaeologists have found extensive evidence of reindeer and reindeer hunting. They have also found clothing, shoes, dead packhorses, and a pair of skis.
The preservation conditions in the ice have meant that organic material, such as wood, leather, and textiles, have also survived.
“This year, we found 48 prehistoric arrows. That's a lot,” Espen Finstad, who leads Secrets of the Ice, tells Science Norway.
He explains that, with these latest discoveries, more than 100 arrowheads and arrow shafts have now been recovered from a single ice patch over the years.
The oldest arrowheads are made from slate, freshwater mussel shells, and bone. More recent arrowheads are made from iron and are 'only' between 1,000 and 1,500 years old.
Archaeologist Åsa Rommetveit Celius from Innlandet County Municipality documents the discovery of a 1,000-year-old arrow shaft. (Photo: May-Tove Smiseth / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice)
Archaeologist Kjetil Loftsgarden from the Museum of Cultural History in Oslo holds a complete 1,800-year-old arrow with a bone arrowhead and a wooden shaft. (Photo: Espen Finstad / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice)
A brutal backdrop
But this year’s fieldwork carries an added sense of gravity.
Finstad explains that the work of recovering archaeological artefacts from the ice has always carried a certain duality.
“It’s fun going around looking for things. It’s exciting, and finding something is just really cool," he says.
Yet behind the excitement lies the reality of climate change. Finstad points to the recent landslide in Nepal and the glacier collapse in Jotunheimen.
“We have always acknowledged this contradiction and the reality behind our work. But this is the first time it has truly affected us on an emotional level,” Finstad says, adding:
“This year, there was a much deeper sense of seriousness and sadness. Only patches of ice remain where we once had large ice patches. It's brutal. And this year, that reality struck us more forcefully than ever before."
ANNONSE
Participants in the field from the Glacier Archaeology Programme in Innlandet, Secrets of the Ice. (Photo: Frys Film / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice)
The glacial archaeologists’ tent camp in Jotunheimen at sunrise. Fresh snow on the ground. (Photo: Espen Finstad / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice)
Finstad and his colleagues estimate that most of the ice patches containing archaeological artefacts will have disappeared within the next 20 years.
“There has been ice here for 6,000–7,000 years. Nature has been warning us and sending signals for many years. But now it's giving up. Now it is simply going to melt,” says the glacial archaeologist.
'For thousands of years, ancient ice has safely preserved unique objects from the past. Now that ice is disappearing,' the archaeologists write in a press release about the finds. 'We have been at the edge of the ice. We have seen it happening. And we are witnesses to a rapidly changing archaeological landscape.'
The lower section of one of the ice patches at Hanklefonne. It was once large. Now only a small, steep section remains. 'The ice is disappearing much faster than we expected. The landscape has changed dramatically, and large areas that were recently covered by ice are now ice-free,' the glacial archaeologists write in a press release. (Photo: Espen Finstad / Innlandet County Municipality / Secrets of the Ice)
More fieldwork ahead
Finstad and his colleagues are planning more fieldwork in the coming weeks, weather permitting.
So far, they have secured finds in the Kvittingskjølen mountain area of Jotunheimen, specifically at Langfonne, Storefonne, and Hanklefonne.
Several of the finds are already on display at the Norwegian Mountain Centre in Lom, just a few days after they were discovered.
———
